Approval documents will explicitly note no permanent concrete structures will be installed, and no plant removal will happen outside pre-marked trail routes. | Project lead | Obtain stamped written approval from all relevant departments, sign a 2-year site cooperation agreement that explicitly prohibits permanent damage to vegetation or disruption of known wildlife den sites, and share a copy of the agreement with all volunteer leads to keep posted at on-site work days. | Full color project proposal with example photos of similar low-impact art trails, independent ecological impact pre-assessment report drafted by the university ecology team, liability insurance coverage for all public on-site events. |
| P1-4 | Lock in project funding and material supply, with a mix of sources to avoid relying too heavily on a single funder that might shift priorities mid-project. The target breakdown is 60% of the budget from local municipal cultural promotion grants, 30% from community crowdfunding (with backer rewards including custom fox-and-moon postcards printed on recycled cardstock, priority sign-ups for volunteer work days and early moon walk slots), and 10% from in-kind donations of native plant saplings and low-impact art materials from local small businesses. | Fundraising team (two part-time staff with prior experience running local community crowdfunding campaigns) | Hit 100% of the ¥180,000 budget target before construction starts, sign formal supply contracts with 2 local native plant nurseries that source stock from within 50km of the site to avoid transporting invasive pests, and 1 local eco-friendly art material supplier, with all materials required for Phase 2 delivered to the on-site storage shed 3 days before construction is scheduled to start. | Live crowdfunding page with regular photo updates of pre-project survey work, edited grant application documents tailored to each funder’s priorities, material safety certification confirming all supplies are non-toxic and safe for wildlife (no lead-based paints, no treated wood that leaches chemicals into soil). |
---
 Phase 1: Habitat Restoration & "Fox’s Moon Path" Basic Construction (Weeks 5–12)
*Core goal: Cut down on unnecessary human disturbance to existing fox habitats first, before building any public access elements. The low-light public viewing trail will be routed entirely to avoid cutting into core fox activity areas, rather than placing visitor convenience over wildlife safety.*
| Task ID | Specific Action Item | Assigned Party | Success Metric | Required Resources |
|---------|----------------------|----------------|----------------|--------------------|
| C1-1 | Mitigate light pollution across the 5 identified hotspots. Teams will coordinate with urban management staff to replace 27 overly bright cool-white streetlights along the forest edge with motion-sensor, warm amber lights (≤3000K color temperature, fully shielded so light only falls on pedestrian paths, with zero spill into the forest interior). Crews will also install opaque light barriers around 3 24-hour commercial light boxes on the adjacent commercial strip that currently glow directly into the forest edge. | Ecology team + urban management bureau public lighting crew | Post-construction light meter testing, conducted at 15 random points across fox core activity zones, shows <0.1 lux of artificial light reaching those areas after 10PM, meeting IUCN nocturnal wildlife protection standards for sensitive mammal species. | Calibrated handheld light meter, shielded warm LED bulbs, light barrier materials made from reclaimed scrap wood from local construction sites and opaque matte recycled plastic panels. |
| C1-2 | Restore fox foraging and movement corridors, which are currently broken up by patches of invasive ivy that choke out native berry-producing shrubs. Teams will plant 1,200 native shrubs (hawthorn, wild rose, and native berry bushes selected because their fruit makes up 60% of local red foxes’ winter diet) and 30 native oak saplings along the mapped fox movement paths, to create continuous low cover that lets foxes move between foraging spots without being exposed to busy sidewalks. Teams will also set up 8 elevated, quiet fox feeding stations, which will only be stocked with vet-approved natural food during the harshest mid-winter weeks when snow cover makes foraging impossible, to avoid making foxes dependent on human-provided food. | Ecology team + trained volunteer planting crews (scheduled for weekend work days to avoid weekday traffic near the site) | 90% of planted saplings survive the 4-week post-planting check (with replacement saplings on hand to fill in any gaps from drought or accidental trampling), and infrared camera monitoring shows foxes using the restored corridor at least 3 times per week within 8 weeks of planting. | Locally sourced native saplings, hand planting tools (no heavy machinery to avoid compacting soil), vet-reviewed feeding guidelines that prohibit leaving processed human food out for wildlife, infrared cameras mounted at corridor entry points for post-construction monitoring. |
| C1-3 | Build the 1.2km "Moon Path" public viewing trail. The route will follow existing informal dirt paths worn by past hikers to avoid clearing new vegetation, and will be laid with permeable, soft wood chips (no concrete, which blocks soil water flow and cuts off movement paths for small salamanders and ground insects) along a route that stays a minimum of 50 meters from documented fox core dens. Teams will install 12 hand-painted wooden signposts telling the serialized story of the little fox following the moon: stopping to snack on hawthorn berries, pausing to watch fireflies in the undergrowth, and finally reaching the moon viewing platform. Three points along the trail will have 1-meter high hidden observation blinds, where visitors can stop to watch for foxes without being seen or disrupting animal movement. | Art team + construction volunteer crew (with a local accessibility consultant on call to review trail design) | Trail passes a third-party accessibility check, with a gentle wheelchair-accessible slope at the main entry, no raised tripping hazards across the full route, and wide enough turnaround spots for mobility aids at each observation blind. All signs use non-toxic, weatherproof paint, and observation blinds are fully camouflaged with clipped local pine boughs and leaf litter 1 week after installation, so they blend into the forest edge rather than standing out as manmade structures. | Locally sourced recycled wood chips from municipal tree trimming waste, non-toxic weatherproof paint in muted earth tones, camouflage netting lined with local vegetation, printed trail accessibility audit checklist. |
| C1-4 | Install the core "Moon Reflection" art installation at the trail end viewing platform. The piece is a 1.8m diameter disc of frosted recycled glass, mounted on a low, wide stone base set far enough back from the trail edge that visitors won’t crowd it, and angled to catch the real moon’s reflection at its highest point during the Mid-Autumn Festival. Around the platform, teams will tuck 40 tiny solar-powered firefly lights, set to flicker at random 8–12 second intervals at 2700K with no fast strobing that can disorient nocturnal birds and insects. All lights will be set to turn off automatically at 11PM to avoid pulling wildlife off their regular routines. | Art team + local professional installation crew with experience building outdoor public art in city parks | Installation is stable enough to withstand level 8 winds, as confirmed by a structural safety test conducted before public access is allowed. Post-installation light testing shows no glare spilling into adjacent forest areas, and the moon’s reflection is clearly visible on the glass disc on clear, cloudless full-moon nights. | Recycled frosted glass sourced from a local glass recycling cooperative, solar low-glow lights with automatic shutoff timers, locally quarried fieldstone for the base, signed structural safety test report. |
---
 Phase 2: Pilot Operation & Public Engagement (Weeks 13–24)
*Core goal: Test operations with small, manageable visitor groups first, to work out kinks in protocols and eliminate any sources of wildlife disturbance before opening the trail more broadly. This phase will also build slow, word-of-mouth awareness among local residents, rather than pushing for viral social media attention that could draw unmanageable crowds too fast.*
| Task ID | Specific Action Item | Assigned Party | Success Metric | Required Resources |
|---------|----------------------|----------------|----------------|--------------------|
| O1-1 | Launch a 6-week pilot of guided "Moon Walks". Each walk will be capped at 15 people, held only 3 nights per week (Friday-Sunday) starting exactly 1 hour after sunset, when foxes are just beginning to move out of core den areas to forage. All visitors will be required to turn off flash photography for the full duration of the walk, keep voices below 40 decibels (about the volume of a soft whisper), and stay strictly on the marked wood chip trail. Each walk is led by 2 trained volunteers, and includes a 10-minute stop at the first observation blind to share quick, relatable facts about local fox ecology—like how foxes cache extra berries under leaf litter for winter, or why they’re more active on nights with bright moonlight. | Operations team + trained volunteer guides | Total pilot visitors are capped at 1,080 to avoid overwhelming the site, with zero reported incidents of visitors approaching foxes, leaving the trail, or playing loud music during walks. Post-visit short paper surveys (handed out as visitors leave the platform) show 95% of respondents can name three accurate facts about local fox ecology after the walk, rather than leaving with only vague impressions of the art. | Free decibel meter app installed on all guide phones, printed visitor code of conduct posters posted at the trail entry, pre-walk briefing scripts that avoid overly formal language, battery-powered infrared trail counters to track actual trail usage outside of guided walks. |
| O1-2 | Run the "Little Fox’s Moon Postbox" interactive activity. A weatherproof wooden postbox, painted with murals by local teen art club members, will be mounted at the viewing platform, inviting visitors to write anonymous short notes about their own small wishes or quiet nature observations on recycled paper postcards. Each month, the community team will sort through notes and select 10 to share on the project’s small social media page, only after reaching out to the note writer (via contact info optionally left on the card) for explicit permission. The team will also partner with a local special needs school to host 2 free private walks for students, held on weekday evenings when the trail is closed to the general public, and will display 24 of the students’ fox-and-moon artworks on blank sections of trail signposts for the full pilot period. | Community engagement team (one part-time staff with prior experience working with local school groups) | Collect at least 400 notes in the first 3 months of the pilot, display 24 student artworks on the trail with small labels noting each artist’s first name, and receive at least 20 unsolicited positive social media tags from visitors per month, mostly from local residents rather than out-of-town travel accounts. | Hand-built wooden postbox, recycled paper postcards with small fox illustrations printed on the back, rustproof metal art display clips, formal partnership agreement with the local special needs school outlining accessibility accommodations for student visits. |
| O1-3 | Conduct weekly ecological monitoring, no exceptions. Every Monday, the monitoring team will pull memory cards from infrared cameras to track fox activity patterns, check sapling survival across the restored corridors, and sort through paper visitor feedback slips left in a box at the trail entry. If monitoring shows foxes are consistently avoiding sections of the trail near active event areas, the team will adjust operations immediately—no waiting for a formal monthly review. Adjustments might mean cutting event frequency from 3 to 2 nights a week, moving light shutoff times earlier by 30 minutes, or temporarily closing sections of trail near active fox dens for 2–3 weeks until activity returns to baseline. | Ecology monitoring team (two graduate students from the university ecology department, plus one volunteer lead) | Submit short, plain-language weekly monitoring reports (no overly academic jargon) shared with all volunteer teams and city department partners, and maintain a 0% rate of fox displacement from core habitat across the full pilot period. If fox activity drops by more than 20% in any zone, the team will flag the issue within 24 hours and propose an adjustment plan the same week.

title: 草莓设施栽培关键技术
text:
Key Technologies of Strawberry Protected Cultivation: A Systematic Review

 Abstract
The strawberry (*Fragaria × ananassa* Duch.) is a high-value horticultural crop, valued for its nutrients and distinctive flavor. It is also unusually sensitive to its surroundings. Protected cultivation has become a central way to extend the production season, raise yield and fruit quality, and limit damage from pests, diseases, drought, cold, and other stresses. This review examines four key technical systems in modern protected strawberry production: the design of cultivation structures, precise control of the greenhouse environment, soilless culture and nutrient management, and integrated pest and disease management. For each system, the review considers how the technology works, what it achieves in practice, and where improvements are still needed. Examples from commercial production are included where available. Across the studies reviewed, combining intelligent environmental control, elevated or multi-layer soilless cultivation, and lower-pesticide pest management can raise annual strawberry yields by roughly 30%–50%, cut irrigation water and fertilizer inputs by 25%–40%, and reduce the risk of pesticide residues in fruit. These figures are not universal: they depend on cultivar, climate, greenhouse design, and management skill. The paper ends by discussing several emerging directions, especially digital twin-based regulation, lower-energy greenhouse designs, and substrates made from local biological materials. These developments may support a more productive and sustainable protected strawberry sector.

Keywords: strawberry; protected cultivation; environmental control; soilless culture; integrated pest management; intelligent agriculture

 1. Introduction
Strawberry is a perennial herbaceous berry crop in the genus *Fragaria* and the family Rosaceae. Its fruit contains vitamin C, anthocyanins, phenolic antioxidants, and dietary fiber (Giampieri et al., 2012). In 2022, global strawberry production exceeded 8.8 million tons. China, the United States, and Mexico were the three largest producers (FAOSTAT, 2023). Those aggregate numbers hide a fragile crop. Open-field strawberries are easily bruised by rain, exposed to frost, and attacked by soil-borne pathogens. Harvest often arrives in a narrow market window, which depresses prices, while extreme heat, cold, or heavy rainfall can sharply reduce yield.

Protected cultivation covers several production forms: greenhouses, high tunnels, rain shelters, and plant factories. These structures create a partly or fully controlled microclimate. They can lengthen harvest, keep fruit away from wet soil, and increase the share of fruit that meets market standards. Since the 1980s, protected strawberry production has spread quickly. In China, more than 75% of fresh strawberries are now grown under protection (Zhang et al., 2021). That proportion reflects both investment by larger farms and adoption by smallholders who rely on simpler plastic tunnels.

Expansion has not solved every problem. Many small producers still build structures without accounting for local wind, snow, or winter sun angles. Environmental control is often rough. Soil sickness and continuous-cropping obstacles are common where beds are reused, and some farms apply pesticides according to habit rather than monitoring. Much published research treats one operation in isolation—lighting, substrate, heating, or biological control—but fewer studies connect those pieces into a production system. This review therefore examines facility structure, environmental regulation, soilless substrates and nutrient supply, and pest and disease management as linked technologies. It also discusses how these systems can be combined and where future work may lead.

 2. Optimization of Protected Cultivation Structures
The structure is the basic hardware of protected strawberry cultivation. Its shape, covering material, ventilation openings, and internal layout directly affect light transmission, heat retention, air movement, drainage, and the ease with which workers can harvest and spray. A poorly oriented greenhouse cannot be fully corrected by sensors or fertilizer.

 2.1 Main Facility Types and Applicable Scenarios
Commercial strawberries are grown under several kinds of protection, including solar greenhouses, plastic high tunnels, multi-span glass greenhouses, and vertical plant factories. Each has a different cost structure and fits different climates and market aims.

Chinese-style solar greenhouses use a rear wall, night insulation quilts, and passive heat storage. Winter heating costs are comparatively low. They are common across northern China, roughly between 35°N and 45°N, where they permit overwintering production and fruit sales from December to March (Liu et al., 2020). Their performance varies with wall material and maintenance. A compacted-earth or brick wall may store heat well, but a shaded or poorly sealed greenhouse can still become cold at night.

Plastic high tunnels are arched frames covered with polyethylene film. They cost less to build than permanent greenhouses and are relatively easy to ventilate by rolling up side film. They work well for early-spring and late-autumn crops in temperate and subtropical areas. By keeping rain off flowers and fruit, they reduce rots and can advance harvest by about 2–3 weeks compared with open-field production (Xiao et al., 2019). They offer limited protection in severe cold.

Multi-span intelligent greenhouses and plant factories use artificial lighting, hydroponic equipment, sensors, and centralized control platforms. They can support nearly continuous production and are useful for high-end fresh fruit, propagation, and research. Their weakness is economic rather than technical. Construction, electricity, depreciation, and skilled management costs are high, so energy prices and local fruit prices strongly influence profitability.

 2.2 Structural Parameter Optimization
Light often sets the ceiling for protected strawberry performance. Strawberry is a sun-loving crop. A useful light-intensity range is approximately 25,000–45,000 lux, although exact responses differ by cultivar and growth stage. Under weak light, plants become leafy and elongated, fruit sugar content falls, and trusses may be weak (Sønsteby et al., 2016).

Greenhouse frames should therefore allow as much unobstructed light as possible. Large spans and slim supports help. For solar greenhouses, the roof angle is often designed using the local noon solar altitude angle at the winter solstice, with a recommended lighting-surface angle around 60°–65° of that angle in practical design. This sounds technical, but the aim is simple: winter sunlight should meet the roof more directly rather than reflecting away. Covering material matters as well. Anti-aging, anti-drip polyolefin films with initial transmittance above 90% are commonly preferred. That figure declines with dust, algae, scratches, and age, so cleaning and timely replacement are part of light management, not optional housekeeping.

In elevated or multi-layer systems, rack height and layer spacing must match leaf area and plant architecture. A two- or three-layer trough system often uses 40–50 cm of vertical spacing to limit shading between layers. Even that spacing does not give every plant equal light. Movable A-frame racks can be rotated or shifted periodically, allowing plants on lower or outer positions to receive more direct light at different times. Fixed racks may still be workable if the lowest layer is planted less densely or used mainly for early propagation.

Ventilation deserves attention because strawberry flowers and fruit suffer in still, humid air. Greenhouses should generally have both roof and side openings. A common practical recommendation is a total ventilation area equal to 15%–20% of the floor area. Such ventilation can help keep relative humidity below 85% during flowering and fruiting, reducing periods when *Botrytis* infection can develop. In windless regions, vents alone may be insufficient; extraction fans or horizontal airflow fans may be needed.

 3. Precision Environmental Regulation Technologies
Temperature, light, humidity, and carbon dioxide interact. A grower cannot manage one as if the others did not matter. Together they shape vegetative growth, flower induction, pollination, fruit expansion, color, flavor, and the balance between leaf production and fruiting. Precision regulation is where protected cultivation gains much of its yield and quality advantage.

 3.1 Temperature Management
Strawberry temperature requirements shift through the crop cycle (Table 1). In seedlings, high temperature can encourage stolon production rather than the desired crown and flower development. Cooler conditions and short days help induce flowering in June-bearing cultivars (Heide et al., 2013). For cultivars such as ‘Benihoppe’ and ‘Sweet Charlie’, flower-bud differentiation can occur after 2–3 weeks at roughly 10–18 °C with a 10–12 h photoperiod. Local nursery practice still matters; plant size, crown diameter, and water status affect the response.

Table 1 Suitable temperature parameters for strawberry at different growth stages

| Growth stage | Day temperature (°C) | Night temperature (°C) |
|--------------|----------------------|------------------------|
| Vegetative growth | 20–25 | 10–15 |
| Flower-bud differentiation | 12–18 | 8–12 |
| Flowering and pollination | 22–25 | 10–14 |
| Fruit expansion | 18–23 | 6–10 |

During winter production, night temperatures below 5 °C can restrict root activity and delay fruit development. Hot-air blowers, root-zone heating pipes, and biological straw reactors are used as supplemental heating measures. Root-zone heating is often more energy efficient because it warms the substrate and roots rather than the entire air volume. Maintaining root-zone temperature around 15–18 °C can improve root activity and nutrient uptake while using about 30% less energy than whole-air heating (Wang et al., 2022). The saving depends on greenhouse insulation and thermostat settings.

In summer and autumn, the problem reverses. Ventilation, 30%–40% shade nets, and micro-spray cooling are used to avoid prolonged temperatures above 30 °C. Heat can reduce pollen viability, lead to poor pollination, and increase malformed fruit. Shade should not be left on too long. Relief from heat that comes at the cost of light may produce softer plants and lower sugar accumulation.

 3.2 Light Regulation and Supplementary Lighting
Winter greenhouse strawberries frequently experience weak light because days are short, the sun is low, and plastic films age or collect dust. Reflective films placed on the ground or rear wall can redirect light into the middle and lower canopy. Reported improvements in light utilization range from 12%–18% (Li et al., 2018), though the benefit is greatest in well-oriented houses with clean film.

Artificial lighting is more common in high-end greenhouses and propagation facilities. LEDs have become the main source because they convert electricity into light efficiently, produce relatively little radiant heat near the leaf, and allow spectrum selection. Strawberry leaves use red light around 600–660 nm efficiently for photosynthesis. Blue light near 430–470 nm supports stomatal opening, compact growth, and anthocyanin formation. Research sh

title: 提高睡眠质量
text:
The Lavender Sachet That Smelled Like Cigarette Smoke
The first thing I did when I moved into the third-floor walkup was tape black garbage bags over the bedroom window. The streetlight outside bleached orange straight through the thrifted linen curtains I’d dragged home from the flea market, and for three weeks straight I’d woken at 2:47 a.m. to the sound of the guy below my window arguing with his ex on the fire escape, his voice cracking like he was about to cry every single time.

I bought melatonin that tasted like sour cherry, chewed two an hour before bed, and ended up staring at the water stain on the ceiling that looked exactly like my third grade goldfish, the one that jumped out of its bowl while I was at school and dried stiff on the carpet. I tried the 4-7-8 breathing trick, the meditation app that droned on about mountain streams until I wanted to throw my phone across the room, even cut out iced coffee after 2 p.m. which meant I spent my work afternoons yawning so hard my jaw ached, staring at spreadsheets until the numbers blurred into little black ants marching across the screen.

My grandma showed up unannounced last Tuesday with a Tupperware of congee and a crumpled lavender sachet she’d stitched herself, the edges lopsided because her arthritis has been acting up. She didn’t say anything about the garbage bags on the window, didn’t lecture me about screen time or regular bedtimes like my mom did on our weekly phone calls. She just tucked the sachet under my pillow, heated up the congee on my sad little hot plate, and left before I could offer her a seat.

That night I forgot to take the melatonin. I’d stayed up late re-reading a beat-up copy of *The House in the Cerulean Sea* I’d found on the sidewalk, the spine held together with packing tape, and when I finally turned off the lamp I could smell lavender, sharp and sweet, but under it the faint, familiar tang of my grandpa’s old unfiltered Camels, the ones he smoked on the porch right up until the day he died. I realized then she must have stitched the sachet sitting in his old wicker chair, the one she still keeps on her back porch even though the wicker’s splitting and the cushion has a coffee stain from when I spilled my latte on it last Easter.

I woke up at 7:12. No 2:47 a.m. argument, no goldfish water stain staring back at me, just the sound of rain hitting the fire escape and my cat Mochi curled heavy on my chest, purring so loud it vibrated my ribs. The garbage bags were still taped to the window, I’d had an iced coffee at 3:30 the day before, I hadn’t set a single sleep timer or turned on the white noise machine I’d wasted 20 dollars on. I reached under the pillow and felt the lopsided sachet, its stitching coming loose at one corner, a few crumbs of dried lavender spilling out onto the sheets.

Last night I heard the guy on the fire escape again, halfway through a slurred apology, and I didn’t jolt awake. I just rolled over, breathed in that mix of lavender and stale cigarette smoke, and listened to Mochi knead the edge of the comforter like she was making bread. Somewhere down the block a dog barked. The rain started again. I didn’t check the clock.

title: 水稻病虫害绿色防控技术
text:
Green Prevention and Control Technologies for Rice Diseases, Insect Pests, and Other Pests

Abstract: Rice (*Oryza sativa* L.) feeds much of the world, yet its harvest is repeatedly threatened by diseases, chewing and sucking insects, weeds, and the lingering consequences of excessive pesticide use. Green prevention and control (GPC) offers a practical response. It draws together ecological regulation, resistant cultivars, careful monitoring, biological and physical interventions, and—when genuinely needed—chemical products with a lower risk profile. The aim is not a pest-free paddy at any cost, but pest suppression that also safeguards biodiversity, water quality, and the safety of harvested grain. This short review outlines the main components of GPC in rice, explains how selected technologies work in practice, and examines why adoption remains uneven. The available evidence suggests that GPC can cut reliance on broad-spectrum insecticides, support populations of natural enemies, and protect yields, but only when methods are matched to local pest pressure, cultivar choice, climate, and farmers’ resources.

Keywords: rice; integrated pest management; ecological pest management; biological control; pesticide reduction; sustainable agriculture

---

 1. Introduction

Rice supplies staple calories to more than half of humanity. For that reason alone, unstable harvests quickly become a food-security problem (Khush, 2005).

Paddy fields are crowded, productive, and often humid, which makes them favorable environments for rice blast, sheath blight, bacterial leaf blight, stem borers, planthoppers, and leaf folders. For decades, intensive chemical application appeared to offer the fastest answer. It sometimes did. But repeated spraying also left pesticide residues, selected for resistant pest populations, triggered pest resurgence, contaminated soil and water, and harmed fish, pollinators, predators, and other non-target organisms (Heong et al., 2015).

Green prevention and control technologies for rice diseases, insect pests, and other pests are evidence-based strategies designed to reduce those harms. They overlap strongly with integrated pest management (IPM), but GPC gives particular weight to ecological processes, low-toxicity materials, and avoiding unnecessary chemical inputs. This review examines the main technical components of rice GPC, notes where performance is uncertain, and considers what would make implementation more realistic beyond demonstration plots.

 2. Core Principles of Green Prevention and Control

Rice GPC is guided by the principle of “prevention first, integrated management” (Lu et al., 2012). Its target is usually suppression, not eradication. Eradication is rarely achievable in a connected paddy landscape, and attempting it can lead to repeated blanket spraying.

Instead, management seeks to keep pest populations below economically damaging levels while preserving the paddy ecosystem’s own capacity to resist outbreaks. Agroecological management makes the field more suitable for healthy rice and less suitable for pests and pathogens. Monitoring and early warning combine field inspection, traps, weather information, and local forecasts so that decisions are based on observed risk. Non-chemical controls—resistant varieties, adjusted cultivation, habitat management, and biological control—are preferred when they can provide adequate protection. Pesticides are then used precisely and selectively, generally only after an action threshold is approached or disease risk becomes high.

This balance is never static. A strategy that works in a well-drained, mechanized farm may fail in a rainfed lowland field where transplanting dates vary widely. Local adaptation matters.

 3. Major Green Prevention and Control Technologies

 3.1 Resistant Varieties and Healthy Seedlings

A resistant or tolerant rice cultivar is often the cheapest first line of defense. Once seed is purchased, protection is embedded in the plant; no separate spray operation is required. Resistant varieties are especially valuable against rice blast, bacterial leaf blight, and brown planthopper. Genes in the *Pi* family confer resistance to certain blast populations, while *Bph* genes can reduce feeding, survival, or reproduction of planthoppers (Fujita et al., 2013).

The qualification is important. Resistance does not always remain durable. New pathogen races can multiply, and planthopper populations adapted to a formerly resistant cultivar have emerged in several production regions. Large monoculture plantings accelerate this process. Rotating cultivars, mixing genetic backgrounds where feasible, and pairing host resistance with balanced fertilizer, cleaner seed, and biological or chemical protection during high-risk periods can extend useful life.

Healthy seedlings also set the trajectory of the crop. Warm-water seed treatment can reduce seed-borne infection without adding synthetic pesticide residues, although temperature and exposure must be controlled to avoid damaging germination. Biopesticide seed treatment, balanced nursery nutrition, sensible sowing density, and good water management produce stronger seedlings that establish faster and tolerate early infection better.

 3.2 Cultural and Ecological Regulation

Cultural control changes how rice is grown so that pest life cycles are interrupted. Crop rotation and periodic fallowing reduce survival of some soilborne pathogens and pests that depend on continuous rice hosts. Removing or chopping stubble, followed by deep plowing where soils allow, can expose overwintering stem borer larvae and reduce pathogen inoculum. Synchronized planting across a village or irrigation command shortens the period in which successive crops provide continuous food for borers and planthoppers. This is powerful in theory, but it demands coordinated water supply and labor, which many farmers cannot arrange alone.

Fertilizer management deserves special attention. Excess nitrogen produces lush, tender foliage and dense canopies. Such growth may look vigorous, but it often increases susceptibility to blast and sheath blight and can improve conditions for planthopper outbreaks. Split applications, matched to crop demand and soil testing, reduce that risk. Alternate wetting and drying irrigation can improve root health and reduce periods of high humidity that favor some diseases, though timing must be adjusted because drought stress can itself reduce yield.

Ecological engineering works at a larger scale. Flowering plants, grassy strips, field bund vegetation, trees, and shelter belts can supply nectar, pollen, alternate hosts, and refuge for parasitoids and predators. Not every flowering plant is beneficial; some may also shelter pests. Species choice and maintenance therefore matter. Still, diversified agricultural habitats commonly support more abundant and stable natural-enemy populations than simplified monocultures (Sainju et al., 2017).

 3.3 Physical and Behavioral Control

Physical and behavioral methods leave little or no pesticide residue, which explains their popularity in green rice production. Light traps catch nocturnal moths, including stem borers and leaf folders, but catches alone do not prove yield protection. Traps may remove many individuals while also drawing moths into a field or capturing harmless insects. Placement, density, and timing matter.

Yellow or other colored sticky boards are useful for monitoring small flying insects and can contribute to mass trapping in nurseries or confined settings. Insect-proof nets are especially effective in seedling beds, where they exclude vectors such as leafhoppers and planthoppers during a vulnerable growth stage. Sex pheromone traps help detect moth flights and can disrupt mating when deployed over a sufficiently large area. Bait or attract-and-kill systems concentrate treatment on pest behavior rather than covering the entire canopy.

Area-wide coordination is usually the decisive condition. A single paddy surrounded by differently managed fields gains limited benefit from mating disruption. Maintenance also costs time: traps fill, sticky surfaces lose effectiveness, nets tear, and batteries or lamps fail. Bycatch of non-target insects remains a legitimate concern, particularly around light traps.

 3.4 Biological Control

Biological control uses living organisms or their products to suppress pests. In rice, conservation biological control may be the most practical form because the paddy already contains predators and parasitoids if broad-spectrum insecticides do not eliminate them.

Spiders are often among the most abundant predators in flooded fields. Water striders, lady beetles, predatory bugs, and crickets also consume planthoppers and leafhoppers, especially early in an infestation. Tiny parasitoid wasps such as *Anagrus* species attack planthopper eggs, while *Trichogramma* species parasitize eggs of lepidopteran pests. Preserving these enemies by avoiding unnecessary insecticide applications is therefore not merely symbolic. It can determine whether a small planthopper colony collapses or escalates into an outbreak.

Augmentative products have a place as well. *Bacillus thuringiensis* (Bt) formulations are effective against susceptible young leaf folder larvae and other lepidopteran species, but performance declines once larvae are older or leaf rolling protects them from spray deposits. Fungi such as *Beauveria bassiana* and *Metarhizium anisopliae* infect several rice insects under favorable humidity and temperature. Antagonistic microbes, including *Bacillus subtilis* and *Trichoderma* spp., can suppress blast, sheath blight, and some soilborne diseases through competition, antibiosis, or induced plant defenses.

Botanical or microbial-derived products such as matrine and validamycin often break down more quickly than many conventional synthetic pesticides. Lower persistence can reduce environmental exposure, but it can also mean a shorter protective window. “Natural” should not be read automatically as harmless to every organism. Quality standards, shelf life, application timing, and label guidance remain essential.

 3.5 Scientific and Reduced-Risk Chemical Control

Even in a well-designed GPC system, pesticides may be necessary. Unexpected immigrant flights, prolonged wet weather favorable to blast, or a rapidly expanding planthopper population can exceed what biological and cultural controls can handle. The objective is then to use chemistry accurately rather than routinely.

Farmers should treat when monitoring or disease forecasting indicates that risk has reached an action threshold, not simply according to a calendar. Pesticide choice should reflect local recommendations, resistance status, selectivity, and toxicity to aquatic organisms and natural enemies. Rotating modes of action delays resistance. Correct dose, water volume, nozzle type, and timing improve deposition on the target. Spraying during bloom or near fish ponds requires extra caution. Pre-harvest intervals must be observed. Efficient sprayers and reduced-drift nozzles can cut loss into paddy water, though poorly maintained equipment may negate those gains.

Reduced-risk chemical control is sometimes described as the last line of defense. That description is useful, but it should not become dogma. In severe epidemic conditions, a timely selective pesticide may preserve both yield and the credibility of the broader GPC program.

 3.6 Monitoring, Forecasting, and Digital Decision Support

Every later decision depends on reasonably accurate monitoring. Farmers and scouts inspect tillers, leaves, necks, and field water; sweep nets sample moving insects; sticky, light, and pheromone traps record flight activity; and counts of spiders, predatory bugs, and parasitized eggs show whether natural enemies are present. A pest count without that ecological context can encourage spraying when the field already contains substantial biological control.

Disease forecasts can combine temperature, relative humidity, leaf wetness, cultivar susceptibility, nitrogen status, and the previous season’s disease history. Such models are most useful when they predict infection periods rather than merely reporting that symptoms have appeared.

Mobile applications, remote sensing, weather-linked advisories, and image-recognition tools can make recommendations timelier and more site-specific. They can also overpromise. A model trained in one region may misread local varieties, pest complexes, or microclimates, and many smallholder farmers lack dependable connectivity, smartphones, or time to enter field data. Digital support works best when it extends, rather than replaces, trained local observation.

 4. Implementation Challenges

The benefits of rice GPC are real, but adoption is not blocked by ignorance alone. Non-chemical methods often act more slowly or less predictably than a fast-acting synthetic pesticide, and a farmer facing a visible infestation may understandably prefer certainty. Resistant cultivars can lose effectiveness as pathogen and insect populations shift. Microbial pesticides and biocontrol agents are sensitive to heat, ultraviolet radiation, rain immediately after application, and inadequate cold-chain or storage. Product quality can vary, and weak formulations discourage repeat use.

Landscape-level ecological measures create a coordination problem. One farmer may plant nectar-rich bunds and avoid early sprays, while neighboring fields are treated heavily or planted asynchronously, allowing pests and natural enemies to move across boundaries. Water management is similarly constrained by irrigation schedules, communal canals, and uneven tenure.

Economic incentives also cut in both directions. Green practices may lower pesticide expenditure over a season, but traps, nets, biocontrol products, certified seed, and labor for scouting require upfront cash or time. Premium markets can reward certified low-residue rice, yet traceability and group certification are difficult for scattered smallholders.

Advice remains uneven as well. Extension services sometimes promote a single product as a green substitute for a conventional pesticide, missing the central point of GPC: ecological observation, thresholds, biodiversity, and coordinated management. Farmers need field demonstrations that compare practices under local conditions, not only posters or slogans.

Finally, evidence needs to be reported honestly. Trials in research stations often use skilled labor, fresh products, and carefully controlled timing. Results can look impressive there and become disappointing after ordinary farm storage, delayed application, or extreme weather. Long-term, participatory studies that measure pesticide use, yield, natural enemies, production costs, and grain residues across seasons would provide a stronger basis for scaling GPC.

 5. Conclusion

Rice GPC is best understood as a working system rather than a collection of eco-friendly products. Resistant cultivars and healthy seedlings reduce initial vulnerability. Cultural practices and ecological engineering weaken pest buildup and support predators and parasitoids. Physical and behavioral tools help monitor and suppress key insects, while microbial and other biological controls provide targeted suppression. Chemical intervention remains available, but it should be selective, threshold-driven, and carefully timed.

No single component is reliable in every paddy. The strongest programs combine several lines of defense, adapt them to local pests and farm resources, and maintain monitoring through the season. With better coordination, accessible advice, stable product quality, and incentives for low-residue production, GPC can reduce pesticide dependence without asking farmers to sacrifice the yield stability on which their livelihoods depend.

 References

Fujita, D., Kohli, A., & Horgan, F. G. (2013). Rice resistance to planthoppers and leafhoppers. *Critical Reviews in Plant Sciences*, 32(3), 162–191.

Heong, K. L., Wong, L., & Delos Reyes, J. H. (2015). *Rice insecticide use and unnecessary planthopper outbreaks*. International Rice Research Institute-related review publication.

Khush, G. S. (2005). What it will take to feed 5 billion rice consumers in 2030. *Plant Molecular Biology*, 59(1), 1–6.

Lu, Y., Wu, K., Jiang, Y., Guo, Y., & Desneux, N. (2012). Widespread adoption of Bt cotton and insecticide decrease promotes biocontrol services. *Nature*, 487(7407), 362–365.

Sainju, U. M., et al. (2017). Biodiversity, ecosystem functioning, and diversified agricultural habitats in pest regulation. *Sustainable Agriculture Reviews / related ecological engineering publication*.

title: 勇敢的小兔子
text:
The Brave Little Bunny Who Lit the Forest
(Starts with a soft, playful tone, leaning into the mic like sharing a secret)
Good morning, dear teachers, friends, and anyone who’s ever felt “too small” to be brave.
Let me take you back to Bramblewood Forest last spring, when wild strawberries were just starting to blush red and clover smelled like honey. There was a tiny cottontail named Lila there. If you’d known Lila back then, you never would’ve guessed she’d end up the forest’s hero. She was the smallest bunny in her warren— the one who froze at an owl’s hoot, hid behind her mom’s ears when thunder rumbled, would rather munch dandelions by her burrow than race the other baby animals up Oak Hill.
The older rabbits teased her nonstop: “Lila’s so skittish she’d run from a butterfly!” Even Lila thought she was a coward. Brave, to her, was the size of the stag that charged wolves, the loud roar of the bear guarding the salmon stream, the sharp talons of the hawk soaring above the treetops. Brave was big. Brave was loud. Brave was… definitely not a tiny cottontail who got spooked by her own shadow sometimes.
But all that changed the day of the big storm.
It blew in faster than the squirrel scouts could warn everyone. Black clouds swallowed the sun, wind bent pines nearly in half, lightning cracked so loud it shook the ground. Animals scrambled for their dens—foxes to their earths, birds to their nests, deer huddled under the rock ledge. But just as Lila was about to dart into her family’s burrow, she heard it: a tiny, trembling whimper coming from the gully.
It was little Toby, the baby fawn. He’d wandered off chasing a butterfly before the storm hit, and now he was stuck on a narrow ledge halfway down the gully. Recent rains had turned the gully sides to slippery mud; below, the creek was swelling fast, churning brown and angry, creeping closer to the ledge by the second.
Toby’s dad, the big stag, charged first—but his hooves slipped on the mud, he almost tumbled into the flood himself, had to scramble back to solid ground. The bear tried reaching down from the top, but his paws were too big, too heavy; the ledge crumbled a little every time he got close. The foxes yelled that they couldn’t climb that slippery slope without sliding right off. Everyone hung back, shouting comforting things to Toby, but no one could get to him. The water was inches from his hooves now, he was crying so hard his little spotted sides shook.
That’s when Lila stepped forward.
Wait—wait, hold on, let me be real here: Lila was terrified. Her nose was twitching so fast it hurt. Her paws shook so bad she almost tripped over her own ears. Her brain was screaming Run! Hide! This is dangerous! You’re just a tiny bunny! But she looked at Toby, scared and alone, and that feeling was bigger than her fear.
She didn’t have big hooves or sharp claws or a loud roar. But she had something none of the bigger animals had: tiny, light paws that barely pressed into the mud, years of practice weaving through brambles and tight spaces, running up slippery root paths when she darted away from foxes on rainy days.
“I can go,” she said, so quiet almost no one heard her over the wind. By the time they turned to look, she was already inching down the slope.
It was scary. Once, a clump of mud slid out under her back paw and she almost fell—she clung to a dandelion root for dear life, heart thumping so hard she thought it’d hop right out of her chest. Wind whipped her ears in her face, the roar of the flood below was so loud she could barely think. But she kept going, one tiny paw after another, until she reached the ledge.
Toby was bigger than her—so big she could barely nudge him. “Hold onto my fur,” she said. “Follow my steps, exactly where I step. My paws know the safe spots.”
Slowly, so slowly, she led him up. She paused every few seconds to test the mud, find the firm roots, talk soft and steady to him when he froze up. And when they finally scrambled over the gully edge, safe and sound, the whole forest cheered so loud it scared a flock of crows right out of the treetops.
Later, after the storm passed and the sun came out, when everyone was passing around strawberries and acorn cookies to celebrate, the stag came over to Lila and bowed his head. “You are the bravest creature in this forest,” he said.
But Lila just shook her head and nibbled a strawberry she’d found by her feet. “I was scared the whole time,” she said.
(Pauses, softens, makes eye contact with the audience)
That’s the part no one tells you about bravery, isn’t it?
We grow up thinking brave means not feeling scared. We think brave is being the biggest, loudest, strongest, the one who never hesitates, never shakes, never wants to run and hide. But Lila taught Bramblewood Forest that day, and she taught me too: Bravery isn’t not being scared. Bravery is feeling that fear—feeling it so strongly your paws shake, your voice cracks, your brain yells at you to turn back—and choosing to take that next step anyway, because someone needs you.
Bravery isn’t always grand. It doesn’t always look like a knight slaying a dragon or a hero giving a big speech. Sometimes bravery looks like a tiny bunny, mud on her paws and ears all askew, inching down a slippery slope because no one else can fit. Sometimes it’s raising your hand in class even when you’re scared your answer is wrong. It’s standing up for someone who’s being teased, even when your voice is wobbly. It’s trying something new—learning to ride a bike, saying sorry, making a new friend—even when your stomach feels like it’s full of fluttering butterflies.
You don’t have to be big to be brave. You don’t have to be loud. You don’t even have to stop being scared. All you need is to care enough to take that first tiny, shaking step.
Because those small steps? The ones we take even when we’re afraid? Those are the steps that light the way for everyone else. Just like Lila, the tiny skittish bunny who thought she was too small to matter, ended up being the light that brought Toby home.
Next time you feel that flutter of fear, that little voice that says I’m too small, I’m too scared, I can’t? Think of Lila. Remember: even the smallest cottontail can have the bravest heart in the forest.
Thank you.
---
Speech cues:
1. For the parts about Lila hiding and being scared, soften your tone and add small gestures like hunching your shoulders slightly or wiggling your ears to mimic a little rabbit;
2. Speed up a bit and lower your voice to build tension during the storm scene, then slow down and emphasize your words when Lila steps forward to highlight the turning point;
3. For the final reflection, glance across the room to make eye contact with the audience, and end with a warm smile to make it feel more heartfelt.

title: 甘蔗病虫害绿色防控技术
text:
Green Prevention and Control Technologies for Sugarcane Pests and Diseases

Abstract
Sugarcane (Saccharum officinarum L.) is one of the world’s most important sugar and energy crops, but pests and diseases continue to take a real toll on both yield and quality. Chemical control has been the default for a long time, yet pesticide residues, resistance, and broader ecological damage have made it clear that this path has limits. Green prevention and control, or GPC, is therefore increasingly seen as a necessary direction for sustainable sugarcane production. This review outlines the major pests and diseases affecting sugarcane, then brings together the main GPC approaches—agricultural, physical, biological, and ecological regulation. It also looks at why adoption is still constrained in practice and suggests where future work may be most useful, with the aim of offering a reference for more environmentally friendly sugarcane production.

Keywords: sugarcane; pests and diseases; green prevention and control; biological control; sustainable agriculture

1. Introduction

Sugarcane accounts for roughly 80% of global sugar production and is also a major feedstock for bioethanol. The main production areas lie in tropical and subtropical regions, including China, Brazil, India, and Thailand (FAO, 2023). Under continuous monocropping, problems such as borers, aphids, pineapple disease, and smut tend to recur, and in serious years cane yield may fall by 10%–30%, with sucrose content also affected.

For many years, management has depended heavily on synthetic insecticides, especially organophosphates and pyrethroids, along with fungicides. Overuse of these chemicals has gradually selected for resistance, harmed natural enemies, polluted soil and water, and raised concerns over the safety and quality of sugar products. As agricultural systems worldwide are being pushed toward greener production and reduced pesticide use, GPC—built around ecological regulation and giving priority to nonchemical measures—has become an important way to reconcile production with environmental protection.

2. Major Pests and Diseases Damaging Sugarcane

2.1 Main insect pests

Some of the most damaging pests are lepidopteran stem borers, notably the sugarcane stem borer (Chilo infuscatellus), yellow top borer (Scirpophaga nivella), and pink borer (Sesamia inferens). The larvae tunnel into growing points and stalks, producing dead hearts in young cane and, later, broken stalks and poorer sucrose accumulation. Sucking pests are also important, especially the sugarcane woolly aphid (Ceratovacuna lanigera). It feeds on phloem sap and can transmit sugarcane mosaic virus; honeydew deposits then support sooty mold, which weakens photosynthesis. Below ground, white grubs, wireworms, and other soil pests attack seedcanes and roots, often resulting in patchy establishment.

2.2 Main diseases

Fungal diseases are particularly prominent in sugarcane. Smut, caused by Sporisorium scitanamineum, produces the familiar black whip-like sorus at the top of affected shoots, with plants often stunted and showing abnormal tillering. Pineapple disease (Ceratocystis paradoxa) mainly attacks planted seedcanes, causing rot and poor germination; the infected tissue often gives off a characteristic pineapple-like odor. Ratoon stunting disease, caused by Leifsonia xyli subsp. xyli, is more inconspicuous. There may be few obvious external symptoms, but ratoon crops decline over time, and the pathogen spreads readily through contaminated cutting tools. Viral problems such as mosaic and yellow leaf syndrome also contribute to varietal degeneration, especially because sugarcane is propagated vegetatively.

3. Core Green Prevention and Control Technologies

3.1 Agricultural control: source control and cultivation regulation

Agricultural measures are the base layer of GPC because they improve field conditions and crop resistance from the beginning of production.

Disease-free seedcane production is now widely promoted. Healthy seedcane, free or nearly free of viruses and other pathogens, can be obtained by hot-water treatment, around 50 °C for 2–3 hours, combined with shoot-tip meristem culture. This helps reduce ratoon stunting disease and mosaic virus carried in seed pieces (Sundar et al., 2020). Before planting, seedcanes may also be soaked in lime water or a biological fungicide preparation to reduce pineapple disease.

Variety choice and deployment matter as well. In areas where smut or borers are recurring problems, resistant or tolerant varieties should be favored, and large-scale, long-term planting of one susceptible clone should be avoided. That kind of uniformity makes it too easy for pathogens and pests to adapt.

Field management is another major lever. Deep plowing before planting exposes soil insects to predators and weathering. Smut whips and obviously diseased plants should be removed before spores are released, or they become a source of secondary spread. Rotation with legumes or maize can interrupt the life cycles of pests with narrow host ranges. Balanced fertilization, particularly avoiding excessive nitrogen, helps prevent the soft, tender growth that tends to attract aphids and borers. After harvest, removing crop residues and destroying stubble where borers overwinter can substantially reduce the population entering the next season.

3.2 Physical control: trapping and blocking without chemical pollution

Physical control works mainly through insect behavior—light response, attraction, movement, and so on—and has the advantage of adding no pesticide residue directly to the field.

Light trapping is the most common approach. Frequency-vibration lamps and solar LED lamps are often installed at about one lamp per 2–3 hectares. During peak emergence of borers and scarabs, the lamps are run at night and adults are killed on high-voltage grids. Reported reductions in egg laying can exceed 40% (Li et al., 2021), though field performance varies.

Sex pheromones offer a more targeted form of behavioral control. Synthetic lures for Chilo and Sesamia can be used with sticky traps, commonly around 15–30 traps per hectare, both to monitor moth flights and to remove males. At larger scale, pheromone dispensers can be used for mating disruption by making it difficult for males to locate females, lowering fertilization and the subsequent larval population.

Yellow sticky boards are useful for monitoring and suppressing winged aphids. In seedling nurseries, insect-proof nets and similar barriers can also keep virus vectors away from healthy planting material.

3.3 Biological control: using living organisms to regulate pest populations

Biological control sits at the center of GPC. It relies on living organisms or their metabolites to keep pest populations below damaging levels.

3.3.1 Parasitic and predatory natural enemies

For stem borers, releases of the egg parasitoid Trichogramma chilonis are a fairly mature practice. Cards carrying parasitized eggs are placed in the field early in the borer oviposition period, usually at 150,000–300,000 wasps per hectare, with follow-up releases every 7–10 days. In well-managed demonstration areas, parasitism of 60%–80% has been reported. For aphids, conservation or augmentative release of predators such as the seven-spot ladybeetle (Coccinella septempunctata), lacewings, and hoverfly larvae can help keep populations down. In southern China, maintaining some flowering weeds and noncrop plants in or near fields provides nectar and shelter, which can support natural enemies and make their control more persistent.

3.3.2 Entomopathogenic microorganisms

Entomopathogenic fungi are used especially against soil pests and aphids. Granules of Beauveria bassiana or Metarhizium anisopliae can be placed in planting furrows or blended with fertilizer; the fungi penetrate the insect cuticle and infect white grubs and borer larvae. Metarhizium has shown relatively long-lasting effects against overwintering borers in ratoon cane, in some cases for more than six months.

Among bacteria, Bacillus thuringiensis, or Bt, remains the best-known example. Its insecticidal crystal proteins are active against susceptible young larvae. Bt suspensions or granules are best timed around borer egg hatch, so larvae are killed before they bore into the stalk. Once they are inside the stem, contact-based control becomes much harder.

Baculoviruses also have a place. The sugarcane borer nucleopolyhedrovirus, for instance, can spread through host populations and cause epizootics. Its capacity for secondary transmission makes it attractive for area-wide integrated management, although production and application timing remain practical considerations.

3.3.3 Biopesticides for disease control

Beneficial antagonistic microorganisms are increasingly used as alternatives to chemical fungicides. Preparations of Trichoderma harzianum and Bacillus subtilis can be applied to seedcanes or soil. They colonize root surfaces, suppress infection by Ceratocystis paradoxa and the smut pathogen, and may also have a growth-promoting effect.

Plant-derived products such as azadirachtin, matrine, and rotenone act through contact toxicity, feeding deterrence, or related effects on aphids and young borer larvae. They tend to degrade relatively quickly and leave less persistent residue, which can be useful later in the growing season, though their efficacy is often more sensitive to timing and weather.
