title: 老人和他的狗
text:
The Crabapple Stick
The linoleum by the back door sticks a little when you step on it right, right where Mabel spilled a whole jar of dill pickles the summer before she died, brine seeped under the edge before either of us noticed. I kick at the sticky spot every morning when I pull my work boots on, same as I did when she’d holler from the kitchen that I was gonna scuff a hole right through the floor if I kept it up.
Jake’s already waiting on the step, tail thumping so hard the whole porch rail shakes. He’s got that gray fuzz around his muzzle now, same as the white that’s been creeping up my sideburns for ten years, and he can’t chase squirrels up the old oak anymore without huffing so bad I have to sit with him on the grass for ten minutes after, rubbing the spot behind his ear where he likes it. Last month the vet said his hips are going, said I should think about keeping his walks shorter, no more tramping all the way down to the creek like we used to. I didn’t say nothing. When we left the office he tugged on the leash so hard he nearly pulled my shoulder out, heading straight for the trail that cuts through the pine grove, like he knew exactly what the vet had said and was having none of it.
We took the long way today, past the empty lot where the general store used to be. Mr. Henderson’s kid sold the land last year to some folks from the city who put up one of those tiny houses with a metal roof that glints so bright in the sun it hurts your eyes. Jake stopped to sniff every dandelion along the fence line, stopped to lift his leg on the same fence post he’s peed on every day since he was a puppy, like he was leaving a note for whoever moved in that this was still his route, same as it’s been for twelve years.
Halfway to the creek he stopped short, nose twitching, and bolted off into the underbrush before I could grab his collar. I yelled after him, my voice cracking a little—last time he ran off like that he came back limping, a thorn stuck deep in his front paw, and I sat on the kitchen floor for an hour with him draped over my lap, prying it out with tweezers while he whined like I was killing him. I tramped through the brambles, my jeans catching on thorns, calling his name until my throat was raw, and then I heard it: that high, excited yip he only makes when he’s found something he thinks is a prize.
He was sitting in the middle of a patch of wild blackberries, tail going a mile a minute, and when I got close I saw what he had: a gnarled old crabapple stick, about two feet long, chewed at one end like some dog had carried it around years ago. He dropped it at my feet, slobber all over the bark, and looked up at me like he’d just found a gold bar.
I picked it up. It was smooth from rain and rot, lighter than it looked, fit perfect in my hand like it had been carved just for me. I threw it a little ways, soft, because I didn’t want him to run too hard, and he loped after it, slow, his back legs hitching a little like they do when he’s tired, but he picked it up and brought it right back, dropped it at my feet again.
We sat on the creek bank after that, him curled up at my feet, the stick between his paws. The water was low this time of year, so shallow you could see the minnows darting between the rocks, same as when I was a kid, same as when Mabel would bring us down here with a picnic basket and Jake would jump in after every leaf that floated by, shaking water all over the blanket until she’d pretend to be mad and swat at him with her napkin.
A couple of kids on bikes went past on the path, yelling so loud a flock of geese took off from the other side of the creek, and Jake lifted his head, growled low in his throat like he was gonna chase them, but then he put his head back down on his paws, huffed, and went back to chewing on his stick.
The sun got low enough that it turned the pine needles gold, and my knee started aching, the one I messed up falling off a ladder back in ‘07, so I pushed myself up, brushed the grass off my jeans, and whistled for him. He didn’t move at first, just looked up at me, his eyes all cloudy around the edges like they get when he’s tired, so I leaned down, scratched that spot behind his ear, and picked up the crabapple stick.
“C’mon, old man,” I said, and he stood up, slow, his joints creaking loud enough I could hear them over the water.
We walked back slow. He stopped twice to sniff at rabbit holes, stopped once to lap at a puddle left over from last week’s rain, and I didn’t rush him. When we got to the house I left the stick propped up by the back door, right next to my work boots, right where the pickle brine stain still sticks to the linoleum.
He’s asleep on the rug by the stove now, his paws twitching like he’s chasing squirrels in his sleep, and every so often he makes that little snuffling noise he makes when he’s dreaming about something good. I heated up a can of soup for dinner, split a piece of bread with him like I always do, and when I sat down in my chair I could see the crabapple stick through the screen door, propped up where I left it, the last of the sunset hitting the chewed end so it glowed a little.
The crickets started up a while ago. The floor still sticks when I step on that spot by the door. Tomorrow I’ll probably kick at it again when I put my boots on, and Jake will be waiting on the step, tail thumping, and we’ll go back down to the creek. I’ll bring the stick.

title: 旅游业高质量发展路径
text:
High-Quality Development Paths for the Tourism Industry: Connotation, Challenges, and Strategic Choices

Abstract

As the global economy continues to transform and upgrade, tourism is gradually moving away from a scale- and speed-driven growth model toward one centered on quality and efficiency. High-quality tourism development has become an important direction for industrial restructuring in many countries, as it seeks to balance economic returns, social equity, ecological protection, and cultural continuity. This paper outlines the core meaning of high-quality tourism development, examines the major challenges now facing the industry, and suggests practical pathways in areas such as product innovation, digital transformation, green development, institutional improvement, and inclusive growth. The study argues that meaningful progress depends on cooperation among governments, businesses, local communities, and tourists. Sustainable industrial upgrading can only be achieved when innovation, environmental responsibility, and a people-centered approach are pursued together.

Keywords: tourism industry; high-quality development; sustainable tourism; digital transformation; industrial upgrading

1. Introduction

Tourism is a broad, cross-cutting industry with economic, social, cultural, and ecological significance. It supports economic growth, creates employment, facilitates cultural exchange, and improves people’s quality of life. Over recent decades, global tourism expanded rapidly. Before the COVID-19 pandemic, international tourist arrivals reached 1.3 billion in 2019, and the sector contributed more than 10 percent of global GDP, according to the United Nations World Tourism Organization (UNWTO). Despite this expansion, the traditional extensive model—reliant on resource inputs, homogeneous competition, and low-value output—has revealed serious weaknesses, including ecological pressure, the commercialization of culture, and unequal distribution of the benefits generated by tourism.

Policymakers in different parts of the world have begun to place greater emphasis on the quality of tourism development. China, for instance, has made “high-quality development” a key part of its national tourism strategy, while the European Union has introduced its Transition Pathway for Tourism to support green and digital upgrading. In this context, it is both theoretically and practically important to clarify what high-quality tourism development means and to identify realistic ways of advancing the sustainable transformation of the global tourism industry.

2. The Core Meaning of High-Quality Tourism Development

High-quality tourism development is not simply about receiving more visitors or earning more revenue. It involves a broader upgrading of the sector around quality, efficiency, and sustainability. Its core meaning can be understood through four interrelated dimensions.

2.1 Innovation-Driven Industrial Upgrading

This dimension emphasizes reducing reliance on natural resources and low-cost factors. Tourism products, business formats, and operating models need to be upgraded through technological, product, and managerial innovation. Rather than focusing mainly on sightseeing, tourism should offer richer experiential and integrated activities, extend industrial chains, and create greater added value.

2.2 Ecological Priorities and Green Development

High-quality tourism follows the principle that lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets. Development should be based on the carrying capacity of local resources and ecosystems. Tourism operations should reduce carbon emissions, pollution, and ecological damage across different segments of travel, so that tourism growth and environmental protection can reinforce one another.

2.3 Cultural Continuity and the Enhancement of Value

Culture should be treated as the soul of tourism rather than as a superficial commercial element. High-quality development avoids excessive commercialization and cultural homogenization. Through creative transformation and innovative expression, it can support the protection and continuation of valuable local cultures while deepening tourists’ understanding, identity, and experience.

2.4 Inclusive Sharing and People-Centered Development

The benefits of tourism should be shared by a wide range of stakeholders, especially local communities and residents. While improving tourist satisfaction, destinations should also create jobs, raise household incomes, narrow regional gaps, and strengthen social well-being. The aim is to integrate economic benefits, social fairness, and improved livelihoods.

3. Major Challenges to High-Quality Tourism Development

The global tourism industry still faces several structural constraints as it moves toward higher-quality development. The most prominent issues are outlined below.

3.1 Homogeneous Products and Inadequate Effective Supply

Many destinations remain overly dependent on conventional natural scenery and historical sites. Products are often limited in form, while scenic areas, homestays, and cultural activities can look and feel much the same from one place to another. A large share of tourism remains at the basic sightseeing level, with insufficient supply of immersive, customized, premium, and integrated experiences. As a result, the industry struggles to meet increasingly diverse, personalized, and quality-conscious consumer demand. In addition, tourism value chains are often short. Revenue is concentrated in tickets and accommodation, while cultural and creative products, study tours, health and wellness services, and other high-value segments remain relatively weak.

3.2 Uneven Digital Transformation and Inefficient Resource Allocation

Big data, cloud computing, artificial intelligence, and other digital technologies are increasingly being used in tourism, but adoption varies sharply across regions and firms. Small and medium-sized tourism enterprises, together with remote destinations, often lack the funding and skilled personnel needed for intelligent management and online operations. Data silos are also common across government departments, scenic areas, and companies. Information on visitor flows, spending patterns, and tourist feedback is not always shared in a timely manner, contributing to mismatches between supply and demand and slowing responses to emergencies.

3.3 Tensions Between Development and Ecological Protection

Some tourism development has followed a “develop first, protect later” approach. Core scenic areas may be overbuilt, visitor numbers may exceed ecological carrying capacity, and disposable products may be used extensively. Such practices can lead to soil erosion, waste pollution, and loss of biodiversity. Tourism transport, particularly road travel and aviation, is also a major source of carbon emissions. At the operational level, hotels, homestays, and scenic spots often lack a strong low-carbon awareness, while standards and incentives for green tourism remain underdeveloped.

3.4 Unclear Benefit-Sharing Mechanisms and Weak Community Participation

In certain tourism projects, outside capital controls planning and operation, while local residents are largely excluded from the higher-value parts of the industry. They may receive only low-wage jobs in cleaning, security, or basic services, while also facing rising prices and living costs associated with tourism. Communities often have limited channels to participate in planning and decision-making. This can generate friction between residents and tourists and weaken the authenticity and long-term appeal of destinations.

3.5 Institutional Gaps and Shortages of High-Quality Talent

The institutional framework needed for high-quality tourism is still incomplete in areas such as ecological compensation, intellectual property protection, and service-quality supervision. Problems such as forced shopping, misleading advertising, and irregular service continue to appear from time to time. The talent structure is also mismatched. While traditional service workers may be relatively abundant, there is a serious shortage of professionals skilled in digital operation, cultural creativity, low-carbon management, and international communication. This shortage limits innovation and industrial upgrading.

4. Pathways for Promoting High-Quality Tourism Development

To address these challenges, tourism development should be advanced through a coordinated framework involving product upgrading, digital and green transformation, stronger institutions, and broader participation.

4.1 Deepen Supply-Side Reform and Develop a Diversified, High-Quality Product System

Destinations should promote the integrated development of “tourism plus culture, education, health, sports, and agriculture.” Local cultural resources can support immersive experiences, intangible cultural heritage workshops, and history-based study tours. Rural areas can develop distinctive homestays, pastoral complexes, and agricultural experience activities. At the same time, destinations can plan high-end formats such as wellness tourism and outdoor sports tourism according to local conditions, reducing dependence on ticket revenue and extending the tourism value chain.

title: 读书的意义
text:
I found that beat-up paperback copy of *Where the Red Fern Grows* in the back of my grandma’s hall closet last month, tucked between a stack of old Christmas cards and a jar of rusty screws. The spine was held together with packing tape, pages 73 and 74 were stuck together with what I’m pretty sure was 30-year-old Kool-Aid, and someone had scribbled a bad drawing of a coonhound in the margin of page 112. I sat down on her scratchy wool carpet right there and read for an hour, and I didn’t think once about the work email piling up in my pocket, or the leaky faucet I’d been putting off fixing for three weeks, or the fight I’d had with my roommate the night before about who left the milk out.

I don’t buy the stuff people say about books making you smarter, or more successful, or whatever self-help garbage they peddle on BookTok. I still forget how to do long division, I burned toast this morning, and I’ve never gotten a promotion because I could quote Mary Oliver. Last year I read a 400-page book about 19th century beekeepers in the Appalachians, and I can’t tell you a single fact about beekeeping now, not really. I remember the part where the old beekeeper sat on his porch after his wife died and watched the bees swarm the old apple tree, and how he didn’t cry for three weeks until one of the bees landed on his wedding ring and stayed there for seven minutes. I thought about that part last April when I sat in the hospital waiting room while my mom got knee surgery, and the clock above the front desk ticked so slow I thought it had stopped, and I didn’t know what to do with my hands. I didn’t have the book with me, but that part was just there, sitting in my head, and I breathed a little easier.

Sometimes I read stupid stuff. Last week I binged three terrible 90s romance novels I got for a quarter each at the library book sale, the ones with shirtless cowboys on the cover and plots so predictable you could guess the ending by page 5. I didn’t learn anything. I didn’t have any grand epiphanies about love or life. But I’d had a garbage day at work—my boss yelled at me for messing up a spreadsheet, my bike got a flat tire on the ride home, it poured rain and I forgot my umbrella—and for two hours, I got to sit on my couch and not be the girl who messed up the spreadsheet or got caught in the rain. I got to be the girl who watched the cowboy realize he was in love with the ranch vet, right as she was about to move to Montana. It was dumb. It was exactly what I needed.

My 10th grade English teacher made us read *The Bluest Eye* over spring break, and I complained the whole time. I wanted to be at the mall with my friends, getting Orange Julius and trying on lip gloss we couldn’t afford, not sitting in my room reading about a little girl who thought blue eyes would fix everything. I wrote a half-assed book report about “themes of racial beauty standards” because that’s what I thought she wanted to hear, got a B+, and forgot most of the book for 10 years. Then last summer I was waiting for the bus, and I saw a little girl standing on the sidewalk with her mom, staring at a billboard for a skin lightening cream, and she reached up and touched her own cheek, quiet, like she was checking something. That book didn’t give me a line to say to her, or a fix for the billboard, or any answer at all, really. But I saw her, in a way I don’t think I would have if I hadn’t read that book when I was 16, half-bored and complaining about missing the mall. I didn’t walk over and say anything. I just stood there, and I knew what that quiet little touch on the cheek meant, even a little bit. That counts, I think.

I don’t read every day. Sometimes I go weeks without picking up a book, when work is crazy or I’m binging a stupid reality show or I just can’t sit still long enough to make it through three pages. I don’t have a fancy bookshelf organized by color, I don’t post my reading list online, I don’t keep a reading journal with pretty tabs and notes. Last week I left a library book on the bus, and I had to pay a $12 fine, and I cursed the whole walk home.

Last night I sat up till 1 a.m. reading that beat-up *Where the Red Fern Grows* copy from grandma’s closet, and when I got to the part where Old Dan dies under the oak tree, I cried so hard I had to blow my nose on a paper towel from the kitchen. I’d read that part three times before, when I was 8, when I was 14, when I was 22. I cried every time. This time, though, I thought about how grandma gave me that book for my 8th birthday, wrote “For the kid who chases stray dogs home” on the inside cover, and how she died two years ago, and how I still sometimes reach for my phone to call her when I see a coonhound on the street. The book didn’t tell me how to grieve her. It didn’t make the fact that she’s gone hurt any less. But when I closed it, I could smell her closet, that mix of cedar and lemon Pledge and the peppermints she always kept in her coat pocket, for a second. The lamp on my desk was too bright, the neighbor’s dog was barking through the wall, and for a minute, I wasn’t alone in the room.

Current Situation and Countermeasures of Sugarcane Industry Development: A Global Perspective
Abstract

Sugarcane is one of the world’s most important sugar and bioenergy crops. Beyond its role as a raw material, it supports food security, renewable energy transition, and rural employment in many tropical and subtropical regions. In recent years, global output has continued to grow, largely because demand for sugar, ethanol, and various bioproducts has kept rising. But the industry is also under considerable pressure. Yields have become more unstable under climate change; many smallholder areas still have low mechanization; production costs are increasing; links within the industrial chain are often weak; and intensive cultivation has created new environmental problems.

This paper examines the current state of the global sugarcane industry from three angles: production layout, industrial structure, and technology use. It then identifies the main constraints affecting higher-quality development and suggests several responses. These include accelerating the breeding of climate-smart varieties, promoting mechanization across the production process, strengthening integrated development along the industrial chain, improving policy support, and expanding green circular production models. The aim is not to offer a single universal model, but to provide useful reference points for making the sugarcane industry more sustainable, efficient, and value-driven in different producing countries.

Keywords: Sugarcane Industry; Industrial Development; Mechanization; Industrial Chain Integration; Climate-Smart Agriculture; Sustainable Development

1. Introduction

Sugarcane (Saccharum officinarum) is a perennial C4 grass grown in more than 100 countries. It supplies about 80% of the world’s sugar and around 40% of bioethanol feedstock (Food and Agriculture Organization [FAO], 2023). Because it serves both as an economic crop and an energy crop, the sugarcane industry plays a central role in the agricultural economies of countries such as Brazil, India, Thailand, China, and Australia. It connects cane production, sugar processing, bioenergy manufacturing, and the use of byproducts.

Since the beginning of the 21st century, world sugarcane output has risen from 1.3 billion tons in 2000 to 1.9 billion tons in 2022. This increase has come partly from expanded planting areas and partly from higher per-unit yields (FAO, 2023). Even so, the industry is now going through major structural changes. On the demand side, population growth and the expansion of food processing continue to support strong demand for sugar. At the same time, the transition toward renewable energy has created larger markets for sugarcane ethanol and biodegradable materials. On the supply side, extreme weather, aging farm labor, and fluctuations in international sugar prices have made the weaknesses of traditional production models much more visible.

In this context, understanding where the sugarcane industry stands, where its bottlenecks lie, and what transformation paths may be feasible has become an important issue for both research and practice. Existing studies tend to concentrate on particular regions or on individual technologies. There is still relatively little systematic discussion of global industrial characteristics together with multi-dimensional policy and industry responses. To address this gap, this paper draws on macro-level industry data and cases from major producing countries. It analyzes the current development and constraints of the global sugarcane industry and then proposes a set of interconnected countermeasures to support industrial upgrading.

2. Current Development Status of the Global Sugarcane Industry

2.1 Production Layout: Concentration in Major Producing Regions and Continued Output Growth

Global sugarcane production is highly concentrated geographically, mostly in tropical and subtropical areas. In 2022, Brazil, India, and Thailand were the three largest producers, accounting for 38%, 21%, and 8% of total output, respectively. Together, these figures reflect a production pattern led by South America and Asia (United States Department of Agriculture [USDA], 2023). Brazil has the world’s strongest sugarcane processing and ethanol conversion capacity, with about 45% of its sugarcane directed to ethanol production. India and Thailand remain more focused on sugar. In China, production is concentrated in Guangxi, Yunnan, and Guangdong, with Guangxi alone contributing more than 60% of the country’s sugarcane output (Li & Wang, 2022).

Yield differences across regions are substantial. The global average sugarcane yield reached 72.5 tons per hectare in 2022. In major producing regions of Australia and Brazil, improved varieties and intensive management can support yields of 90–110 tons per hectare. By contrast, many smallholder-dominated areas in South Asia and Africa still record yields of only 50–60 tons per hectare, often because farming technology is outdated and infrastructure remains weak (FAO, 2023).

2.2 Industrial Structure: Moving beyond Sugar toward More Diversified Use

For a long time, the sugarcane industry was organized mainly around raw sugar and white sugar processing. In recent years, the growth of the bioeconomy has pushed the industrial structure in a more diversified direction.

One major change is the rapid expansion of sugarcane ethanol. Brazil has developed a relatively mature “sugar-ethanol cogeneration” model. Mills can adjust the share of cane going to sugar or ethanol in response to market prices, and sugarcane ethanol now accounts for about 30% of the country’s road transport fuel (Brazilian Sugarcane Industry Association [UNICA], 2023).

Byproduct utilization has also become an important source of additional value. Bagasse is widely used for biomass power generation, papermaking, and degradable tableware. Molasses is processed into alcohol, yeast, and amino acids, while filter mud can be turned into organic fertilizer. In this way, a basic circular industrial chain has begun to take shape.

Still, development along the chain is uneven. Many small and medium-sized sugar mills in developing countries continue to depend on sugar processing as their main source of profit. Byproduct use often remains limited to relatively low-value products, while sugarcane-based bioplastics, functional sugars, and health-related products are still at an early stage (Chen et al., 2024).

2.3 Technological Application: Variety Improvement and Mechanization Are Progressing, but Unevenly

Variety improvement has been one of the key drivers behind higher cane yields and sugar content. Major producing countries have bred high-yield, high-sugar, disease-resistant, and stress-tolerant varieties through both conventional hybridization and molecular breeding. Brazil’s RB series and China’s Guitang series, for example, now cover more than 70% of local planting areas and have helped raise sucrose content by 0.5–1.2 percentage points (Zhang et al., 2023).

Mechanization tells a more divided story. In countries with large-scale planting, especially Brazil and Australia, mechanized harvesting exceeds 90%, greatly reducing labor costs and improving harvest efficiency. But in hilly and mountainous sugarcane areas across China, India, and parts of Southeast Asia, where smallholders dominate, the overall mechanized harvest rate remains below 30%. Planting and harvesting still depend heavily on manual labor (Li & Wang, 2022). Digital and precision agriculture tools, including drones, soil sensors, and farm management platforms, have started to be tested on larger plantations, but their global adoption is still limited.

3. Main Constraints on Sugarcane Industry Development

3.1 Climate Change and Disasters Are Making Production Less Stable

Sugarcane has a long growing season and requires substantial water and warmth, so it is highly sensitive to climatic conditions. In recent years, droughts, floods, and frosts have become more frequent in major producing areas. The 2021–2022 drought in Brazil’s Center-South region reduced sugarcane yield by 12% year on year. In 2023, floods in Thailand damaged nearly 15% of sugarcane planting areas and contributed to sharp movements in international sugar prices (USDA, 2023).

Over the longer term, climate change is also worsening soil degradation and salinization, while creating more favorable conditions for the spread of pests and diseases such as smut and yellow leaf disease. These pressures add to production risk. Smallholders are often the most exposed because they lack agricultural insurance, irrigation and drainage infrastructure, and other disaster-prevention facilities.

3.2 Low Mechanization and Rising Costs Are Squeezing Returns

A major bottleneck in many producing areas is the mismatch between fragmented smallholder planting and machinery designed for larger-scale operations. In hilly and mountainous areas, plots are often irregular and field roads are poor, making large combine harvesters difficult or uneconomical to use. At the same time, as rural labor moves into non-agricultural sectors, the cost of planting and harvesting sugarcane has continued to rise.
