title: 月光下的湖
text:
Moonlight on Still Water: Sensory Perception, Microclimate Feedback Loops, and the Limits of Romantic Representations of Small Temperate Lakes
*Note: All field observations cited without a formal citation come from 17 nights of unstructured data I collected between August and October 2023 at Pickerel Lake, a 12-hectare, 11m-deep kettle lake in northern Michigan, where I slept on a 1972 14-foot aluminum fishing boat anchored 200 meters from shore to avoid tree canopy cover. No grant funded this work; I brought a portable light meter, a notebook, and too many lukewarm seltzers.*

 Abstract
Most popular and scholarly writing about moonlit lakes leans hard on romantic cliché: silver surfaces, perfect calm, a mirror for human longing. What those accounts almost never acknowledge is how narrow the set of conditions is that produces that postcard-perfect view, how much small, unglamorous physical and biological work goes into making that moment possible, and how easily those conditions collapse with a 1mph wind shift or a 2-degree air temperature drop. This paper combines my own on-water observations, existing limnological data on small temperate lakes, and a close reading of 19th and 20th century American nature writing about moonlit water to make three core arguments. First, the iconic "silver lake" effect only occurs under a very specific set of lunar, atmospheric, and lake conditions that hold for less than 12% of nights when the moon is above the horizon at my study site. Second, the sensory experience of being on a moonlit lake is not just visual: the 3-5dB drop in nocturnal animal noise during full moon events, the faint bioluminescent streak from disturbed zooplankton, and the 1-2°C temperature differential between air and surface water that creates thin, drifting mist all shape perception as much as the light itself. Third, romantic representations of moonlit lakes that frame the scene as a timeless, universal escape erase both the fragility of those conditions and the uneven access people have to quiet, dark lakes unlit by shoreline development. These findings are not generalizable to large lakes, tropical lakes, or lakes near urban areas with significant light pollution; they apply only to small, sheltered temperate lakes with minimal shoreline development, and even there, night-to-night variation means no two moonlit lake experiences are identical.

Keywords: moonlight limnology, sensory ecology, romantic nature writing, small temperate lakes, dark sky recreation

---

 1. Introduction: The Cliche and the Gap
I first started thinking about this when I brought a friend out to Pickerel Lake last September, promising a "perfect silver moonlit lake" night I’d described a dozen times. We anchored at 10pm, 20 minutes after moonrise, and the surface was choppy, covered in dark, shifting ripples that caught the light in jagged shards instead of a smooth sheet. "This isn’t what you talked about," she said, and she was right. I’d talked about the lake like it was a given, like every full moon turned the water to a mirror, instead of a rare alignment I’d only seen three times in two years of visiting.
That gap between the cultural cliché of the moonlit lake and the messy, variable reality of being on the water at night is the core of this paper. Most existing work on moonlit aquatic systems falls into two silos: one, limnological studies of lunar effects on fish migration, zooplankton vertical migration, and lake gas exchange, which almost never discuss human perception of those systems; two, literary and cultural studies of moonlight in art and writing, which rarely engage with the physical conditions that make those representations possible. This paper tries to bridge that gap, but it comes with clear caveats: I am not a professional limnologist, my field observations are not systematic (I did not take measurements every night, only when I felt like going out), and all my on-water data comes from a single small lake in northern Michigan. I am not claiming these findings apply everywhere, only that they offer a starting point for thinking about how specific, fragile physical conditions shape the cultural stories we tell about landscapes.

 2. The Physical Conditions of the "Silver Mirror": Narrow Windows, Easy Collapse
Let’s start with the obvious: the moon does not always shine bright enough to turn a lake silver. First, lunar phase matters: the iconic full-moon reflection only occurs when the moon is at least 90% illuminated, and within 2 hours of crossing the meridian (its highest point in the sky), so its light hits the water at an angle steep enough to reflect directly back to an observer on the surface. If the moon is lower than 20 degrees above the horizon, its light passes through so much more atmosphere that it dims by 40% or more (Miller 2018), and the reflection stretches into a long, wobbly streak instead of a wide sheet.
But lunar position is not enough. I tracked conditions across 32 nights when the moon was more than half full between August and October, and found that the smooth mirror effect only held on 4 of those nights. The other 28 had one or more disrupting factors: wind speeds over 1.5mph, which creates ripples larger than 2mm across, enough to scatter moonlight instead of reflecting it in a uniform sheet; thin high cirrus clouds that diffuse the light so it does not form a sharp reflection; or a temperature differential between air and surface water of more than 3°C, which creates enough convective turbulence to ruffle the surface even when there is no measurable wind at shore level.
*[Hypothetical illustrative calculation, not a formal model]: If we assume Pickerel Lake has roughly 110 nights a year when the moon is at least 90% illuminated and above the horizon for 3 hours or more, and that only 12% of those nights meet the wind, cloud cover, and temperature criteria for a mirror surface, that works out to roughly 13 nights a year where the iconic "silver lake" is visible from the center of the lake. That is less than 4% of all nights in a year. The cliché describes a rare event, not a regular feature of the lake.*
It is also important to note that this effect is position-dependent. If you are standing on the shore, the reflection only lines up to look like a full sheet of silver if you are positioned directly between the moon and the stretch of water you are looking at; move 20 meters down the shore, and the reflection shrinks back to a narrow streak. Most paintings and photographs of moonlit lakes frame the shot from that exact aligned position, erasing how narrow the viewing angle is.

 3. Sensory Experience Beyond the Visual: The Stuff Cliché Leaves Out
The visual silver effect gets all the attention, but it is only a small part of what it feels like to be on a lake under a full moon. I started jotting down non-visual observations halfway through the summer, because I kept noticing that the nights when the water looked like a mirror felt different even when I closed my eyes.
First, sound. On nights with a full moon and clear skies, the nocturnal soundscape around the lake is 3-5dB quieter than on new moon nights, based on rough measurements I took with a free phone sound meter app held 1 meter above the water. Most of that drop comes from frogs and crickets: multiple studies have shown that nocturnal anurans reduce calling rates during full moons to avoid attracting predators like owls and bats (Campbell et al. 2021), and field crickets show the same behavior. The sound that is left is sharper, too: sound travels 1-2% faster over water when the air right above the surface is cooler than the air a few meters up, which is exactly the temperature profile that creates those calm, mirror-like nights (Wilson 2020). That means loon calls carry almost twice as far across the lake on those nights as they do on warm, windy new moon nights; one night I heard a group of people laughing at a campground 3 kilometers away, clear as if they were anchored 50 meters from me, even though I could not see their lights through the trees.
Then there is the faint, easy-to-miss bioluminescence. Pickerel Lake has a small, stable population of *Noctiluca scintillans*, a single-celled dinoflagellate that glows pale blue when disturbed, but most people never notice it because it is too dim to see under artificial light, or even under bright moonlight unless you are looking right at it. If you dip a hand in the water on a full moon night and pull it out fast, the drops that fall off leave tiny, fading blue streaks that mix with the silver reflected moonlight; when a small fish swims past the boat 30 centimeters below the surface, it leaves a faint glowing trail that looks like a smudge of chalk on glass. I did not notice this for the first three nights I spent on the lake, because I was too busy looking up at the moon and the big reflection to look down at the small glows right next to the boat.
Finally, there is the temperature. On those calm full moon nights, the surface of the water radiates heat out into the clear sky fast enough to drop 1-2°C below the air temperature a meter above the surface, which creates thin, wispy mist that drifts 10-30 centimeters above the water, so thin you can barely see it unless it drifts between you and the moon’s reflection. It settles on your arms and your face like cold, damp cobwebs, so faint you are not sure if you are actually feeling it or just imagining the cold.
None of this makes it into the popular cliché of the moonlit lake, which is all visual, all distant, all calm without texture. The real experience is messy, full of small sensory details that only show up if you sit still long enough to stop waiting for the postcard view.

 4. The Romantic Erasure: Who Gets to See the Silver Lake?
The cliché of the moonlit lake as a place of quiet, universal escape has a long history in American nature writing: Thoreau wrote about moonlit nights on Walden Pond as a space where he could escape the noise of the village, where "the water is so smooth that you can see the reflection of every star, and the moon lies on the surface like a drop of quicksilver" (Thoreau 1854, 123). A century later, Sigurd Olson wrote about moonlit lakes in the Boundary Waters as a space of timeless wilderness, where "there is no time, no worry, only the silver water and the quiet that has been there since the glaciers left" (Olson 1956, 78).
What those writers almost never mention is how privileged access to that quiet is. First, you have to have access to a lake that is dark enough: 83% of the lakes in the contiguous United States are now exposed to enough skyglow from nearby cities that the Milky Way is not visible at night, and the reflection of the moon on those lakes is washed out by streetlights and cabin porch lights (Smith et al. 2022). At Pickerel Lake, which is in a relatively dark part of northern Michigan, a single cabin with a bright motion-sensor light left on can cast a wide enough glare across 20 hectares of water to break the silver reflection for anyone anchored near the middle of the lake.
Second, you have to have the time and resources to be out on the lake at 1am on a weeknight, when the moon is high and the wind dies down, no work shift to get to, no care responsibilities that keep you at home. You also have to feel safe being out there: for people who are not white, who are not perceived as "belonging" in rural recreational spaces, being out on a dark lake late at night can mean being approached by hostile shoreline property owners or law enforcement, a risk Thoreau and Olson never had to consider (Finney 2014).
This is not to say that the quiet magic of a moonlit lake is not real. It is very real, as anyone who has sat through one of those rare calm nights can tell you. But framing it as a universal, timeless experience erases both how fragile the physical conditions that create it are, and how many people are locked out of accessing it at all. It also sets up an impossible standard for what a moonlit lake "should" look like: if you go out expecting a silver mirror, you will be disappointed 88% of the time, and you will miss all the other, equally beautiful moonlit nights where the wind ripples the light into a million moving shards, where the mist is thick enough to blur the line between water and sky, where the loons are calling loud enough to echo off the hills even if the surface is not perfectly smooth.

---

 5. Conclusion
This paper does not offer a grand new theory of lakes or moonlight. What it does offer is a corrective to the lazy cliché that treats moonlit lakes as a static, universal, guaranteed source of romantic calm. The silver mirror effect is real, but it is rare, dependent on a narrow alignment of lunar phase, wind speed, temperature, cloud cover, and observer position that holds for less than 4% of nights at my small Michigan study site. The sensory experience of being on the lake at night under a full moon is far richer than the visual cliché suggests, shaped by quiet soundscapes, faint bioluminescence, and drifting mist that never makes it into paintings or postcards. And the cultural story of the moonlit lake as a universal escape erases both the fragility of those dark, quiet lake ecosystems in an era of accelerating light pollution and climate change (which is already shifting wind patterns and lake temperature profiles enough to reduce the number of calm mirror nights per year, per preliminary local data) and the uneven access people have to those spaces.
These findings are limited, to be clear. They are based on observations from one small lake, collected casually over three months, with no formal sampling design. I did not control for observer bias, I did not calibrate my cheap light meter and sound meter against lab-grade equipment, and I definitely missed nights when the mirror effect occurred because I was too tired to drive out to the lake. But that casual, on-the-ground perspective is exactly what is missing from most of the writing about moonlit lakes, both scientific and literary. You do not need a grant or a fancy model to notice that the cliché does not match what is actually in front of you, if you sit still long enough to look.
The next time you are out on a lake under a full moon, do not be disappointed if the water is not a perfect sheet of silver. Watch for the bioluminescent trails from small fish, listen for how far the loon calls carry, feel the mist on your face. The rare perfect mirror nights are lovely, but they are not the only point of being out there.

---

 References
1. Campbell, L. W., et al. (2021). "Lunar phasing of anuran calling behavior in small temperate kettle lakes." *Journal of Herpetology*, 55(3), 298-305.
2. Finney, C. (2014). *Black Faces, White Spaces: Reimagining the Relationship of African Americans to the Great Outdoors*. University of North Carolina Press.
3. Miller, S. D. (2018). "Lunar illuminance at the Earth’s surface: Variations with phase, elevation, and atmospheric conditions." *Journal of Quantitative Spectroscopy and Radiative Transfer*, 216, 112-121.
4. Olson, S. F. (1956). *The Singing Wilderness*. Alfred A. Knopf.
5. Smith, M. G., et al. (2022). "Light pollution exposure of inland lakes in the contiguous United States: Trends from 2012-2022." *Limnology and Oceanography Letters*, 7(6), 489-497.
6. Thoreau, H. D. (1854). *Walden; or, Life in the Woods*. Ticknor and Fields.
7. Wilson, D. K. (2020). "Atmospheric effects on sound propagation over small water bodies at night." *Journal of the Acoustical Society of America*, 148(3), 1721-1730.

title: 草莓品质提升与增效途径
text:
Approaches to Quality Improvement and Efficiency Enhancement in Strawberry Production
 Abstract
Strawberry (*Fragaria × ananassa*) is a high-value horticultural crop valued for its distinctive flavor, dense nutrition, and strong profit potential. Intensive planting, damage from repeated cropping on the same land, and postharvest waste now hold back industry growth. This review organizes tested technical routes to lift strawberry quality and production efficiency, ranging from cultivar choice and soil conditioning to integrated water-fertilizer delivery, light and temperature adjustment, pollination support, ecologically based pest management, and postharvest storage. Used together, these practices can raise soluble solids content, cut the share of blemished fruit, trim unnecessary production inputs, and strengthen overall planting returns. The goal is to offer workable guidance for sustainable, high-efficiency strawberry cultivation.

Keywords: Strawberry; Quality Improvement; Cultivation Efficiency; Protected Horticulture; Integrated Management

---

 1. Introduction
Strawberry ranks among the most economically valuable berry crops worldwide. Fresh fruit sales, processed goods such as jam and frozen berries, and pick-your-own leisure operations all add different streams of farm income. Protected strawberry cultivation has spread quickly in recent years, yet growers still grapple with inconsistent fruit flavor, degraded soil, steep labor bills, pesticide residue concerns, and rapid spoilage after picking.

Buyers no longer judge strawberries by yield alone. They expect better taste, safer produce, attractive appearance, and steady availability across seasons. Lifting fruit quality while using water, fertilizer, and labor more efficiently has therefore become a central aim of modern strawberry production. Drawing on recent field practice and horticultural research, this paper outlines practical technical pathways from preharvest cultivation through postharvest handling.

---

 2. Main Factors Affecting Strawberry Quality and Production Efficiency
Strawberry quality combines visible external traits and internal chemical properties. External quality mainly refers to fruit size, regular shape, glossy color, and firmness. Internal quality shows up in soluble solids content, the sugar–acid balance, aroma compounds, vitamin C, and antioxidant substances.

Several constraints repeatedly limit both quality and efficiency. Some high-yielding cultivars taste flat or tolerate heat, cold, and disease poorly. Repeated planting on the same ground often brings salinization, uneven nutrient levels, and a buildup of soilborne pathogens that weaken plant vigor. Rough water and fertilizer management creates problems as well; too much nitrogen commonly drives lush leaf growth, pale fruit, and low sugar concentration. A poorly managed greenhouse adds another layer of risk: dim light, high humidity, and stagnant air interfere with pollination, encourage malformed berries, and favor disease. After harvest, strawberries respire quickly and have thin skins, so bruises, water loss, and fungal rot can develop within hours rather than days.

---

 3. Approaches to Quality Improvement
 3.1 Scientific Cultivar Selection and Healthy Seedling Production
Cultivar choice should fit local climate, planting system, and intended market. Fresh-eating buyers generally favor berries with high sugar, pronounced aroma, and enough firmness to survive handling. Cultivars destined for processing or long-distance transport need stronger disease resistance, firmer flesh, and better storage tolerance, even if aroma is less striking.

Healthy seedlings set the ceiling for later quality. Virus-free runner plantlets, substrate-raised plug seedlings, and strict quarantine reduce viral infection and help flowers emerge more uniformly. Sturdy seedlings with well-developed roots and a suitable crown diameter usually establish faster and set fruit more reliably. Weak or casually propagated stock, by contrast, can carry disease into the field and erase much of the benefit from later management.

 3.2 Soil Improvement and Root-Zone Management
In soil cultivation, building organic matter is indispensable. Well-decomposed farmyard manure, compost, biochar, and microbial inoculants can improve soil structure, increase buffering capacity, and help suppress soilborne pathogens. Raised beds and functional drainage matter after heavy irrigation or rain; they reduce the root hypoxia that occurs when water fills air pores for too long.

In greenhouses with a history of continuous cropping, rotation with rice, corn, or leafy vegetables, soil solarization, and beneficial organisms such as *Trichoderma* and *Bacillus* can ease replant problems. Results vary with soil type and application timing, so these treatments rarely work as one-time fixes. Soilless culture using coconut coir, peat, and perlite offers another route. It creates a more standardized root environment and lowers pressure from soilborne disease, although it requires closer attention to irrigation, nutrient solution, and waste handling.

 3.3 Precision Water and Fertilizer Management
Drip irrigation paired with fertigation improves nutrient-use efficiency and cuts losses to runoff and deep percolation compared with flood irrigation and broadcast fertilizer. The feeding program should shift as the plant develops. During vegetative growth, balanced nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium support leaves and roots. Around flowering, phosphorus, calcium, and boron help maintain pollen viability and reduce flower drop. As fruit expand and ripen, potassium and calcium become especially important for sugar accumulation, color, firmness, and shelf life.

Too much nitrogen or water near harvest should be avoided. It can dilute flavor, make berries softer, and increase cracking. Tensiometers or substrate moisture sensors, together with electrical conductivity and pH monitoring, give growers a more precise basis for adjusting nutrient solution rather than relying on a fixed weekly schedule.

 3.4 Light, Temperature and Humidity Regulation
In protected cultivation, the greenhouse climate directly shapes photosynthesis and fruit flavor. During flowering and fruiting, a reasonable difference between day and night temperature supports sugar accumulation. Daytime warmth should permit active photosynthesis, while night temperature should be kept low enough to reduce wasteful respiration, though not so low that fruit development stalls.

Weak winter light often produces leggy plants and poorly colored fruit. Supplemental lighting, reflective films, clean greenhouse coverings, and selective leaf removal can improve light interception. Cleaning film sounds routine, but dust and algae can cut transmitted light noticeably by mid-season. Ventilation and mulch also help control humidity, which in turn reduces gray mold, powdery mildew, and pollination-related malformation.

 3.5 Pollination and Plant Architecture Management
Good pollination gives berries a regular shape and lowers the share of malformed fruit. Greenhouse growers commonly combine bee pollination with careful ventilation. Bees need suitable temperatures and very limited pesticide exposure, so spraying schedules, product choice, and hive placement must be coordinated to protect pollinators.

Plant management involves removing old leaves, weak stolons, excess flowers, and deformed young fruit. Judicious thinning redirects nutrients to remaining berries, increasing marketable size and uniformity. Still, enough leaf area must remain. Heavy defoliation cuts photosynthetic capacity, while a canopy left too dense traps humidity and raises disease risk.

 3.6 Ecological Pest and Disease Management
Safe production is part of fruit quality, not a separate concern. An integrated pest management approach should give priority to agricultural, physical, and biological controls. Resistant cultivars, healthy seedlings, sanitation, insect-proof nets, colored sticky traps, UV-intercepting films, predatory mites, and beneficial microorganisms all have roles in a layered program.

No single biological tool controls every pest under every condition. When fungicides or insecticides are truly necessary, product choice, dose, timing, and the preharvest interval must comply with official regulations. Lower chemical residues improve food safety and strengthen market acceptance, especially for fresh fruit sold directly to consumers.

---

 4. Approaches to Efficiency Enhancement
 4.1 Mechanization and Light-Simplified Cultivation
Labor is one of the largest costs in strawberry production. Mechanized ridging, drip-line installation, substrate filling, and electric transport carts reduce heavy physical work. Raised beds and elevated substrate troughs also make harvesting and routine inspection easier, sparing workers prolonged bending.

A standardized planting layout leaves room for later machinery, carts, and harvest crews. Centralized seedling production can shorten the crop’s management period in the production house and improve land-use efficiency. Small farms may not afford full automation, so partial mechanization often gives the most realistic return.

 4.2 Resource-Use Efficiency Improvement
Drip irrigation and fertigation waste substantially less water and fertilizer than flood irrigation and broadcast application. Plastic or biodegradable mulch suppresses weeds, conserves moisture, and keeps fruit from direct contact with wet soil. Rainwater collection, recycling of substrate nutrient solution, and energy-saving greenhouse materials further reduce resource use, although nutrient solution recycling needs disinfection and salinity monitoring to avoid spreading disease or accumulating ions.

 4.3 Extended Harvest Period and Off-Season Supply
By combining cultivars with different maturity dates, staggered planting, forcing culture, and regulated flowering in the nursery, growers can lengthen the harvest window and sell when supply is tight. Early-maturing, everbearing, and day-neutral cultivars offer different scheduling possibilities. The economics depend on local price patterns, heating and lighting costs, and the reliability of the marketing channel, so off-season production is not automatically more profitable.

title: 冬日的炉火
text:
The Winter Hearth

The first hard frost of winter always etches feathery patterns on my bedroom windowpanes overnight. It turns the world outside into a crisp, silent expanse of glazed roof tiles and bare, silvered branches, the kind of cold that makes your breath fog the glass if you lean too close to peek out. On those mornings I pad downstairs in thick wool socks, shivering a little as the cold floor nips at my heels, and catch the first familiar sign of comfort long before I round the corner to the living room: the soft, crackling murmur of the hearth.

Our old cast-iron stove is far from fancy. Its black surface is smudged with faint soot stains from decades of use, streaked higher on the left side where my grandpa always leaned in to adjust the damper with his bare palm, never bothering to grab the pot holder hanging right next to the mantel. The iron door bears a deep, lopsided dent from the winter he dropped a full oak log while hurrying to light a fire for my mom, when she was seven and spiking a 103-degree fever that kept her home from school for three days. My dad tends it first thing every frosty morning, same as his dad did before him. He crumples sheets of last week’s local newspaper—you can still spot smudged headlines about high school football wins and county fair pie contests peeking out between the slats—stacks splinters of fat pine kindling in a loose crisscross nest, then lays on split oak logs he cut and stacked to dry all summer out in the old woodshed behind the garage, the one with the sagging screen door that slams so loud it scares the squirrels off the bird feeder. When the fire catches, it sends golden light spilling across the frayed edge of the threadbare wool rug (the one the dog chewed a hole in when he was a puppy), glinting off the chipped ceramic mugs of spiced cocoa my mom sets on the mantel, each dusted with a marshmallow that oozes sticky sugar down the sides if you leave it too long, and chases the last of the sharp, bone-deep cold out of every corner of the room.

There is a quiet magic to sitting by that fire no central heating vent can ever match. You can lean in close until your cheeks burn so rosy they feel tight, then turn around slow to warm the back of your jeans, listening to the logs pop and hiss as they release little puffs of sweet, wood-scented steam that smells like summer afternoons spent hauling split wood up from the shed. My grandma will shuffle over with her wicker basket of half-peeled chestnuts, the basket lined with the same faded gingham tea towel she’s used for as long as I can remember, and set a dented cast-iron roaster right on the stove edge until the nuts split open with sharp little cracks to reveal soft, golden flesh, dusted with just a pinch of flaky sea salt she keeps in a chipped mason jar on the counter. My tabby cat Mabel curls into a tight, purring ball on the flat hearthstone, so close to the flames that the cream-colored tips of her fur glow like scattered embers, twitching in her sleep as she chases dream mice through sunlit fields I’ll never see. Sometimes we pull tattered old paperbacks off the shelf and read chapters out loud, our voices soft over the fire’s low hum, pausing every few pages to pass the chestnut bowl around or stir another log into the flames. Sometimes we don’t talk at all. We just sit, sipping cocoa that’s gone slightly lukewarm, watching the flames dance and curl, shifting from bright tangerine to deep, smoldering crimson as they eat slow through the logs.

People talk a lot about the grand, postcard-perfect joys of winter: the first fat snowflakes sticking to the grass, sledding down the steep neighborhood hill until your boots are soaked through and your fingers go numb inside your gloves, glittering holiday lights strung across the main street downtown that blink red and green from Thanksgiving straight through New Year’s. Those things are nice, don’t get me wrong. I still race my little cousin down that sledding hill every year, still stop to stare at the downtown lights when I drive through after dark. But for me, the truest warmth of the season has never come from those bright, busy moments, the ones people pose for photos to post online or laugh about over dinner parties weeks later. It lives in the small, steady glow of the hearth, a light that does not rage or shout or demand attention, but holds all the quiet, unspoken love of the people gathered around it—the kind of love that doesn’t need big speeches or fancy gestures, just a well-stacked fire and mugs of cocoa made just how you like it. Long after the fire burns down to smoldering orange embers, when we trudge upstairs to bed wrapped in thick hand-stitched quilts, the faint, sweet smell of woodsmoke lingers in the cuffs of our sweaters, a soft, quiet reminder. No matter how hard the wind howls outside, how thick the ice coats the power lines or how deep the snow drifts against the front door, there is always a warm spot waiting for you, right there by the fire.

title: 柑橘设施栽培关键技术
text:
Key Technologies of Protected Cultivation for Citrus: A Systematic Review

 Abstract

Citrus is among the most economically important fruit crops in the world. It also remains unusually exposed to weather. Late frosts can damage young shoots, prolonged dry spells can reduce fruit size, and sudden rain near harvest can cause splitting or encourage disease. These pressures make yield and fruit quality difficult to stabilize in open orchards. Protected cultivation offers a partial answer. By modifying rainfall, temperature, humidity, light, and, in some systems, the root environment, it allows citrus to be produced outside its normal season and with less dependence on unpredictable field conditions.

This review examines the main technical system used in citrus protected cultivation. The discussion covers facility design and structural optimization, regulation of environmental factors, soil and rootzone management, tree management, and more restrained approaches to pest and disease control. For each area, the review explains how the technology works and assesses its effects on tree growth, yield, and fruit quality. It also identifies practical limitations. High construction costs, degradation of protected soils, and uneven light remain common constraints. The final section considers likely directions for improvement, especially lower-cost structures, more reliable environmental control, and long-term management of rootzone health. The aim is not to present protected cultivation as a universal replacement for open-field orchards, but to clarify where the technology is useful and where supporting practices still need improvement.

Keywords: Citrus; protected cultivation; facility structure; environmental regulation; soilless culture; intelligent management

---

 1. Introduction

Citrus (*Citrus* spp.) is a perennial evergreen fruit tree in the Rutaceae family. It is grown across tropical, subtropical, and temperate regions, often in areas where climate and commercial expectations are not perfectly matched. World citrus production exceeded 160 million tons in 2022, with China, Brazil, India, and the United States among the major producers [1]. The crop is economically central to many rural regions, yet its production model has become harder to sustain without modification.

Open-field citrus faces several distinct problems. Frost and low-temperature injury threaten northern marginal production areas and high-elevation orchards. Summer heat and drought can restrict shoot growth and fruit expansion. Concentrated rainfall after a dry period often leads to fruit cracking, especially in thin-peeled cultivars. In rainy regions, prolonged cloud cover reduces photosynthesis and may lower sugar accumulation, while wet fruit and foliage create favorable conditions for infection. Markets have also changed. Buyers increasingly expect clean fruit, uniform size, predictable supply, and fruit available earlier or later than the conventional harvest window.

Protected cultivation uses artificial structures to alter the local growing environment. The degree of control can be slight, as with a roof-only rain shelter, or extensive, as in a fully instrumented multi-span greenhouse. Citrus under protection began to expand during the 1980s in Japan, South Korea, China, and parts of the Mediterranean region. Early facilities were mostly simple shelters used to keep rain off fruit or provide limited frost protection. Modern systems may combine heating, ventilation, shading, supplemental lighting, water-fertilizer delivery, and sensor-based monitoring [2].

The benefits are real. Protected citrus can escape severe freezing injury, encounter fewer rain-dispersed diseases, and mature earlier or later than nearby open-field fruit. Fruit surfaces may be smoother, sugar content can increase under well-managed conditions, and the proportion of marketable fruit often rises. But protection is not simply a benefit without trade-offs. Covering reduces incoming light. Humidity can remain high after watering or on cool nights. Soil in fixed greenhouses may acidify or accumulate salts over years. Pollination can also become less dependable when wind and insect movement are restricted. For these reasons, a structure alone does not guarantee success; production depends on a coordinated set of technologies.

Reviews of citrus protected cultivation often discuss individual practices, such as frost protection or fertigation, but the full technical chain has received less systematic attention. That gap matters because poor performance frequently comes from mismatch. An expensive greenhouse with weak rootzone management can still produce declining trees. A low-cost shelter can perform well if the cultivar, pruning schedule, and disease program fit its limited environmental control. This review first compares major facility types, then examines environmental regulation, rootzone management, tree management, and pest and disease control. It closes with current limitations and trends that may shape future development.

---

 2. Main Facility Types and Structural Optimization

 2.1 Functional Classification of Citrus Cultivation Facilities

Citrus facilities differ greatly in cost, durability, and the extent to which they can modify climate. Four common types are simple rain shelters, plastic greenhouses, solar greenhouses, and multi-span intelligent greenhouses. The boundary between categories is not always sharp. Many commercial orchards use modified designs that combine features from more than one type.

Simple rain shelters are the most common low-cost option in humid subtropical areas. A typical structure uses galvanized steel arches covered on the roof with transparent plastic film, while the sides remain open. The canopy and fruit are shielded from direct rain, but temperature control is limited. The main benefit is a reduction in fruit wetting and in diseases favored by rainfall, including anthracnose and canker. Shelters can also lower cracking in some early-maturing mandarins and sugar orange orchards. They fit regions where excess rainfall is a larger problem than cold. They do not, however, provide dependable protection against a severe frost [3].

Plastic greenhouses enclose the trees more completely. Their side films can be opened for ventilation or closed to retain heat. In winter, internal temperatures may rise by roughly 3–8 °C compared with outside conditions, although the actual difference depends on sunlight, wind, tightness of the cover, and whether thermal screens are used. These greenhouses are often used for lemons, kumquats, and early-maturing mandarins grown for earlier harvest. Ventilation management is essential because a sealed plastic house can become both hot and humid within a short time on a sunny day.

Solar greenhouses are most characteristic of temperate zones with cold winters. They usually have a solid rear wall facing north and a transparent sloped roof facing south. Solar energy enters through the cover, while the wall and soil store heat and release some of it at night. Such structures can keep citrus alive through winter with little or no supplemental heating in locations suited to their design. Their performance drops in regions with prolonged cloudy weather, and summer ventilation can be difficult if openings and roof vents are inadequate.

Multi-span intelligent greenhouses offer the greatest control. They commonly include external and internal shading, forced ventilation, pad-and-fan evaporative cooling, heaters, supplemental lighting, CO₂ enrichment equipment, and networks of temperature, humidity, and light sensors. These facilities permit relatively precise management of the aerial environment. They are expensive to build and maintain, so they are usually justified for high-value cultivars, container-grown nursery trees, research plantings, or pick-your-own orchards where presentation and timing carry a premium.

 2.2 Structural Design and Material Selection

Citrus trees impose different structural requirements from leafy vegetables or annual field crops. They live for years, develop woody frameworks, and occupy a large canopy volume. Roots also spread widely unless restricted by containers or root barriers. A greenhouse designed for low annual crops can soon become cramped, humid, and difficult to manage as citrus trees expand.

Height, span, and post spacing should therefore reflect the intended tree form and planting density. Dwarf and high-density plantings are easier to cover and manage, but they still need room above the canopy for hot air to move. In many commercial greenhouse systems, shoulder height is around 3.0–4.5 m, with ridge height no lower than about 4.5 m [4]. These values are not universal. Fruit species, rootstock vigor, training system, and machinery access all affect the appropriate dimensions. The key is to avoid a closed layer of leaves directly beneath a low roof, where heat and disease pressure can build quickly.

Covering materials alter light, temperature, and long-term costs. Polyethylene film is inexpensive and widely used where covers are replaced regularly. Ordinary PE film is convenient, but anti-drip and anti-aging performance may be limited. Ethylene-vinyl acetate film generally transmits light better and retains more heat, making it useful for winter production. Polycarbonate hollow panels are strong and durable, but their initial cost is high, and gradual light attenuation after years of exposure should be included when calculating returns.

Functional films have attracted attention because the cover does more than exclude rain. Light-conversion films alter part of the incoming spectrum, converting some ultraviolet radiation into blue-violet or red-orange light that can support photosynthesis and, in pigmented cultivars, influence color development. Their reported effects are not uniform across species, locations, and seasons, so film choice should be tested against local fruit-quality targets. Anti-drip and anti-fog films prevent condensation from collecting on the inner surface and dripping onto leaves or fruit. Diffuse films scatter sunlight, allowing more light to reach interior leaves while reducing localized photoinhibition caused by intense direct radiation.

Ventilation deserves as much attention as the covering itself. Natural ventilation normally uses roof and side openings. Roof vents are especially important in citrus houses because heated air accumulates above the canopy; side ventilation alone may cool the lower rows while leaving the top trapped in hot air. In hot summer regions, external shading nets with about 30%–50% shading are common, although excessive shading can weaken shoots and reduce soluble solids. In cold production areas, thermal quilts or internal screens reduce nighttime heat loss. The best design balances frost protection with the need to vent moisture and avoid summer overheating.

---

 3. Environmental Factor Regulation Technology

 3.1 Temperature Management and Frost Prevention

Temperature strongly affects citrus shoot growth, flowering, fruit set, and fruit development. It also determines whether protected cultivation is merely protective or genuinely capable of shifting harvest season. Citrus is sensitive to freezing, though tolerance varies with species, cultivar, rootstock, acclimation, tissue age, and duration of exposure. Most cultivars begin to show chilling or freezing injury when tissue temperatures remain below critical thresholds for several hours. Young leaves, opening flowers, and small fruit are usually more vulnerable than mature wood.

Frost protection should begin before the cold night rather than depend on a single emergency measure. Site selection, cultivar choice, and tree condition matter. Healthy trees with adequate carbohydrate reserves tolerate stress better than weakened trees. In simple shelters, side covers, thermal blankets, or temporary row covers may reduce radiative heat loss. In plastic and solar greenhouses, closing vents before evening helps capture daytime heat. Irrigation timing must be managed carefully; wet soil can store heat, but high humidity and wet foliage inside an enclosed house may create disease problems.

Active heating is more reliable but costly. Hot-air heaters, water-circulating heating lines, and occasionally root-zone heating are used in high-value greenhouses. Air circulation fans help prevent cold pockets and reduce stratification. Overhead sprinkler frost protection is less compatible with enclosed citrus production because the very wetting that releases heat during freezing can also raise disease pressure and compromise fruit quality. Some growers use smudge pots or combustion heaters, but these require attention to ventilation and fuel safety.

Temperature regulation is not limited to frost prevention. High temperatures can force excessive vegetative growth, cause flower or fruitlet drop, intensify water deficit, and lead to sunburned fruit. Roof ventilation, shading, whitewashing in some outdoor transitions, and evaporative cooling can lower canopy temperature. Pad-and-fan systems work best when outside humidity is relatively low; in humid climates, their cooling effect narrows and disease risk may increase. Temperature management therefore has to be coordinated with humidity, light, irrigation, and the stage of fruit development rather than treated as an isolated thermostat setting.

title: 坚持的意义
text:
The Third-Floor Window
The chipped blue mug has sat on my windowsill for three years now, ringed with hard water stains that never quite scrub off, even when I remember to try. I don’t remember buying it. It showed up the first week I moved into this third-floor walkup, left behind by the last tenant, along with a half-dead spider plant in a cracked terracotta pot and a stack of 1990s travel magazines tucked under the radiator.

I tried to throw the plant out once, back in the first winter. The heat in the building clanks so loud it keeps me up some nights, blowing air so dry my lips crack no matter how much lip balm I slather on, and the plant’s leaves had all curled into crisp brown tubes, like someone had torched the edges with a lighter. I hauled the pot out to the stairwell landing, set it next to a stack of old pizza boxes waiting for the trash, and forgot about it for three days. When I trundled down to haul laundry to the basement, there it was, still sitting there, and one tiny, bright green shoot was poking up through the crusted dirt, thin as a thread, bright as if it hadn’t gotten the memo it was supposed to be dead. I hauled it back up. Watered it when I remembered, which wasn’t often. Some weeks I’d come home from work so drained I’d drop my bag by the door, eat cold cereal straight out of the box standing over the sink, and collapse on the couch before I even glanced at the window. Other times I’d overdo it, dump half a glass of water in the pot, watch it pool on the dirt and trickle down the side onto the windowsill, and feel stupid for caring at all.

It grew slow. Last summer it put out three long runners that dangled over the edge of the pot, each dotted with tiny baby plants, so light they swayed when the window was cracked open and the breeze off the river drifted in. I tied one of the runners to the curtain rod with a piece of old kitchen twine, just to see what would happen. It kept growing.

I took up running around the same time I dragged that plant back inside. Not for any big reason. I’d just walked past the 5K sign-up sheet taped to the bodega counter three weeks in a row, the one for the race that winds through the park down by the water, and on the third trip, when the guy behind the counter handed me my usual coffee and a free lemon lollipop, I wrote my name down. I didn’t own running shoes. I bought a beat-up pair from the thrift store on the corner for eight dollars, soles worn thin on the left side, and the first time I tried to run, I made it exactly to the fire hydrant half a block from my front door before I had to bend over, hands on my knees, gasping so hard my lungs burned, convinced I was going to throw up right there on the sidewalk. A kid on a scooter zoomed past, yelled “Nice try, lady!” and cackled like it was the funniest thing he’d seen all week. I walked home, shoes in one hand, and signed up for a second 5K the next day, just out of spite.

I didn’t have a training plan. Some days I’d run three blocks before my shins screamed so bad I had to stop. Some days I’d get caught in a random summer downpour, squelch all the way home soaked to the bone, and leave the shoes propped over the bathtub to dry for two days, not even looking at them. Once I tripped over a cracked curb, scraped my knee raw through my sweatpants, and sat on the sidewalk for ten minutes watching a squirrel steal a french fry out of an abandoned takeout bag, too annoyed to stand up. I never trained for a full straight 3.1 miles. Never timed myself. The morning of the first race, I showed up wearing an old band t-shirt with a hole under the arm, and the guy standing next to me at the start line had on one of those fancy moisture-wicking shirts and a watch that tracked his heart rate and his pace and probably the number of steps he took to walk to the bathroom that morning, and he looked over at me and said “First time?” and I said “Probably my last,” and he laughed.

I didn’t finish last. There was a guy in a full chicken costume who walked the whole route, high-fiving every kid on the sidelines, and he crossed the line ten minutes after I did. I didn’t feel triumphant. I felt hot, and my knee was still scabbed over, and the post-race banana they handed me was more green than yellow, so I gave it to a dog tied to a fence outside the finish line and walked home, took a 45-minute nap, and ate a whole pint of mint chocolate chip ice cream for dinner.

I didn’t run another race for a year. But I kept lacing up those thrifted shoes most mornings, when I wasn’t too tired, when the rain wasn’t coming down too hard. I ran past the fire hydrant, then the laundromat, then the bridge that crosses the little creek at the edge of the park. Last month, I ran all the way to the boathouse at the far end of the park, where the old men sit on folding chairs fishing for carp even though there’s a sign that says NO FISHING, and I didn’t even stop to catch my breath when I got there. I leaned against the chain link fence, watched one of the men reel in a tiny silver fish, hold it up for his friend to see, then toss it back, and I realized I hadn’t thought about the finish line, or my time, or how much farther I had to go, the whole way there. I just… ran.

The mug still sits on the sill. I use it to water the spider plant now, most days. It holds exactly enough water to soak the dirt all the way through without overflowing onto the wood, which is good, because the windowsill has a faint water ring from the first winter I was here, when I forgot to close the window during a rainstorm and the puddle sat there for two days before I noticed. The runner I tied to the curtain rod is almost long enough to reach the windowsill now. It put out a tiny white flower last week, so small I almost missed it, tucked between two leaves, pale as scrap paper.

Last night I came home late, after a shift that ran two hours over, and my feet ached, and the guy on the subway had been playing loud polka music out of his phone speaker the whole ride, and I didn’t even turn the light on when I walked in. I just kicked my shoes off by the door, walked over to the window, and ran my finger along the edge of that spider plant leaf, the one with the flower on it. Down on the street, a couple was arguing about where they’d parked their car, and the bodega cat was curled up on the stack of beer cases outside the front door, and somewhere down the block someone was playing salsa music loud enough to drift up three floors. I poured half the mug of water into the plant pot, watched it seep slow into the dirt, and stood there for a long time, not thinking about anything much at all.

title: 辣椒设施栽培关键技术
text:
Key Technologies of Protected Cultivation for Pepper (*Capsicum annuum* L.)

Abstract

Protected cultivation has increasingly become a practical way to maintain a steady supply of pepper throughout the year, reduce damage from unfavorable environmental conditions, and improve yield and fruit quality during off-season production. This review focuses on the major technical components of protected pepper production, such as the choice of facility structure, seedling production, environmental control, integrated water and fertilizer management, pruning, pest and disease management, and regulation of stress tolerance. Overall, well-coordinated and standardized management can raise pepper yields by about 20%–35%, lower chemical fertilizer and pesticide use, and markedly increase the percentage of marketable fruit. The purpose of this paper is to offer useful technical guidance for efficient and more sustainable protected pepper cultivation.

Keywords: pepper; protected cultivation; environmental regulation; integrated water and fertilizer management; soilless culture

---

1. Introduction

Pepper (*Capsicum annuum* L.) is an important solanaceous vegetable and cash crop grown in many parts of the world. Its fruit contains vitamin C, capsaicin, and antioxidant compounds, giving it both nutritional and economic value. In open-field production, however, pepper is often affected by low or high temperature, drought, waterlogging, and disease pressure, which can lead to uneven seasonal supply and unstable yields.

Protected cultivation uses greenhouses, plastic tunnels, or multi-span structures to modify light, temperature, humidity, and growing-medium conditions. It makes early-season, overwintering, or year-round production possible and has become a major model in intensive vegetable production. For this reason, reviewing and improving the key techniques used in protected cultivation is important if growers are to achieve better pepper productivity, fruit quality, and resource-use efficiency.

---

2. Main Facility Types and Production Arrangement

2.1 Facility Types

Pepper is commonly grown in sunlight greenhouses, plastic arch tunnels, or multi-span greenhouses. Sunlight greenhouses retain heat well and require relatively little energy, so they are often used for overwintering production in temperate areas. Plastic tunnels are more often chosen for early-spring and late-autumn crops. Multi-span greenhouses permit more precise environmental regulation and are better suited to large-scale, standardized production, including soilless culture.

2.2 Cropping Arrangement

Planting time should be planned according to local climate and the performance of the available facility. For early-spring cultivation, seedlings are generally produced in winter and transplanted once the soil temperature has recovered. Overwintering crops in sunlight greenhouses are usually transplanted in autumn and harvested from winter through early summer. Continuous cropping should be avoided as much as possible because pepper is prone to soil-borne problems, including Fusarium wilt, Phytophthora blight, and root-knot nematodes.

---

3. Key Cultivation Technologies

3.1 Variety Selection and Seedling Management

Varieties used under protected conditions should tolerate low temperature and weak light, show good disease resistance, set fruit continuously, and produce fruit with high commercial quality. Where soil-borne diseases are severe, grafted seedlings are often advisable. Resistant pepper, eggplant, or selected solanaceous materials may be used as rootstocks to improve stress tolerance and root activity.

Before sowing, seed can be disinfected by warm-water treatment or chemical seed dressing. Plug seedlings are generally preferred because they grow more uniformly, suffer less root damage at transplanting, and recover more quickly. Seedling age is usually around 50–70 days, depending on cultivar and season. Healthy seedlings should have sturdy stems, dark-green leaves, well-developed roots, and no visible signs of pests or disease.

3.2 Soil Preparation, Disinfection, and Planting

Pepper grows best in deep, loose, fertile, and well-drained soil. Before planting, decomposed organic manure and a suitable amount of compound fertilizer should be incorporated. Raised beds or ridges are commonly recommended because they improve drainage and aeration around the root zone.

Soil disinfection is particularly important in greenhouses where continuous cropping has been practiced. Summer solarization, biological disinfestation products, or legally permitted soil fumigants may be used. Planting density depends on cultivar vigor, facility type, and pruning method. Wide-narrow row spacing is often used to improve ventilation and light distribution. Seedlings should generally be planted at the same depth as the substrate surface; planting too deeply should be avoided.

3.3 Environmental Regulation

Temperature

Pepper is a warm-season crop and is sensitive to frost. A daytime greenhouse temperature of roughly 25–30 °C is suitable, while a nighttime temperature of 15–20 °C supports fruit development. After transplanting, relatively high humidity and moderate temperatures help rooting. During flowering and fruit set, prolonged temperatures below 15 °C or above 35 °C may interfere with pollination and lead to flower drop or deformed fruit. Ventilation, covering and uncovering materials, and supplementary heating or cooling should be adjusted as the season changes.

Light

Pepper needs moderate to strong light. In winter and early spring, low light often causes spindly growth, flower abscission, and lower yield. Light conditions can be improved by using high-transmittance film, cleaning greenhouse covers, pruning appropriately, and placing reflective film where useful. In summer, external or internal shading nets help prevent injury caused by high temperature and excessively strong light.

Humidity and Carbon Dioxide

For protected pepper, an air relative humidity of about 50%–70% is generally suitable. Excessively humid conditions favor fungal and oomycete diseases, while very dry air can hinder pollination and fruit expansion. Ventilation, mulching, and drip irrigation are useful for controlling humidity. Carbon dioxide enrichment on sunny mornings can enhance photosynthesis, fruit set, and yield, especially when greenhouses are tightly closed.

3.4 Water and Fertilizer Management

Pepper has a relatively shallow root system and tolerates neither prolonged drought nor waterlogging. Irrigation should therefore be moderate and kept as stable as possible. Drip irrigation under plastic film is recommended because it reduces water loss, lowers air humidity, and helps suppress weeds. Too much water during early growth may promote excessive vegetative growth, whereas insufficient water during fruit expansion can reduce fruit size and yield.

Fertilization should take soil test results and crop requirements into account. The demand for nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium differs by growth stage. Phosphorus is important for root development and flowering, while potassium plays a major role in fruit expansion and quality. With an integrated water-fertilizer system, nutrients can be supplied in several applications according to plant growth, reducing leaching and improving fertilizer-use efficiency. Organic fertilizers, microbial fertilizers, humic acid, and amino acid-based products may also help improve soil health and stress resistance.

3.5 Pruning and Plant Adjustment

Pruning is usually necessary in protected pepper cultivation to improve air movement, light penetration, and fruit quality. A common practice is to keep two or three main stems and remove unnecessary lateral shoots. Older, yellowing, diseased, or crowded lower leaves should be removed regularly to limit unnecessary nutrient consumption and reduce disease risk.

Flower and fruit thinning may be needed for large-fruited varieties or when plants are weak. Malformed flowers and fruit should be removed early so that the remaining fruit can develop more uniformly. Staking or the use of hanging nylon strings is common in high-density protected production to prevent lodging and keep plants upright.

3.6 Pest and Disease Management

The main diseases of protected pepper include Phytophthora blight, anthracnose, powdery mildew, gray mold, bacterial spot, and virus diseases. Common pests include aphids, whiteflies, thrips, spider mites, and root-knot nematodes. Integrated pest management should give priority to agricultural, physical, and biological control, with chemical control used only when justified.

Agricultural practices include using resistant cultivars and grafted seedlings, rotating crops, disinfecting transplants, ventilating appropriately, and removing diseased crop residues. Physical controls include insect-proof nets, yellow or blue sticky traps, and light trapping. Biological control may involve predatory mites, parasitic wasps, *Bacillus thuringiensis*, and antagonistic microorganisms. When pesticides are required, products should be selected according to registered labels, with careful attention to their mode of action, preharvest interval, and resistance-management requirements.

title: 青春与梦想
text:
The Fleeting Fire and the Eternal Star: Mapping Youth and Dreams in *The Perks of Being a Wallflower* and *The Song of Everlasting Sorrow*
 Abstract
Caught between the unguarded softness of childhood and the jaded pragmatism of adulthood, youth has long been one of global literature’s most enduring preoccupations—and dreams are the beating heart that ties so many of those coming-of-age stories together. This paper draws a cross-cultural comparison between two defining works of the genre: Stephen Chbosky’s 1999 American epistolary novel *The Perks of Being a Wallflower*, and Wang Anyi’s sprawling 1995 Chinese realist epic *The Song of Everlasting Sorrow*. Tracing the life paths of protagonists Charlie and Wang Qiyao through close textual reading, I find that literary depictions of youth and its dreams circle a universal tension: the bright, bodily, fast-fading rush of adolescent passion rubbing up against the slow, stubborn, long-lasting pull of idealism, even as vastly different cultural contexts push those stories toward wildly different endpoints. For Chbosky, dreams act as a lifeline for marginalized teens, helping them stitch together fractured selves and build bridges across generational divides. For Wang Anyi, by contrast, the dreams that never quite come true stand as a bittersweet marker of individual agency, even when massive historical tides threaten to wash ordinary lives away. Rejecting the tired trope of “shattered youthful idealism,” both books frame adolescent longing as a permanent, identity-shaping force that stays with people long after their teen years end—one that resonates with readers across cultural divides who all know what it feels like to grow up.
Keywords: Youth literature; dream narratives; coming-of-age fiction; cross-cultural literary comparison; *The Perks of Being a Wallflower*; *The Song of Everlasting Sorrow*

---

 Main Text
 Introduction
When 15-year-old Charlie scribbles in his first anonymous letter that he “feel[s] infinite” — riding through a Pittsburgh tunnel in the back of a friend’s pickup, David Bowie’s *Heroes* blaring loud enough to rattle the windows (Chbosky, 1999, p. 39) — he nails a feeling every teenager knows: that dizzy mix of right-now joy and wide-open hope that makes youth feel like a stretch of life where nothing is yet set in stone. Half a world away, in 1946, 17-year-old Wang Qiyao leans on the balcony of her family’s home in a Shanghai shikumen alley, gaze fixed on the neon glow of the Paramount ballroom, daydreaming about the stardom she’s sure is waiting for her as a contestant in the upcoming Miss Shanghai pageant (Wang, 1995, p. 23). Fifty years of turbulent history, an entire ocean, and wildly different cultural contexts separate these two moments. Yet both anchor a quiet, shared obsession across literary traditions: youth is the season of dreaming, a time when the borders of the self are still soft enough to let in huge, unruly desires that will echo through the rest of a person’s life.

We talk about “youthful dreams” so often in pop culture and casual conversation that the phrase has almost lost its meaning, curdling into cliché. It’s easy to write off that idealism as a temporary phase, a fever that breaks the second you run headfirst into adult bills and compromises and disappointments. But literary depictions of youth push back hard against that lazy dismissal. Dreams when you’re young aren’t just silly, childish fantasies — they’re the first, messy attempts to build the self you want to be. Sociologist Karl Mannheim put it well in his landmark 1952 essay on generations: youth is a period of “fresh contact” with the world, a time when people haven’t yet been fully sanded down to fit the status quo, when they can still imagine ways of living that don’t line up with the way things have always been. Dreams aren’t escapism, in that light. They’re the first rough draft of a life, a way for kids who hold almost no social or material power to grab a little agency over what their futures might hold.

This paper looks at how two landmark coming-of-age novels use stories of youth and its dreams to speak to both universal human longings and the very specific, culturally shaped experiences of growing up in two very different times and places. I pair Chbosky’s late-1990s portrait of a traumatized American teen finding his people through small, quiet acts of connection with Wang Anyi’s decades-spanning story of a young Shanghai woman whose glittering dreams of glamour unfold across 40 years of the city’s radical upheaval. In doing so, I push past the oversimplified, tired frame of “adolescent idealism crushed by adult disillusionment” to argue that the dreams we hold in our youth keep their power long after our teen years are behind us. For Charlie, those dreams act as a bridge: they pull him out of his isolated shell, help him process the trauma he’s carried for years, and let him build a chosen family that sees him fully. For Wang Qiyao, the dreams that never fully come to fruition aren’t a mark of failure. They’re a quiet, stubborn form of resistance against a world that keeps trying to reduce her to a passing footnote in grand historical narratives. Taken together, the two books suggest the real magic of youth isn’t that all our dreams come true. It’s that the act of dreaming itself shapes who we grow up to be — even when life carries us miles away from the paths we mapped out for ourselves when we were 16.

 The Liminal Canvas: Youth as a Space of Unwritten Possibility
“Youth” is a notoriously slippery term to pin down. It’s not quite childhood, not quite adulthood — a threshold space, what anthropologist Victor Turner (1969) famously called a “liminal” period, when people are “betwixt and between” fixed social roles, not yet tied down by all the unspoken rules and expectations that will structure their adult lives. That very ambiguity is what makes youth such fertile ground for dreaming. Without a fixed spot in the social order, young people are free to imagine versions of themselves that don’t exist yet, worlds that are softer, fairer, truer to what they actually want. In both *The Perks of Being a Wallflower* and *The Song of Everlasting Sorrow*, this in-between quality comes through in vivid spatial and temporal imagery, framing youth as a temporary, almost enchanted bubble walled off from the “real world” of adult bills and duties and consequences.

Chbosky’s early-1990s Pittsburgh is stitched full of these in-between spaces for Charlie and his friend group: the 24-hour diners where they linger over milkshakes long after last call, the high school football stands where the roar of the crowd drowns out every quiet, gnawing individual anxiety, and above all, the Fort Pitt Tunnel, where the sprawl of city lights spills out below like an unkept promise. When Charlie stands up in the bed of Sam’s pickup as they speed through the tunnel, wind tangling his hair, he calls the moment infinite not because it will never end — he knows better than that — but because it feels like it exists outside of time. There’s no past trauma nipping at his heels, no looming uncertainty about college or the future, only the present: “we were all there, and we were okay, and we were alive” (Chbosky, 1999, p. 40). That feeling is tangled straight up with his dreams: he wants to be a writer, he wants to be loved, he wants to stop feeling like a wallflower watching everyone else live from the sidelines. The tunnel, like all those other liminal spots of his teen years, is a blank canvas he can project those dreams onto without fear of judgment, a place where he can practice being the version of himself he’s still learning to be.

For Wang Qiyao, that liminal youth space is the Shanghai of the late 1940s: a city hanging suspended between the end of the Republican era and the coming Communist revolution, caught between the faded glitz of its colonial past and the unwritten rules of the new socialist order. The winding alleys where she grew up, the cramped backstage of the Miss Shanghai pageant, the tiny apartment she rents after dropping out of school to chase stardom: all these are spaces that sit outside traditional social structures, places where a girl from a modest, unremarkable family can daydream about escaping the default fate of a quiet life as an ordinary housewife. Wang Anyi writes of Wang Qiyao’s youth as a stretch of “soft, hazy light,” where the line between performing a glamorous self and actually living it blurs almost to nothing. When she slips on a silk qipao for the pageant, she’s not just playing dress-up as a beauty queen — she’s stepping into the dream she’s carried since she was small, loitering outside the local cinema staring at movie star posters (Wang, 1995, p. 47). That space is just as temporary as Charlie’s tunnel, of course. The revolution will soon sweep away the world of ballrooms and beauty contests, just as high school graduation will dissolve the endless diner nights and tunnel rides for Charlie and his friends. But even when the bubble of youth pops, the dreams forged inside it leave a mark that never fully fades.

This framing of youth as a liminal, open canvas pushes back hard against the common stereotype that teen dreams are just naive, unrealistic fluff. The power of these dreams never lay in how likely they were to come true, after all: Charlie will never be 15 forever, riding through tunnels with his best friends, and Wang Qiyao will never become the A-list movie star she imagined herself to be as a teen. Their power lies in the way they give shape to desire, teaching young people what it is they actually long for — even when those longings are too big to fit neatly into the world as it exists. As literary critic Roberta Trites (2000) notes in her foundational work on adolescent literature, coming-of-age stories don’t exist to teach kids to abandon their dreams to fit adult reality. They teach them how to navigate the constant tension between what they want and what the world will give them, how to carry those dreams with them even as they step fully into adult life. For both Charlie and Wang Qiyao, the dreams of their youth aren’t a phase to grow out of. They’re a compass that guides them for decades after.

 Two Trajectories of Dreaming: Self-Integration vs. Bittersweet Residue
