title: 葡萄高效种植模式与经济效益分析
text:
The Magical Vineyard: A Grape-Growing Fairy Tale

There was a valley once, soft with sunlight and ringed all around by green hills. In that valley lived a small rabbit named Lulu, and she kept a little vineyard. Lulu truly loved sweet grapes. The trouble was, her vines did not grow very well. The leaves looked thin, and too many of the grapes were small or sour. She often stood among the rows with her ears drooping a little and thought, “What am I doing wrong? How can I grow grapes that actually taste sweet?”

Then one moonlit night, when the whole valley was blue and quiet, a tiny fairy came fluttering to Lulu’s window. Her wings looked like grape leaves, thin and veined and gleaming at the edges.

“Dear Lulu,” whispered the fairy, “I can teach you something. Call it efficient grape-growing magic, if you like. But you must listen carefully.”

The First Magic: The Upright Trellis Spell

“First,” the fairy said, “give your vines tall, strong trellises. Do not let them lie and crawl along the ground. Guide the branches upward, and help them grow neatly along the frames—almost like arranging your storybooks on a shelf, though vines, of course, are never quite that neat.”

She fluttered her leaf-wings once as she spoke.

“When the leaves are lifted up,” she went on, “each one can meet the sunlight. Air can move between them too. The grapes have a better chance to swell and sweeten, and some of those little bugs will find fewer damp corners to hide in.”

Lulu nodded at once. She was already picturing rows and rows of green climbing up toward the sun.

The Second Magic: The Smart Spacing Charm

“Then give the vines room,” the fairy said. “Do not tuck them too close together, simply because more vines feel like more grapes. Their roots need space to stretch and find water. The vines need room to breathe.”

She tilted her head.

“If they are crowded, they spend their strength struggling against one another. If they are spaced well, they can grow strong. You may even find fewer weeds choking your rows, and that means less weary work for you.”

The Third Magic: The Wise Feeding Enchantment

“Feed them gently,” the fairy said, smiling now. “Use compost—fallen leaves, fruit peels, things that have softened back into earth. Be careful with strong fertilizer. More is not always better.”

“And in spring,” she added, “pinch away the tiny extra buds. It can feel wasteful at first, but not every bud should become a branch. Keep the good ones, and let the vine’s sweetness go where it matters. Sunshine and water should help make grapes, not disappear into a tangle of leaves no one needs.”

Before dawn, the fairy left Lulu one glowing grape seed. Then she floated off into the pale dark.

Lulu planted the seed immediately. She built trellises, measured the spacing as well as her rabbit paws could manage, mixed compost into the soil, and came back to the vineyard every day. Some days she tied a branch. Some days she pulled a weed. Some days she simply sat and watched the new leaves open.

By autumn, the vineyard had changed. It looked like a green gallery draped with clusters of purple and emerald grapes. The bunches were round, heavy, and shining in the sun. When Lulu tasted one, it was sweet all the way through. Even the birds paused after a small stolen bite and sang as if they had something to be pleased about.

It was not long before animals came from other parts of the forest to buy Lulu’s grapes. Squirrel bought armfuls for jam. Bear carried off baskets to make juice. The little mice strung grapes on thread and wore them as sweet, wobbling necklaces. Lulu dried some into soft raisins and put up jars of jelly too.

Because her methods were efficient—less wasted water, less wasted growth, more good fruit—she earned a neat little pile of shiny coins. She bought colorful umbrellas to shade the youngest vines in the hottest summer weeks. She also built a cozy stall near the road. And because she did not think a good secret should stay buried like a stone, she showed her neighbors how to build trellises and space their vines.

After a while, sweet, fruitful vineyards spread through the whole valley.

That night, Lulu sat beneath her grape trellis eating one grape at a time and watching the stars come out. The leaf fairy returned quietly, almost hidden in the shadows.

“You see?” she laughed softly. “Farming is not only hard work. It is also smart work. Respect the sun, respect the soil, and pay attention to the little vines. Then they give back sweetness.”

Lulu smiled. Fireflies blinked around the vineyard, and the air smelled of leaves and ripe grapes. At last she curled into her soft bunny bed, warm and happy and still a little full of grapes, and drifted into a sweet, grape-scented sleep.

The end. 🌙🍇

title: 傲慢与偏见
text:
The Tension Between Social Hierarchy and Moral Autonomy in *Pride and Prejudice*: A Re-examination of Austen’s Romantic Ethics
Course: 19th-Century British Literature  
Student Name: [Redacted]  
Date: October 26, 2024  
Word Count: 3,287  

---

Abstract
When Jane Austen’s *Pride and Prejudice* hit shelves in 1813, no one could have predicted it would become one of the defining romantic comedies of manners in the Western canon—beloved for generations for its sharp, playful wit and the slow, smoldering courtship between Elizabeth Bennet and Fitzwilliam Darcy. Most mainstream film and TV adaptations, plus a lot of the earliest critical writing on the book, boil it down to a straightforward personal growth story: two flawed people let go of their respective hang-ups, work past their snap judgments, and earn their happy marriage. This paper pushes back against that oversimplified take, arguing Austen was making a far bolder intervention into Regency-era social norms than those readings give her credit for. Elizabeth and Darcy’s slow-burn romance isn’t just a satisfying love plot—it’s a sustained, sharp-eyed critique of how rigid class hierarchies claimed false moral authority, how gendered economic rules stripped women of power, and how easily people confused high social standing with inherent goodness.
By digging into key turning points in the text—Darcy’s first, disastrous proposal, the long explanatory letter he sends Elizabeth after that rejection, and the messy resolution of the Lydia-Wickham elopement subplot—this paper shows Austen never argued for tossing out social structure entirely. Instead, she laid out a quiet but radical ethics of moral autonomy: a person’s worth isn’t tied to their birth family, bank account, or how well they can perform polished gentility for others. It shows up in how carefully they reflect on their own mistakes, how empathetically they judge the people around them, and how willing they are to unlearn their own biased assumptions. Framed that way, the novel reimagines marriage as an equal partnership rather than a cold economic transaction—an incredibly radical stance for a time when most popular writing for and about women framed wifely compliance to social expectations as a core moral duty.
Keywords: Jane Austen; *Pride and Prejudice*; class hierarchy; moral autonomy; Regency gender norms; romantic ethics

---

1. Introduction
It’s hard to find a line in English literature more quoted than the opening of *Pride and Prejudice*: “It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife” (Austen 1). That sharp, layered irony hits on the first page, immediately cluing readers in that the book will circle the messy collision between cold economic pragmatism and messy romantic desire in Regency England. For the gentry class Austen wrote about, marriage was rarely about personal affection first—it was a tool for reproducing social status across generations. This was especially brutal for women, who were locked out of property ownership, barred from most formal respectable work, and stripped of independent legal personhood entirely under the doctrine of coverture. For many, marriage wasn’t a choice so much as the only reliable way to avoid destitution (Poovey 73).
The Bennet family’s precarious position drives that structural pressure home immediately. Their Longbourn estate is entailed away to a distant male cousin, Mr. Collins, which means none of the Bennet daughters will inherit a penny after their father dies. Mrs. Bennet’s frantic, often comedic scramble to lock in eligible suitors for her five girls isn’t just silly, over-the-top maternal fuss—it’s a completely rational response to the very real threat of poverty and social erasure hanging over the whole household once Mr. Bennet is gone.
Back in the early 20th century, critics like D.W. Harding famously framed Austen as a “detached satirist”: someone who poked gentle, affectionate fun at her society’s silly quirks without ever challenging its foundational rules (Harding 349). But later feminist scholarship has repositioned her as a far sharper critic of patriarchal constraint, pointing out that her heroines always navigate incredibly narrow, restrictive sets of options to claim agency on their own terms, rather than simply playing by the rules they are given (Johnson 22).
This paper builds on that body of work to argue that the core tension running through *Pride and Prejudice* is a clash between two totally opposed value systems. On one side is the rigid hierarchical logic of Regency class society, which judged people’s moral worth first and foremost by their rank, wealth, and family name. On the other is Austen’s own quiet humanist ethics, which locates real worth in individual character, a person’s capacity to grow and change, and mutual respect between equals. The novel’s parallel courtship plots—Elizabeth and Darcy, Jane and Bingley, Lydia and Wickham, Charlotte and Collins—aren’t just there to mix up the narrative. Each acts as a kind of test case for those competing value systems, laying bare the harm that comes from mindlessly deferring to social hierarchy, while also mapping out how hard it is to build the kind of independent moral judgment that lets people push back against those unspoken rules.

---

2. The Performance of Gentility: Class as Moral Mask
Austen’s takedown of class hierarchy starts by stripping away the facade to show the wide, often absurd gap between performative gentility and actual moral worth. The Regency gentry justified their massive privilege by leaning hard into the ideology of “politeness”: a rigid code of manners, taste, and public decorum they framed as an outward sign of inherent, inborn inner virtue (Langford 112). Austen picks that ideology apart line by line, filling her novel with characters who nail every rule of polite performance yet lack basic moral integrity, alongside characters dismissed as “low” for their lack of rank who show consistent, quiet virtue every time it counts.
George Wickham is the most obvious example of that gap. The charming militia officer wins over the entire Meryton community, and Elizabeth right along with it, with his easy, relaxed manners and knack for making whoever he’s talking to feel seen and flattered. When he first spins Elizabeth the false story of Darcy’s supposed cruelty—claiming Darcy cheated him out of the clerical living old Mr. Darcy had promised him, leaving him penniless—Elizabeth buys every word without a second thought. It doesn’t hurt that his polished public persona lines up perfectly with her already existing grudge against Darcy, who she’d written off as arrogant after their first awkward meeting at the ball. As she puts it later, the respect she felt for Wickham’s supposed good qualities “was at first strong; but…his countenance and voice established him at once as the possessor of all that was amiable” (Austen 73).
That polished gentility was nothing more than a con. Wickham racks up gambling debts all across Meryton, then runs off with 15-year-old Lydia Bennet with zero intention of marrying her—a choice that would have dragged the entire Bennet family’s reputation through the mud, ruining marriage prospects for all her sisters in the process. He only agrees to go through with the wedding when Darcy secretly pays him a massive sum to cover his debts and buy his compliance. His whole nice-guy act was a mask, tailor-made to exploit a social system that automatically equates a pleasant demeanor with goodness.
Flip that dynamic, and you find the characters dismissed for their lower class status often show far more moral backbone than their wealthy, titled counterparts. Take the Gardiners, Mrs. Bennet’s brother and sister-in-law: they live in Cheapside in London, working in trade for a living, a fact the snobbish Caroline Bingley sneers at constantly, writing them off as “low” and unfit to mix with gentry circles (Austen 36). But the Gardiners are the steady, reliable voice of good judgment throughout the whole novel. They’re the ones who first warn Elizabeth that it’s reckless to trust Wickham as much as she does. They chaperone her on her trip through Derbyshire, when she visits Pemberley and starts to rethink her judgment of Darcy. And their own marriage is a warm, stable, equal partnership—a model of companionate marriage totally absent from the Bennet house, with its sniping parents and chaotic energy. Even Darcy, after he’s done the work to unlearn his own class snobbery, recognizes their worth, striking up a genuine, easy friendship with Mr. Gardiner in the middle of the chaos of Lydia’s elopement.
Then there’s Mr. Collins, the most absurd walking example of class-based moral pretension in the whole book. The obsequious clergyman owes his entire livelihood to Lady Catherine de Bourgh’s patronage, and he never lets anyone forget it. He rambles on endlessly about the grandeur of Rosings Park, fawns over every offhand comment Lady Catherine makes like it’s divine wisdom, and his proposal to Elizabeth is almost comically unromantic: he lists his reasons for marrying as a messy mix of perceived social duty, a direct order from Lady Catherine, and a vague, self-satisfied desire to “set the example of matrimony in his parish” (Austen 97). Every line of his dialogue lays bare the hollow core of class hierarchy: status rarely goes to the people with the most merit. It goes to the people best at performing cringing deference to anyone ranked higher than them on the social ladder.
Lady Catherine herself, the novel’s loudest, most unapologetic defender of rigid class boundaries, is painted as rude, overbearing, and completely entitled. When she gets wind that Darcy might propose to Elizabeth, she storms over to demand Elizabeth turn him down, to preserve the planned arranged marriage between Darcy and her own sickly, quiet daughter. She treats other people’s most personal life choices like they are subject to her old-fashioned feudal authority, no questions asked.
What ties all these character portraits together is Austen’s total rejection of the core lie of Regency class ideology: that rank is a reliable stand-in for virtue. After Elizabeth finds out the truth about Wickham, and realizes how wrong she was about both him and Darcy, she berates herself fiercely: “How despicably have I acted!…I, who have prided myself on my discernment! I, who have valued myself on my abilities! who have often disdained the generous candour of my sister, and gratified my vanity in useless or blameable distrust” (Austen 185). Her mistake wasn’t just a one-off personal error in judgment. It was the mistake of buying into society’s default assumption: that polite, charming performance equals moral worth, and that reserved, unapologetic pride of the kind Darcy showed at their first meeting equals moral corruption.

---

3. Pride and Prejudice as Structural Failures, Not Personal Flaws
Critics have long treated the novel’s title as a straightforward reference to the two leads’ personal flaws: Darcy’s overweening pride in his rank and fortune, and Elizabeth’s prejudice against him, rooted in the sting of his snub at the Meryton ball where he refused to dance with her, calling her “tolerable but not handsome enough to tempt me” (Austen 13). It’s true that personal growth sits at the heart of the novel’s arc—both Elizabeth and Darcy have to confront their own blind spots to get to their happy ending. But that reading misses how much both “pride” and “prejudice” aren’t just individual quirks; they’re baked into the structure of the class system they live in.
Darcy’s initial arrogance isn’t some random personal failing. It’s the default mindset he’s been taught his whole life. From childhood, he was told his wealth, family name, and position at the top of the social ladder made him inherently better than the people around him, that his judgment should carry more weight, that he didn’t owe basic courtesy to people he considered beneath his notice. That’s why his first proposal is so cringingly offensive, even when he’s trying to be sincere: he spends half the speech rambling about how hard he fought his feelings, because marrying Elizabeth would mean lowering himself by connecting to her embarrassing, unrefined family (Austen 161). He genuinely thinks he’s making a huge, generous sacrifice by offering for her, and he can’t understand at first why she’s furious rather than flattered.
Elizabeth’s prejudice, too, isn’t just a product of her own quick temper or wounded vanity. She’s spent her whole life watching people with money and rank get away with behaving badly, while people without those advantages are expected to defer to them no matter how rudely they act. She’s also primed to distrust people who act like they’re better than everyone else, in large part because she’s seen how empty that performative superiority is in people like Mr. Collins and Miss Bingley. So when Darcy acts like he’s too good for the Meryton ball, and when Wickham rolls up with his charming manner and a story about Darcy abusing his power, she doesn’t just take Wickham’s side on a whim. She’s taking the side of the person who seems to push back against the unearned arrogance she’s resented her whole life.
It’s not just the two leads, either. The whole Meryton community is quick to judge Darcy as cold and cruel after that first ball, just as they’re quick to fawn over Wickham, because those judgments line up with what they’ve been taught to expect: the charming, friendly man must be good, the quiet, reserved rich man must be stuck up and unkind. Even the Bennet family’s judgment of Bingley as a perfect match for Jane is tied up in that structural bias: they assume his wealth makes him a desirable catch before they even get to know his character, just as they write off Darcy as a bad person because he doesn’t perform politeness the way they expect a wealthy man to.
Take Charlotte Lucas’s choice to marry Mr. Collins, for example. Most readers are quick to judge her for marrying a ridiculous, obsequious man she doesn’t love, but her choice isn’t a failure of personal morals—it’s a rational response to the structural pressure she faces as a 27-year-old woman with no fortune, no family connections, and no other way to secure a home and social standing. As she tells Elizabeth plainly, “I am not romantic, you know; I never was. I ask only a comfortable home; and considering Mr. Collins’s character, connections, and situation in life, I am convinced that my chance of happiness with him is as fair as most people can boast on entering the marriage state” (Austen 109). She isn’t being greedy or shallow. She’s working within the narrow set of options the system gives her, and the fact that readers often judge her harshly for it is a sign of how easy it is to mistake structural constraints for personal failure—exactly the mistake Elizabeth makes about both Darcy and Wickham early on.
Even Wickham’s manipulations are enabled by that structural bias. People don’t trust him because he’s a uniquely good liar; they trust him because he knows how to perform the markers of moral worth that Regency society taught people to look for, and because his story of being wronged by a wealthy aristocrat feels satisfyingly consistent with people’s quiet resentment of class privilege. It never occurs to most people in Meryton to fact-check his story, because his manners fit the mold of what a good, wronged gentleman is supposed to act like.
That’s what makes Darcy’s letter such a turning point in the novel, not just for Elizabeth’s personal growth, but for the book’s broader argument. After Elizabeth rejects his first proposal, Darcy doesn’t lash out or double down on his class privilege. He writes her a long, unflinching letter laying out two truths she’d refused to see: that Wickham is a con artist who tried to elope with Darcy’s 15-year-old sister to steal her 30,000 pound fortune, and that he’d talked Bingley out of pursuing Jane not out of snobbery alone, but because he genuinely believed Jane didn’t care for Bingley, in large part because Mrs. Bennet was so loud and obvious about chasing the match for financial gain (Austen 174). When Elizabeth reads that letter, she doesn’t just realize she misjudged two people. She realizes that the “discernment” she was so proud of was actually just a set of pre-programmed biases, fed to her by the society she lives in. She’d taken the easy, obvious judgments that lined up with social expectations, instead of doing the slow, hard work of actually thinking through what she saw.
That slow, deliberate self-reflection is the core of the moral autonomy Austen argues for. It’s not enough to just reject class hierarchy out of hand, or to assume that all rich people are bad and all charming people are good. Moral judgment requires constant self-questioning, a willingness to admit you were wrong, and a commitment to judging people by their actions rather than the social markers they carry. Darcy, too, has to do that work after Elizabeth’s rejection. He doesn’t just change his mind about marrying her; he changes how he acts toward people he’d previously dismissed as beneath him. When he finds out about Lydia’s elopement, he doesn’t stand on his rank and let the Bennet family be ruined. He tracks Wickham and Lydia down in London, pays off Wickham’s debts, negotiates the marriage settlement, and does it all in secret, not because he expects praise or a reward, but because he recognizes it’s the right thing to do—even though it means associating with people his aunt would dismiss as unworthy of his time.
By the time Lady Catherine shows up at Longbourn to demand Elizabeth reject Darcy, insisting that the marriage would be a violation of class boundaries and family honor, Elizabeth is able to push back clearly, without apology. She tells Lady Catherine, “I am a gentleman’s daughter; I am a gentleman’s daughter” (Austen 306), but more importantly, she refuses to let someone else make her most intimate choices for her, no matter how high that person’s rank is. “I am only resolved to act in that manner, which will, in my own opinion, constitute my happiness, without reference to you, or to any person so wholly unconnected with me,” she tells her (Austen 308). That’s not just a romantic declaration of love for Darcy. It’s a rejection of the entire idea that social rank gives anyone the right to dictate another person’s choices, or to assign moral worth to someone based on their family name.
The novel’s ending, then, isn’t just a satisfying romantic payoff. When Elizabeth and Darcy finally get engaged, their marriage isn’t the kind of economic transaction most Regency novels framed as the ideal. It’s a partnership between two people who have both done the hard work of unlearning the biases their society taught them, who respect each other’s judgment, and who see each other as equals regardless of the gaps in their rank and fortune. Even the other secondary plots circle back to that point: Jane and Bingley end up together because Bingley lets go of his willingness to let other people’s class-based judgments dictate his choices, and he learns to trust his own feelings for Jane. Lydia and Wickham’s marriage, by contrast, is a constant reminder of what happens when people perform gentility without actual moral integrity: they’re stuck in a loveless, debt-ridden marriage, constantly bailed out by Darcy and the Gardiners, never taking responsibility for their own choices. Charlotte and Collins’s marriage, meanwhile, is a quiet, pragmatic compromise—Austen never judges Charlotte for making the only choice she realistically could, but she also makes clear that it’s a pale shadow of the equal, respectful partnership Elizabeth and Darcy build.
Austen never argues that we can do away with social structure entirely, or that class and wealth don’t matter in the world her characters live in. But what she does argue, through Elizabeth and Darcy’s arc, is that moral worth is never assigned by birth or rank. It’s something you build, through constant self-reflection, through the willingness to admit you were wrong, and through the choice to treat other people with respect regardless of their position on the social ladder. That’s the romantic ethics at the heart of the novel: not the idea that love conquers all, but the idea that love can only thrive when people reject the arbitrary hierarchies that tell them who is worthy and who is not, and choose instead to judge each other as full, complex, fallible human beings. It’s a quiet radicalism, easy to miss if you write the book off as just a fluffy love story, but it’s there on every page, in every sharp line of irony, every moment of self-recognition, every choice a character makes to push back against the rules they were taught to follow without question.

title: 柑橘产业发展现状与对策
text:
The Groves That Stayed  
Marta found her grandfather under the orange tree at noon, his boots caked in the mud that hadn’t dried since last week’s unseasonal rain. He was running a thumb over a split rind—fruit that swelled too fast in the wet, then cracked open to wasps and rot. Three boxes of these sat by the fence, already oozing that sharp-sweet smell of waste.  

She’d driven down from the city the night before, laptop stuffed with spreadsheets about cooperative pricing, emails from a juice brand that asked for “uniform brix, uniform size, zero blemish” and paid less every year. The old man didn’t care about brix. He planted this grove the year her mother was born, back when every family along the valley had a few hundred trees, and trucks from the co-op would rumble through at harvest, horns honking before dawn.  

Last winter half those groves got bulldozed. People planted avocados, or sold the land to people who built white houses with pools. Mr. Lin from the next farm uprooted his trees in March; he said he couldn’t pay for the new organic certification, not when the middlemen cut prices again after the late frost in April. Abandoned groves sat untended now, branches tangling, psyllids drifting from them like dust onto leaves that still got sprayed every month.  

Her grandfather tossed the split fruit into the hedge. “Your grandma used to say oranges know when no one’s watching.”  

Marta had spent three weeks arguing on the phone with a logistics guy who said small batches “weren’t worth the truck.” Then she made an Instagram account, shaky videos of her grandfather shaking a tree, fruit thudding into the canvas, close-ups of peel that had faint scars from wind but tasted like sunlight when you bit in. People commented. A café in the city wrote, asking for forty pounds a week. A teacher drove out last Saturday and paid twice the supermarket price just to pick her own, said her kid had never seen an orange still attached to a branch.  

Not everything worked. The first batch she shipped in reused cardboard boxes arrived half squashed. An old neighbor laughed when she talked about selling directly online, said he was too old to learn phones, that he’d just let his trees go wild when his hands stopped working. She didn’t push. She brought him a jar of her grandma’s marmalade on Sunday and asked if he’d let her sell his fruit alongside theirs, no fee, if his grandson could help him film short clips every now and then.  

Last night they sat on the porch sorting fruit by lamplight. Some were small, some lumpy. None looked like the waxed ones stacked in grocery stores. Her grandfather picked one up, peeled it in one long curl, and handed her half. It was so tart her eyes watered, then sweet right at the center.  

Somewhere down the valley a dog barked. The wind carried the smell of orange blossom even in autumn, strange and stubborn. Tomorrow she’d get up at five to load the car. There’d be wasps in the damaged fruit, more emails saying prices were dropping, more trees falling somewhere over the ridge. But tonight the lamplight glowed on the peels, and the old man was humming a folk tune she hadn’t heard since she was small, and the fruit in the wooden crate was warm still, from holding all summer on the branch.

title: 一次难忘的旅行
text:
An Unforgettable Ecological Journey: Place Attachment, Pro-Environmental Behavior Shifts, and Transformative Learning From the 2023 Sanjiangyuan National Park Community-Led Ecotourism Expedition
*Academic paper submitted to the *Journal of Sustainable Tourism* (Special Issue: Transformative Travel Experiences)*

 Abstract
As nature-focused travel gains traction worldwide for its reported ability to spark individual behavior shifts and support community-led conservation, this paper draws on mixed-methods data from a 14-day community-run ecotourism expedition to Sanjiangyuan National Park (Qinghai, China) held in August 2023— a trip the lead author joined both as a researcher and a full participant in the travel group. Grounded in Mezirow’s (1991) transformative learning theory and Williams & Roggenbuck’s (1989) place attachment framework, the analysis weaves together six months of participatory observation, pre- and post-trip surveys collected from 21 expedition members, semi-structured conversations with 8 Tibetan pastoralist guides, and the lead author’s own reflective field notes to trace how immersive, community-centered travel experiences can drive long-lasting pro-environmental behavior change.

Three interconnected features of the trip stood out as making it uniquely memorable for those who joined. First, knowledge flowed both ways between travelers and the Indigenous land stewards who hosted them, rather than following the one-way “tourist as consumer” dynamic common to scenic travel, where visitors simply take in views without meaningful exchange. Second, unplanned, emotionally raw moments brought the fragility of the plateau ecosystem sharply into focus: for instance, a joint patrol to clear illegal poaching snares from high-elevation pastures, and a small community festival celebrating local milestones in snow leopard habitat recovery. Third, structured group action projects planned for after the trip kept the experience from ending when participants left the park, extending its impact far beyond park boundaries.

Regression analysis of survey data found that the sense of place identity participants built over the two-week trip predicted a 72% rise in self-reported pro-environmental actions in the six months after travel—from cutting back on single-use plastic to joining local conservation advocacy efforts—even when we controlled for participants’ pre-existing environmental values. Put simply, the study finds that “unforgettable travel” is not just a product of pretty views or the thrill of seeing something new. It is a deeply context-dependent transformative process that can connect individual, in-the-moment experiences to tangible, collective conservation gains. The work does have limitations: the sample is small and self-selected, and longer-term longitudinal follow-up will be needed to track how persistent these behavior shifts are over years, not just months. Future work should also explore how these community-centered travel models can be scaled without eroding the Indigenous governance structures that make these transformative outcomes possible in the first place.

Keywords: transformative travel; place attachment; community-based ecotourism; pro-environmental behavior; Sanjiangyuan National Park; Indigenous ecological knowledge

---

 1. Introduction
Popular narratives and much early tourism research tend to frame “unforgettable travel” as a product of hedonic pleasure: jaw-dropping scenery, novel sensory experiences, or a temporary break from the grind of daily routine (Larsen, 2007). But a growing body of work in tourism geography pushes back on this, arguing that the travel memories that stick with people longest are the ones that upend long-held assumptions, build lasting bonds to a place and its people, and push people to make sustained changes to how they act long after they return home (Soulard et al., 2022). These kinds of transformative travel experiences feel particularly urgent right now, as the world grapples with overlapping climate and biodiversity crises. When nature-based travel is designed to center community leadership and mutual learning, rather than extractive visitor enjoyment, it has the potential to turn casual, short-term visitors into long-term advocates and stewards for the places they visit (Stronza et al., 2019).

This paper uses a 2023 expedition to Sanjiangyuan National Park—often called the “Water Tower of Asia” for its role as the headwaters of the Yangtze, Yellow, and Mekong Rivers—as a case study of this kind of memorable, transformative travel. The trip looked nothing like the commercial ecotourism packages common across the region, most of which prioritize scenic photo stops over deep engagement with local communities. Instead, this expedition was co-designed from start to finish by the Tibetan herder cooperative of Namse Village, and participants were selected specifically for their stated commitment to contributing to conservation advocacy after the trip ended. The lead author joined the expedition as part of a longstanding university research partnership with the cooperative, taking part in every scheduled activity alongside other travelers while collecting structured research data in the months before, during, and after the journey.

The analysis centers on three core research questions. First, what specific experiential, social, and structural features of the Sanjiangyuan expedition made it such a lasting, memorable experience for participants? Second, how did the place attachment and emotional connections to the landscape and host community that formed during the trip translate to concrete behavior changes once participants returned to their home communities? Third, what lessons does this case hold for designing ecotourism models that deliver tangible benefits to host communities while also creating space for transformative learning for travelers? The sections that follow lay out the theoretical framing for the work, describe the study context and research methods, present both qualitative and quantitative findings, and close with implications for tourism research and on-the-ground practice.

---

 2. Theoretical Framework
 2.1 Transformative Learning Theory in Travel Settings
Mezirow’s (1991) transformative learning theory holds that lasting shifts in perspective happen when people encounter a “disorienting dilemma”—an experience that does not line up with their existing beliefs about how the world works—followed by critical reflection on that mismatch, open dialogue with others about the experience, and eventual action aligned with their new, revised worldviews. In travel settings, these disorienting dilemmas often look like cross-cultural encounters that challenge taken-for-granted assumptions, unvarnished exposure to ecosystem damage, or deep, immersive engagement with communities whose relationships to the land are fundamentally different from the dominant Western or urban frameworks most travelers bring with them (Coghlan & Weiler, 2018).

Superficial travel experiences often just reinforce what people already believe—for instance, framing nature as a playground for human recreation, separate from the communities that have stewarded it for generations. Transformative travel, by contrast, creates what Pritchard et al. (2011) term “memorable legacy effects”: shifts in how people think, feel, and act that can persist for years after a trip ends.

 2.2 Place Attachment and Pro-Environmental Behavior
Place attachment describes the emotional and functional bonds people build with a specific geographic place, usually split into two connected dimensions: place dependence, or how well a place supports a person’s specific goals or activities, and place identity, or the degree to which a place becomes woven into a person’s sense of self (Williams & Roggenbuck, 1989). A large body of empirical work connects strong place attachment to higher rates of pro-environmental behavior, for the simple reason that people are motivated to protect places that feel central to who they are (Halpenny, 2010). That said, most place attachment research in tourism focuses on long-term residents or repeat visitors to a destination. We know far less about how short, immersive travel experiences can build lasting place bonds strong enough to drive action even after travelers return to their home communities hundreds or thousands of miles away (Ramkissoon et al., 2013).

 2.3 Community-Based Ecotourism as a Space for Transformation
Commercial ecotourism has faced widespread criticism for reproducing neocolonial power dynamics: it often extracts profit from Indigenous lands while giving local communities little say over how operations run, or access to long-term benefits (West & Carrier, 2004). Community-based ecotourism (CBET) models operate very differently: local communities hold full decision-making power, design their own itineraries, and keep the majority of tourism revenue. Research has repeatedly shown these models deliver more equitable outcomes for hosts and create more meaningful, reciprocal cross-cultural exchanges for visitors (Stronza et al., 2019). This study builds on existing CBET scholarship by exploring how community governance of travel itineraries shapes the transformative potential of the travel experience for both visitors and the hosts who welcome them.

---

 3. Study Context and Methods
 3.1 Site Context: Sanjiangyuan National Park and the Namse Village Cooperative
Established in 2021 as China’s first official national park, Sanjiangyuan spans 123,100 square kilometers across the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau, providing critical habitat for endangered species including the snow leopard (*Panthera uncia*), Tibetan antelope (*Pantholops hodgsonii*), and wild yak (*Bos mutus*). Eighty percent of the park’s land is managed by Indigenous Tibetan pastoralist communities, who have sustained traditional rotational grazing and conservation practices on the plateau for millennia (Yeh, 2013).

The Namse Village Community Cooperative, founded in 2018, runs small-scale ecotourism expeditions with a strict annual cap of 100 visitors. One hundred percent of tourism revenue flows directly to community conservation funds, snow leopard monitoring work, and herder livelihood support. The 2023 expedition at the heart of this study included 18 visitors—university researchers, conservation practitioners, and educators from across China—and 3 local trip coordinators, with 8 Tibetan herder guides leading every activity across the 14-day itinerary. Trip activities ranged from grazing land patrols and visits to community-run snow leopard monitoring stations to participation in the annual l

title: 白菜设施栽培关键技术
text:
Reflection on Key Techniques of Protected Chinese Cabbage Cultivation
After reading *Key Techniques of Protected Chinese Cabbage Cultivation*, I have developed a relatively systematic grasp of the standardized production framework for protected Chinese cabbage. Previously, I vaguely equated facility cultivation with "planting vegetables in a simple greenhouse", but this book corrected that misunderstanding completely. It clarifies that facility vegetable production is a precision agricultural technology system covering environmental dynamic regulation, targeted variety selection, whole-growth-cycle fine field management, and low-toxicity green pest control. By integrating front-line production experience with modern agricultural development concepts, the book has brought me a lot of practical inspiration for efficient, high-quality vegetable planting.

What impressed me most was the principle of matching variety selection to specific facility environments. Unlike open-field planting, protected cultivation has distinct microclimate features: generally weaker light intensity, higher relative humidity, and often a larger temperature gap between day and night. The book makes it clear that selecting varieties with low-temperature tolerance, weak-light adaptability, early bolting resistance, and targeted disease resistance is the core prerequisite for stable yield of protected Chinese cabbage. It also compares the adaptability differences of different Chinese cabbage types—including fully heading and semi-heading varieties—across different facility types, such as solar greenhouses and arched plastic tunnels. This helped me realize that there is no universally "superior variety" in actual production. Only when variety traits align with facility conditions, sowing time, and local market demand can the production potential of the facility be fully brought into play. For example, a high-yield open-field variety with high light demand is very likely to grow spindly and form loose leaf heads when planted in a poorly lit old greenhouse in late winter, no matter how much fertilizer is applied.

The refined environmental management measures running through the entire growth cycle also updated my understanding of facility cultivation. The book sets clear temperature and humidity regulation standards for each growth stage. After sowing, appropriately high bed temperature should be maintained to speed up neat seedling emergence. At the seedling stage, ventilation needs to be increased in time to prevent excessive growth caused by high temperature and humidity. At the heading stage, day and night temperatures should be regulated within a suitable range to promote leaf head compactness and dry matter accumulation. It also explains key points of light supplement, water-fertilizer integrated management for protected fields. In response to common production problems, such as diseases induced by long-term high humidity and secondary soil salinization caused by excessive chemical fertilizer application, the book proposes targeted solutions including under-film drip irrigation, high-ridge planting, and soil testing-based formula fertilization. These specific technical details embody the "precision" of protected agriculture: every environmental factor cannot be left entirely to natural conditions, and requires deliberate, scientifically based manual adjustment.

In terms of pest and disease control, the book consistently adheres to the green prevention and control concept, which fits the development direction of modern vegetable production closely. For major diseases and pests affecting protected Chinese cabbage, including downy mildew, soft rot, aphids, and diamondback moths, it builds a whole-chain prevention and control system. Before planting, thorough disinfection of facility space and pre-planting soil treatment should be completed. During the growing period, agricultural measures such as rational close planting and timed ventilation are adopted to reduce the occurrence base of pests and diseases. When damage occurs, physical control measures such as insect-proof nets and yellow sticky boards, as well as biological control agents, are given priority, while chemical pesticides are used in strict accordance with dosage and safety interval regulations. This set of methods can stabilize yield, and also effectively reduce pesticide residues, providing a feasible technical path for pollution-free green vegetable production.

The book also introduces key supporting techniques including strong seedling cultivation, rational crop rotation, and multi-cropping arrangement, which made me realize that protected Chinese cabbage cultivation is a highly interconnected systematic project. Every link, from seedling raising to field planting, from plant adjustment to timely harvesting, is closely linked. Negligence in any single link may affect final yield and commercial quality. For instance, if seedlings are overgrown before transplanting, subsequent root recovery will be slow, and the probability of leaf head deformity will rise significantly. In particular, the annual planting arrangement model designed according to the thermal insulation performance of different greenhouses greatly improves the utilization efficiency of facility space and land, and stabilizes the annual income of growers. This reflects the unique value of facility agriculture in balancing off-season vegetable supply.

After reading the book, I have not only mastered the core technical points of protected Chinese cabbage cultivation, but also felt the pragmatic spirit of agricultural technology research. All the techniques summarized in the book are derived from long-term production practice, and can directly guide front-line planting, with strong pertinence and operability. At the same time, I also recognize that with the continuous development of facility agriculture, new technologies such as intelligent environmental monitoring and soilless substrate cultivation need to be gradually integrated in the future, to further improve the intensification and standardization level of Chinese cabbage planting. Of course, these new technologies cannot be applied mechanically; they still need to be adjusted according to local facility conditions and growers' actual technical level.

Overall, this book is a practical technical guide with both solid theoretical support and strong practical value. It makes me understand that high-quality facility vegetable cultivation depends on scientific, data-based management rather than scattered empirical guesswork. In future study and practical training, I will apply these key techniques, continue to explore and optimize suitable cultivation models, and contribute my part to the high-quality development of the facility vegetable industry.

title: 收割的季节
text:
Harvest Season
The first thing that sticks in my throat when I walk into my grandma’s yard in mid-October isn’t the smell of chaff or sunbaked dirt, it’s the fine, scratchy chaff dust that sticks to the sweat on my upper lip. I drove three hours from the city yesterday, forgot to pack work gloves, and the blister on the pad of my right thumb already popped when I was yanking dried corn stalks out of the west patch an hour after I got here. Grandma didn’t say I told you so. She just spat on a crumpled piece of last year’s lunar calendar, pressed it to the raw spot, and handed me a chipped enamel mug of chrysanthemum tea that had three dead gnats floating on the surface. I fished them out with a corn silk and drank it anyway. It tasted like burnt sugar and rain that fell three days ago.

We don’t use a combine for the half-acre patch behind the pigsty. The path between the rows is too narrow, rutted out from the summer flash flood that washed out half the sweet potato vines back in July, and anyway Grandma says the machine wastes too many kernels that get stuck in the cobs when it thrashes too fast. Last year the neighbor across the valley hired a combine, and we spent two evenings gleaning 27 pounds of leftover corn from his field, enough to feed the three laying hens through December and make a big pot of corn congee for the village old folks’ lunch at the end of the month. This year our corn is a little stunted, because I forgot to come up to help weed when Grandma called in mid-August, I was stuck finishing a work project that didn’t even matter in the end, the client pulled the account two weeks later. I didn’t tell her that. She just pointed to the shorter stalks when we started yesterday and said the dry spell hit harder down this end, no harm done, the cobs are still sweet if you boil them long enough.

My cousin showed up at noon today on his beat-up electric scooter, the one with the broken kickstand that he has to prop against a tree every time he stops. He brought a bag of cheap orange popsicles from the town convenience store, the kind that melt down your wrist before you can take three bites, and his 7-year-old daughter Xiao Man, who immediately ran into the soybean patch at the edge of the field and came back with her socks caked in burrs and a live cricket in her closed fist. She wanted to keep it in a mason jar as a pet, but Grandma told her crickets eat stored grain, so she let it go by the chicken coop, and spent the next hour chasing one of the hens that got out and pecked a hole in a ripe persimmon that fell off the tree by the kitchen door. The persimmon oozed golden, sticky pulp all over the dirt, and the hen ran off with half of it stuck to her beak, leaving a trail of persimmon smudges on the concrete path. We all laughed so hard Cousin dropped his popsicle in the dirt. He didn’t bother picking it up, just wiped his sticky hand on his work pants and grabbed a corn cob, started peeling back the husk to check for worms.

We found three nestfuls of baby field mice in the corn rows today, pink and blind, curled up in beds of chewed corn silk. Xiao Man wanted to bring them inside and raise them, but Grandma said their mom would come back for them if we left them be, so we carefully moved the stalk clumps they were nested in to the edge of the woods, away from where we’d be stepping. Last year we killed a snake that was hiding in the sweet potato vines, and Grandma made us bury it under the peach tree, said even the things that steal eggs have a place out here, you don’t kill something just because it’s eating the same food you are. We found 17 worm-eaten cobs by three o’clock, the kind with the fat white corn worms curled in the kernels, and we tossed those to the pigs, who grunted and snuffled and fought over them like they were the best thing they’d tasted all month. The pigs are getting slaughtered next month, for the winter sausage, but none of us talked about that. We just tossed the cobs over the fence and watched them root around in the mud, their tails flicking at the flies.

My back aches so bad by four o’clock I have to sit down on a split log by the field edge, and my forearms are crisscrossed with tiny cuts from the sharp corn leaves, the kind that don’t bleed right away, just sting when you sweat on them. Grandma sat down next to me, pulled a crumpled pack of hard candies out of her pocket, the plum flavored ones that stick to your fillings, and gave me two. She pointed to the chestnut tree up the hill, said the burrs are starting to split open, we can go pick them tomorrow if we finish the corn today, if the wind doesn’t pick up and blow them all down into the thorn bushes. I nodded, but I was watching a group of sparrows dart into the uncut part of the corn, pecking at the exposed kernels, fattening themselves up for the cold. A little while ago Xiao Man came running over, holding a dandelion that had gone to fluff, and blew all the seeds right into my face. Some of them stuck to my chapped lips, and I spit them out, and she cackled so hard she tripped over a corn stalk and landed in a pile of dried husks. She didn’t cry. She just rolled around in the husks, throwing handfuls up in the air, and yelled that it was snowing corn.

Cousin yelled from the other end of the row that he found a cob with red kernels, the kind Grandma says is good luck, you save it and hang it above the kitchen door for the whole year. He held it up over his head, and the sun hit it so the kernels glowed dark red, almost purple, and Xiao Man went sprinting over to see, tripping over a sweet potato vine halfway there and going down in the dirt again. This time she did have a little scrape on her knee, but she didn’t even notice, she was too busy reaching for the red cob. The air smells like wood smoke now, because the old man who lives alone two houses over started cooking his dinner, and I can hear the distant putter of a three-wheeler on the main road, carrying someone else’s harvest down to the town grain station. My phone died an hour ago, I left the charger in the car, and I don’t feel like walking back to get it. The blister on my thumb is throbbing a little, and there’s a corn silk stuck in my eyelash, and when I breathe in deep the dust makes me cough. Grandma stood up a minute ago, brushed the husk bits off her pants, said we’d better get back to it, if we get the last two rows done before dark she’ll fry up the green beans we picked yesterday with the cured pork from last year’s pig, the piece with the thick layer of fat that crisps up just right when you cook it hot. I pushed myself up off the log, brushed the dirt off my jeans, and grabbed the next corn stalk.

title: 小龙虾高效种植模式与经济效益分析
text:
Phased Implementation Checklist for High‑Efficiency Crayfish Farming Models and Economic Benefit Analysis

Here is a practical, field‑ready checklist for commercial red swamp crayfish (*Procambarus clarkii*) farming. It brings together high‑efficiency production models, including rice‑crayfish co‑cropping and aquatic grass‑crayfish systems, with economic tracking across the full crop cycle. The work is organized into four main phases, each with concrete steps, expected outputs, and KPIs.

---

Phase 1: Pre‑Launch Preparation and Site Baseline Assessment — Weeks 1–4  
*Goal: Confirm the site is suitable, select the farming model, and establish a clear cost‑benefit baseline.*

1.1 Site and Environmental Compliance Audit

- [ ] Measure the pond or paddy area on site. Record water depth—about 0.8–1.5 m for grow‑out and 0.3–0.5 m in broodstock trenches—and sludge depth, preferably no more than 10 cm.  
- [ ] Test the main water‑quality indicators: pH 7.0–8.5, dissolved oxygen at least 5 mg/L, ammonia nitrogen no more than 0.2 mg/L, and nitrite no more than 0.1 mg/L. Send samples to a local agricultural laboratory for confirmation.  
- [ ] Check that the water source is reliable and unpolluted, with enough capacity to exchange at least 30% of total pond water annually. Review flood and drought records from the past three years.  
- [ ] Confirm local aquaculture permits, environmental rules, and land‑use contracts. Finish all registration and filing work before construction begins.  
- [ ] *Output:* A site suitability report showing whether each indicator passes or fails.

1.2 Model Selection and Infrastructure Planning

Choose the model that best fits the local climate, land, and water resources:

- [ ] Rice‑crayfish co‑cropping, the most common high‑efficiency model. Set aside 8–10% of the paddy area for broodstock trenches, roughly 1.5 m deep and 2–3 m wide, while leaving enough ridge and field space for rice.  
- [ ] Intensive pond crayfish‑grass rotation. Lay out broodstock, nursery, and grow‑out ponds separately, using an area ratio around 1:2:7.  
- [ ] Complete the infrastructure design:
  - [ ] Install escape barriers around every plot: 60 cm high plastic film, with about 20 cm buried in the soil.  
  - [ ] Fit both inlets and outlets with double‑layer 40–60‑mesh screens to keep wild fish out and crayfish in.  
  - [ ] Provide about 1.5 kW of aeration for every 3–5 mu (0.2–0.33 ha) of grow‑out area, and keep backup pumps ready.  
- [ ] *Output:* A plot layout map and a bill of quantities for infrastructure.

1.3 Economic Baseline and Benefit Modeling

- [ ] Work out fixed start‑up costs: land rent, pond renovation, aerators, fencing, plant seed, and crayfish broodstock.  
- [ ] Estimate recurring annual costs for feed, aquatic grass seed, lime, probiotics, labor, water and electricity, and disease prevention.  
- [ ] Prepare forecasts under three scenarios:
  - Conservative: 100 kg/mu of crayfish, 70% survival, and a price 10% below the market average.  
  - Benchmark: 150 kg/mu, 80% survival, and the annual average market price.  
  - Premium: 200 kg/mu, 85% survival, and a 20% premium for large crayfish over 40 g each.  
- [ ] Calculate the break‑even point—aiming for no more than 80 kg/mu in the co‑cropping model—and set a 12‑month ROI target.  
- [ ] *Output:* A full‑cycle cost‑benefit spreadsheet.

---

Phase 2: Pre‑Stocking Preparation and Ecological Planting — Weeks 5–10  
*Goal: Establish a grass‑based ecological system, disinfect the ponds, and prepare healthy seed stock.*

2.1 Pond Disinfection and Bottom Improvement

- [ ] Drain the pond or paddy, remove excess sludge, and sun the bottom for 7–10 days until the surface cracks slightly.  
- [ ] Disinfect the whole pond with 75–100 kg/mu of quicklime mixed with water. This helps control wild fish, frogs, and crayfish pathogens.  
- [ ] Three days after disinfection, apply 50–100 kg/mu of fermented organic fertilizer to encourage zooplankton, an important natural food for juveniles.  
- [ ] Install anti‑escape and filtration facilities, then run a 24‑hour water‑filling test to look for leaks.

2.2 Aquatic Grass or Rice Planting — Core of the High‑Yield System

Planting needs to follow the season closely so that plants eventually cover 30–50% of the water surface.

For continuous pond farming:

- [ ] In late winter or early spring, when water temperature is around 5–10°C, plant *Elodea nuttallii* in rows spaced about 3 m × 4 m. Use roughly 15–20 kg of seed material per mu.  
- [ ] In late spring, interplant *Hydrilla verticillata*, which tolerates warmer water. Aim for roughly a 1:1 balance with Elodea to reduce the risk of summer grass decay.  
- [ ] Plant water peanut, *Alternanthera philoxeroides*, along pond edges as shelter for molting crayfish, but keep edge coverage below 20% so it does not take over.

For rice‑crayfish co‑cropping:

- [ ] Choose tall, flood‑tolerant, disease‑resistant rice varieties, such as a suitable local late japonica rice. Transplant around mid‑June using wide row spacing of about 30 cm × 40 cm.  
- [ ] Keep 85–90% of the plot planted with rice; the remaining trench and open‑water areas allow crayfish to move.  
- [ ] Do not use pyrethroid or organophosphorus pesticides, which are highly toxic to crayfish. Where possible, use biological control, such as trichogramma wasps or duck co‑farming.

After planting:

- [ ] Raise the water level gradually, apply root fertilizer to help grass or rice establish, and thin out excessive growth so total surface coverage stays below 50%.  
- [ ] *Output:* At least 85% survival of aquatic grass or rice, supported by photographs and sampling records.

2.3 Seed Selection and Stocking

- [ ] Source disease‑free broodstock or juveniles from certified farms:
  - Broodstock should weigh 30–40 g each, have intact appendages, and move actively. Use a male‑to‑female ratio of about 2:1 or 3:1.  
  - Juveniles should be 2–3 cm long, fairly uniform in size, and test negative for white spot syndrome virus, or WSSV.  
- [ ] Stocking timing and density:
  - Broodstock: 25–30 kg/mu in the trenches during August–September for overwintering reproduction.  
  - Juveniles: 8,000–10,000 individuals per mu in March–April, once water temperature stays above 15°C, for direct grow‑out.  
- [ ] Acclimate the animals before release. Float transport bags in pond water for about 20 minutes to equalize temperature, and dip juveniles in 3% salt water for 3–5 minutes to reduce parasites.  
- [ ] Record each stocking batch, quantity, size, supplier, and quarantine report.  
- [ ] *Output:* A stocking log and seed health inspection report.

---

Phase 3: Farming Management and Dynamic Economic Tracking — Months 3–8 / Full Growth Cycle  
*Goal: Keep survival and growth steady, manage costs as they occur, and improve harvest revenue.*

3.1 Daily Ecological and Feeding Management

Water quality:

- [ ] Check dissolved oxygen, pH, and water transparency twice a week. Transparency should remain around 30–40 cm. Run aerators around noon on sunny days and through the night during rainy or hot weather.  
- [ ] During high‑temperature periods, exchange 10–15% of pond water every 7–10 days. Apply EM bacteria or other probiotics every 15 days to help break down leftover feed.  
- [ ] Every 20 days, use 5–10 kg/mu of quicklime to add calcium and stabilize pH, which supports molting.

Feeding:

- [ ] Use formulated crayfish feed with 28–32% crude protein together with natural foods such as snails, soybeans, and corn. In April, stock 200–300 kg/mu of live snails as a continuing animal food source.  
- [ ] In spring, feed about 3–5% of total crayfish body weight each day; reduce this to 2–3% in summer. Adjust according to the amount left the next day, aiming for leftover feed below 5%.  
- [ ] Feed once at dusk, since crayfish feed mainly at night. Scatter feed evenly along shallow edges and among grass gaps.

Grass and predator control:

- [ ] In summer, trim back overgrown Elodea tops before they can decay. Remove dead grass promptly so water quality does not deteriorate.  
- [ ] Patrol ponds at dawn and dusk. Control birds, frogs, and wild fish, and inspect escape barriers after heavy rain.  
- [ ] *KPI:* Juvenile survival of at least 75%, a 7–10‑day molting interval, and no large‑scale disease outbreak.

3.2 Disease Prevention and Emergency Response

- [ ] Put prevention first. Disinfect feeding platforms with bleach each week and never use moldy feed.  
- [ ] Watch for WSSV, black gill disease, and enteritis. Isolate abnormal crayfish immediately; if mortality rises above 2% within 24 hours, send samples for testing.  
- [ ] Keep emergency materials on hand, including aerators, oxygen tablets, quicklime, and probiotics. Have a 48‑hour response plan for hypoxia, rainstorm flooding, and pesticide runoff.  
- [ ] Maintain complete medication records and follow local withdrawal periods strictly. As a rule, stop treatments at least 21 days before harvest.

3.3 Staged Harvest and Revenue Optimization

- [ ] Starting in May–June, use baited cage nets with mesh sizes suited to the target market. Harvest rotationally: take crayfish over about 35 g and leave smaller animals to continue growing.  
- [ ] Leave cages out overnight for 8–12 hours rather than too long, because extended confinement causes injury. Grade the catch into large, medium, and small sizes so it can be sold at different price points.  
- [ ] Plan sales around market demand: sell about 60% of the stock during the May–June peak consumption season,

title: 麦田里的夏天
text:
Summer in the Wheat Fields: Ecological Resilience, Agrarian Cultural Memory, and Rural Vitalization in the North China Plain
[Your Full Name]
[Department of Humanities/School of Agriculture, Your Institution]
[Course, e.g., ENGL 325: Literature and Rural Studies / AGEC 410: Sustainable Agricultural Systems]
[Submission Date]
Word count: 7,242

Abstract
The summer wheat growing season on the North China Plain—you know, the region that grows 60% of China’s entire winter wheat crop—isn’t just another agricultural production cycle. It’s this messy, living, constantly shifting tangle of ecological processes, intergenerational stories and memory, and all the messy, on-the-ground changes playing out in rural areas right now. Most existing work on NCP wheat systems fixates almost entirely on crop yields and how farmers are adapting to climate change, right? And when cultural studies scholars write about rural China, a lot of the time they frame agrarian life as something that’s slowly dying off as cities expand. I wanted to push back against both those gaps here, drawing on 18 months of ethnographic work I did in three wheat-farming villages in Henan, close readings of 20th century rural writing about wheat summers, and five years of household survey data tracking farming livelihoods in the area. Working with theories of social-ecological resilience and collective memory, I argue that those summer weeks in the wheat fields act as a sort of “living anchor” for rural communities: they keep alive the ecological feedback loops that supported low-input farming in the region for thousands of years, hold all those cross-generational memories of hard work, scarcity, and neighbors helping each other out, and give a concrete cultural and material base for rural vitalization plans that don’t fall into the old trap of top-down, one-size-fits-all development. What I found is that the recent shifts—combine harvesters taking over most of the cutting, new agro-tourism projects around the harvest—haven’t wiped out what wheat summers mean to people. They’ve just reshaped the social practices around them, creating new frictions between the push to get as much grain as possible out of the fields, and people’s desire to hold onto the cultural threads tied to the season. I hope this work adds something both to agrarian studies and rural policy, by making the case that those rooted, seasonal, on-the-ground experiences are a really important thing to center if we want to actually understand what sustainable rural futures might look like.
Keywords: wheat summer; North China Plain; agrarian culture; social-ecological resilience; rural vitalization; collective memory

1. Introduction
Every year in late May, that dry, warm xiaoman wind—you know, the one that comes when the grain is just starting to bud—blows across the NCP, and all 14 million hectares of winter wheat spread across Henan, Shandong, Hebei fade from that soft pale green to a deep, burnished gold. For the 120 million people living in rural villages across the region, that shift means mangzhong, “grain in ear,” is here: that tight two-week summer harvest window that’s structured every part of agrarian life here for more than 3,000 years. For most of the 20th century, wheat summer was all hands on deck, brutal, collective, nonstop work. Schools let out for “wheat harvest holiday,” city workers got sent down to villages to help bring the crop in, families worked from before sunup to long after dark cutting, threshing, winnowing, racing to get every last head of grain in before the summer monsoons hit and rotted everything standing in the fields.
Now? Combines roll north up the national highways every year in this coordinated, almost chaotic “harvest fleet,” finishing in days what used to take weeks of backbreaking labor. A lot of younger villagers come back from coastal factory and service jobs for two or three days tops to help their families out, then turn right around to head back to the city. More and more villages are putting on “wheat harvest festivals” to draw day-trippers out from nearby cities. But if you read popular media or even a lot of scholarship, people frame all these changes as proof that traditional agrarian life is dead. Nostalgic news pieces bemoan the loss of all the old manual labor traditions, policy reports treat wheat summer like a purely logistical problem to solve, all about maximizing grain output, with almost no attention to what the season means socially or culturally for the people who live there.
I had three connected questions going into this project, really. First: how do the ecological processes playing out in the wheat fields over the summer shape, and get shaped by, the resilience practices communities have used for generations? Second: how are those wheat summers held in collective memory, and how are those memories shifting now that so much of the work is mechanized, and so many people leave the villages for work for most of the year? Third: how can the cultural and material legacy of wheat summer support fairer, more sustainable rural vitalization, instead of getting pushed to the side or turned into a hollow commodity no one who lives there recognizes?
To work through those questions, I drew on 18 months of ethnographic fieldwork between 2021 and 2023 in three villages in eastern Henan. There’s Xizhuang, where 90% of the harvest is mechanized and a huge share of the working-age population has migrated out for jobs; Dongzhuang, which is running a pilot for organic wheat farming and agro-tourism; and Beizhuang, where 30% of households still do at least some manual harvesting for high-value heritage wheat varieties they grow. I did 62 semi-structured interviews total, with farmers ranging from 22 to 87 years old, village cadres, people running agricultural cooperatives, and migrant workers who came back for the harvest. I also spent time just being there: helping with harvest work where I could, sitting in on village rituals and cooperative meetings, all the standard participant observation stuff. I rounded out that ethnographic work with analysis of literary depictions of wheat summers from writers like Liu Shaotang, Yan Lianke, and bi Liao, plus five years of household livelihood survey data collected by the Henan Agricultural University Rural Observatory.
I’ve split the rest of the paper into five sections. Right after this intro, Section 2 lays out the theoretical framework I’m using, bringing together social-ecological resilience and collective memory theory, and situates this work against existing scholarship on NCP agriculture and rural cultural change. Section 3 digs into the ecological dynamics of wheat summer, tracing how the old low-input farming practices co-evolved with the region’s climate to build really resilient food systems, and how current climate change and widespread mechanization are shifting those dynamics now. Section 4 looks at wheat summer as a site of collective memory, tracking stories of scarcity, mutual aid, intergenerational connection across three generations of farmers, and unpacking the tensions between nostalgic ideas of the past and people’s actual lived experiences. Section 5 turns to the present, looking at how people are mobilizing the cultural capital tied to wheat summer for rural vitalization work, and pointing out the real risks of commodification and erasure that come with that. The conclusion makes the case that centering those rooted, seasonal experiences of wheat summer points to a way of doing rural development that respects both ecological limits and cultural continuity, instead of treating rural communities like either dusty relics of the past or empty blank slates for top-down policy interventions.

2. Literature Review and Theoretical Framework
Honestly, scholarship on NCP wheat systems has always felt really siloed to me—agronomists over here, cultural studies scholars over there, rural sociologists in another corner, barely talking to each other. The agronomic work on wheat summer is almost entirely focused on productivity and climate risk: there’s papers documenting rising heat stress during the grain-filling period (Liu et al., 2022), work on how efficient that interprovincial combine harvest fleet is (Zhang et al., 2021), studies on the water access problems winter wheat systems are facing as groundwater levels drop (Wang et al., 2020). That work is obviously critical for food security, don’t get me wrong, but most of it treats wheat fields like nothing more than production units, not social and cultural spaces. It reduces the whole summer harvest to a set of technical problems to tweak and optimize, no people involved except as variables in a yield model.
Cultural studies work on rural China, on the other hand, looks at depictions of wheat and agrarian life in literature and film, a lot of the time framing wheat fields as a symbol of national identity and roots (Cai, 2016). For example, scholarship on Yan Lianke’s novels points out how wheat harvests act as a backdrop for stories of suffering and resilience in Henan’s rural communities (Wang, 2019), while work on 1950s and 60s propaganda traces how wheat summer was framed as a site of socialist collective labor and national building (Schmalzer, 2016). The problem with a lot of that work, though, is that it relies entirely on textual analysis, no time spent actually talking to people in villages on the ground. A lot of it also frames contemporary changes to harvest practices as a straight, linear loss of tradition, without accounting for how communities actively reshape what those traditions mean as life changes around them.
Rural sociology work on NCP villages has documented really thoroughly how outmigration, mechanization, land transfer are reshaping village life (Ye, 2018; He, 2020), but that work rarely centers seasonal experience as a core thing worth analyzing. People have studied how migrant workers come home for big family events like Spring Festival, sure, but the annual summer wheat harvest is barely written about as a site of social connection and identity formation, even though it’s the second-biggest annual return migration event in the whole region.
