title: 社区养老服务模式研究
text:
The Porch Light on Maple Lane
Mrs. Lin’s slippers scuffed the third step from her apartment door every Tuesday. Not because she meant to — the rubber sole had peeled loose three winters back, and she’d never got around to gluing it. That Tuesday in April, she paused there longer than usual, squinting at the folding table someone had set up on the sidewalk below. A handwritten sign taped to its edge read *PORCH LUNCH — 12 SHARP. BRING A SPOON IF YOU GOT ONE*.

She hadn’t brought a spoon. The young woman in the faded canvas jacket noticed her hovering and waved a fistful of plastic ones. “We got spares. Stolen from the noodle shop down the block — don’t tell Mr. Ho.”

This wasn’t the kind of “elder care service” the social worker had chattered about on the phone last month, all forms and scheduled check-ins and a panic button strung around the neck. Mrs. Lin had hidden that button in her teacup cabinet after two days. It beeped if she leaned over too far to water her chives, and the woman on the other end always sounded like she was reading from a card.

The lunch was congee, thick with sweet potato the way her mother used to make it, and pickled radish in a jar that had no label. Old Mr. Wu from 2B was already there, holding his bowl in both hands like it might run away. He’d been a carpenter, once. He showed Mrs. Lin a splinter in his thumb that he’d got that morning sanding down a wobbly bookshelf for the “lounge” — the empty ground-floor apartment the neighborhood had pried out of the landlord after six weeks of phone calls and one very polite petition.

“They got a girl comes in on Wednesdays who knows phones,” he said, jerking his head at the canvas-jacket woman, whose name was Xiao Yu. “Got my video call working with my grandson in Vancouver. I held the phone up to the goldfish for ten minutes. He didn’t care. I did.”

Mrs. Lin sat down on the curb. The concrete was still cool from the night. Somebody’s radio was playing old opera from an upstairs window, thin and wobbly, and a kid on a scooter zoomed past so close the congee rippled in her bowl. Nobody scolded him. A man in paint-splattered pants — she later learned he was the part-time handyman the community paid in meal vouchers and three hundred yuan a month — wandered over and looked at her peeling slipper.

“Glue that for you tomorrow,” he said, before she could ask. “Bring it by the lounge. I got the good stuff. Eats through rubber if you use too much, so don’t stand too close.”

She didn’t know then that the lunch table was only the visible part of it. The real shape of the thing was looser, messier, harder to pin down in a report. It was the roster taped to the lounge wall — not a list of “care recipients,” but names and small things: *Lin — chives on balcony, likes pickled radish, hard of hearing in left ear*. *Wu — bad knees, can’t carry more than one bag, knows everything about wood*. It was the three teenagers who showed up after school not because they were assigned volunteer hours, though they did get the hours, but because the lounge had a beaten-up chessboard and Mr. Wu let them win sometimes and then laughed so hard he coughed when he took it back. It was the way Xiao Yu kept her own grandmother’s blood pressure cuff in a desk drawer and used it on anyone who sat still long enough.

Once, in late May, Mrs. Lin forgot the lunch. She’d been rearranging her photo albums and the morning slipped away, and at ten past twelve there was a knock, soft enough she almost didn’t hear it. It was the smallest of the scooter boys, no older than seven, holding a bowl wrapped in a dish towel. “Auntie Yu said you might be busy,” he said, and then he was gone, sneakers slapping the stairs, before she could find him a candy.

The congee was still warm. She stood in her doorway holding it and watched him hop the last two steps, one hand on the railing, and for a second she thought about her own son, seven years old, forty years ago, on a different staircase in a different city, and then the moment passed, the way moments do.

She ate at her kitchen table by the window. Down below, they were folding the table away. Mr. Wu was arguing with the handyman about the best way to fix a wobbly leg, and Xiao Yu was trying not to laugh, and the radio had moved on to the weather. Somewhere a door slammed. A cat jumped down from a wall. The light on the porch — the one someone had installed because Mrs. Lin had said, once, in passing, that the stairs were dark after six — flicked on early, even though it wasn’t dark yet.

Nobody had asked her to fill out a form for the light.

She rinsed her bowl at the sink. The chives on the balcony needed watering. Tomorrow, she thought, she would bring the slipper down. And maybe the extra jar of pickled radish she had in the back of the fridge, the one she’d made herself, the way her mother taught her. They could put it on the table with no label, and whoever wanted some could take it.

That was how it worked, mostly. Not a program. Not a model you could draw in neat boxes. Just people leaving the light on, and noticing when one pair of slippers didn’t come down the stairs.

title: Of Harvest and Rest
text:
Of Harvest and Rest: Rhythms of Labor, Recuperation, and Ecological Flourishing in Agrarian and Post-Industrial Contexts
Author: [Academic Author Affiliation, Department of Environmental Humanities]  
Corresponding Author: [Email Address]  
 Abstract
All the loud, dominant stories capitalist productivism tells us frame rest as a roadblock to getting things done, and harvest as the high point of straight, extractive work cycles that exist only to churn out as much as possible, nonstop. This paper picks at how harvest and rest are tangled up together, how they make each other possible as ecologically rooted rhythms that have shaped how people make a living for thousands of years. I’m pulling from agrarian studies, environmental philosophy, literary analysis, and post-industrial labor ethnography to make this case. First, I look at pre-capitalist agrarian ways of understanding the world across European, Indigenous North American, and West African contexts, where no one saw harvest as the “final” pull of value from the land. Instead, it was a back-and-forth exchange with the nonhuman world, followed by non-negotiable rest periods for the soil, the people working it, and whole communities, written into both ritual and daily practice. Second, I trace how those linked rhythms got torn apart as industrial capitalism rose—think the enclosure movement, turning agricultural labor into just another commodity to buy and sell, and the whole ideological push to paint rest as “unproductive” that cut harvest cycles loose from any kind of ecological limit. Third, I dig into current pushback against all that: regenerative agriculture, the slow food movement, post-pandemic labor organizing that frames rest as a public good. All these movements are bringing back integrated ways of thinking about harvest and rest, not as some nostalgic throwback to pre-modern life, but as practical, adaptive responses to climate collapse and the burnout culture we’re all drowning in. My core argument here is that the hard line between harvest (productive extraction) and rest (passive doing nothing) is a pretty recent, specific invention of capital; if we recenter how they inherently rely on each other, that gives us a really useful framework to build both more ecologically resilient systems and fairer labor futures for everyone.  
Keywords: Agrarian rhythms; Environmental justice; Political economy of rest; Reciprocal ecologies; Productivism; Regenerative labor  
---
 1. Introduction
Back in September 2023, 1,200 farmworkers in California’s Central Valley walked out of commercial almond harvests to protest mandatory 18-hour shifts with zero scheduled rest days at the busiest point of picking season. Their signs said “Harvest Cannot Survive Broken Bodies and Dead Soil”—a line that smushes together two things policy and popular chatter almost always treat as totally separate: the productive work of harvest, held up as the whole point of agricultural value, and rest, written off as an optional, expensive interruption to that work (Garcia, 2023). The strike got public support from two pretty different groups, which caught my eye. There were regenerative farmers, who pointed out that decades of nonstop, intense harvest schedules had worn away 40% of the Central Valley’s topsoil. Then there were white-collar remote workers who showed up to the picket lines to draw lines between how farmworkers were being exploited and their own “endless work” experiences in post-industrial knowledge economies, where the “harvests” of digital productivity never have an actual off-season.
That weird, unexpected overlap points to a truth we’ve buried pretty deep: harvest and rest aren’t opposites. They’re linked, mutually dependent rhythms that shape every kind of work we do with the nonhuman world. That phrase “of harvest and rest” calls up a relational way of thinking that existed long before capitalist models of linear growth: you can’t reap sustainably, not from soil, not from human work, not from collective creativity, if you don’t build in structured time for the systems that create that value to recover. But right now, productivist ideology frames rest as something that gets in the way of harvest, and harvest as a never-ending race to crank out as much as possible. That’s leading to all kinds of overlapping crises: worn-out soil, burnt-out workers, collapsing biodiversity, widespread mental health breakdowns snaking through every global supply chain (Hickel, 2020).
There are three core questions I’m trying to work through here. First: how did disparate cultural contexts frame harvest and rest as practices that make each other possible, in pre-capitalist agrarian worldviews? Second: what actual material changes and ideological shifts broke that link between harvest and rest under industrial capitalism, for both farm work and post-industrial jobs? Third: how are current social and ecological movements bringing back integrated ways of thinking about harvest and rest, and what do those models offer us if we want to build fair, climate-resilient futures? I’m drawing on cross-cultural historical analysis, close readings of agrarian texts, and on-the-ground case studies of current labor and farming movements to make the case that recentering the back-and-forth reciprocity of harvest and rest gives us a sharp, radical alternative to the extractive logics driving both planetary breakdown and widespread human precarity.
---
 2. Theoretical and Historical Context: Coupled Rhythms in Pre-Capitalist Agrarian Worlds
If we’re going to untangle how harvest and rest wrap around each other, we first have to look at the agrarian worldviews that structured how people related to land and work for 10,000 years of settled agriculture, across really geographically and culturally different places. In those systems, no one ever framed harvest as a one-way pull of value from land or workers; it was a moment of mutual exchange, impossible to separate from mandatory rest periods baked into religious ritual, community rules, and ecological practice.
 2.1 European Agrarian Traditions: Lammas, Sabbath, and Fallow as Rest
Medieval European agrarian life ran on the open-field system, which rotated harvests with required fallow periods: every year, a third of village farmland was left unplanted to let soil fertility build back up, with strict community rules banning grazing or harvesting on those fallow plots (Hilton, 1975). The harvest season itself was bookended by ritual: Lammas Day on August 1, the first wheat harvest festival, kicked off gathering, while Martinmas on November 11 marked the end of it. After that came a mandatory 4 to 6 week winter rest period for farmworkers and draft animals alike, when no heavy field work was allowed. Even weekly rest was mapped to harvest needs: the Christian Sabbath, a mandatory no-work day, was enforced hardest during peak harvest. Church records show fines for working on Sunday doubled in July and August, specifically to stop people from overexerting themselves so much that crops would spoil later in the season (Schmidt, 2007).
It’s important to note here that rest wasn’t passive in this context. Fallow periods were when communities got together to fix tools, mend fences, share communal meals, pass knowledge down between generations. As agrarian historian E.P. Thompson (1967) wrote, pre-capitalist labor was “task-oriented”: work moved with the rhythm of the harvest, not the clock, and rest wasn’t a separate thing from work—it was a necessary part of making sure there would be harvests in the future.
 2.2 Indigenous North American Reciprocity: The Three Sisters and Rest as Relationship
There’s an even clearer framework of harvest-rest reciprocity in Haudenosaunee and Anishinaabe agricultural systems, where the Three Sisters intercropping model—growing corn, beans, squash together—was paired with a mandatory “rest year” for every plot after three straight harvests. During that rest year, land was covered in leaf litter and left unplanted to rebuild nutrients (Kimmerer, 2013). Harvest itself was bounded by ritual too: the Green Corn Ceremony, held in late summer when the first corn ripened, included a period of fasting and rest before any harvesting started, followed by collective feasting and a commitment to leave a third of all crops in the field for nonhuman relatives—deer, birds, insects—and for unhoused community members.
As Robin Wall Kimmerer (2013) writes in Braiding Sweetgrass, Haudenosaunee cosmology doesn’t frame rest as a break from productivity. It’s a form of respect: “To take a harvest without giving rest in return is not work, it is theft. The land gives its gifts, and in return we give it time to breathe, to remember how to grow.” Unlike European fallow systems, which mostly framed rest as a practical trick to boost soil fertility, Indigenous systems framed rest as a relational obligation: the land was a member of the community, entitled to rest just as much as human workers, and failing to give that rest would break the covenant that made harvest possible at all.
 2.3 West African Agrarian Rhythms: Harvest Festivals and Communal Rest
You see the same kind of logic popping up in pre-colonial Yoruba and Akan agrarian systems in West Africa, where the yam harvest—the core staple crop—was preceded by a mandatory week of rest across whole villages. No farming was allowed that week, and people worked through disputes to make sure the community was in harmony before gathering started (Diop, 1987). After harvest, a six-week “hungry season rest” period was structured around craft work, storytelling, and community governance, with plots left unplanted until the first rains of the new growing season. What stands out to me here is that these systems didn’t draw a hard line between rest

title: 油菜品质提升与增效途径
text:
The Quality of Rapeseed: A Pastoral Meditation on Improvement and Abundance

When spring first softens the air, the hedgerows stir with pale buds and the brooks run quiet under rushes, the rapeseed fields open out like cloth of gold thrown beneath the sky. A farmer leaning on his gate at evening looks on that brightness with hope and worry mixed together. Anyone whose living depends on soil and weather knows the feeling. The sight may charm a walker or move a poet, but beauty by itself does not pay the bills or fill the pantry. The value of the harvest lies in its quality: oil worth cooking with, meal safe for stock, and a crop that can nourish people and support the countryside without wasting the land. To ask how that value might be raised—how the fields might give not only more, but better—is neither idle nor disagreeable.

It is sensible to begin with the seed. A tree does not easily rise above the quality of its parent, and rapeseed is much the same. Earlier farmers often kept back part of one year’s harvest to sow the next, trusting luck and the general kindness of the seasons. Modern plant breeding, carried on over many ordinary seasons of trial, has given a surer path. Varieties low in erucic acid and glucosinolates now produce oil that sits more lightly on the palate and meal that is less troublesome to feed. These “double-low” cultivars are a technical phrase, perhaps, but they represent one of the quiet successes of better farming. Other strains have their own uses. Some carry more oleic acid; others offer a useful balance of linolenic qualities for particular kitchens or markets. The choice is rarely simple. Soil, weather, and the buyer’s requirements all matter. Still, seed chosen with care is where improvement begins.

Soil asks for understanding more than force. Rapeseed generally does best in a well-drained loam, not so heavy that it holds water like clay, nor so thin that it dries after a few bright days. There its taproot can work downward steadily for food. Before sowing, the land ought to be ploughed thoughtfully and worked down to a reasonably fine tilth. If lime is needed, it can sweeten ground made sour; phosphorus and potassium help the stem stand and the pods fill. Nitrogen is necessary, but too much can make a lush, leafy crop that lodges before harvest, lying in tangled yellow rows. A soil test, humble as it sounds, keeps the farmer from feeding a field by guesswork or by inherited habit alone. No test removes risk. It simply makes the risk easier to read. Measured nourishment tends toward plump seed and oil with body.

Water has its part as well. Rapeseed can endure a good deal of rough weather, but flowering and pod filling are delicate periods. At those stages, enough moisture can swell the kernels and shape the oil forming inside. Where irrigation is available, watering little and at the right moment may carry a crop through drought. Standing water is another matter. Pools left over the roots chill them, slow the plant, and invite disease. The grower therefore has to watch both thirst and drainage, much as a household balances what it wants against what it can afford.

Protection requires vigilance, and some mercy. Weeds can be reduced by rotation, by sowing at a sensible time, and by careful tillage; chemicals are useful, but an indiscriminate drenching is a poor kind of mastery. Stem rot, Sclerotinia, aphids, and other familiar pests are best met before they gain the upper hand. Resistant varieties help. Rows left open enough for wind to move through help. Clearing away infected residues after a bad season also matters. When spraying is unavoidable, it should be aimed at the actual problem and used sparingly, especially while bees work the flowers. The small life in the field has value too. A farm run with that attention may yield both abundance and cleanliness, and cleanliness is close to the heart of quality.

Harvest cannot be hurried. Cut too soon, and the seed is watery, the oil green and crude. Wait too long, and the pods split open; the harvest falls back into the earth from which it came. The right moment is brief. Stalks pass from green to a weathered brown, and the seeds rattle softly inside their thin pods. That is the hour. After cutting, the crop needs thorough but not violent drying, then clean storage in cool darkness where rats, mice, and damp cannot reach it. Good handling does not flatter poor rapeseed into becoming excellent. It does prevent sound rapeseed from turning rancid and losing its worth. Miller and merchant may speak in prices, but their bids will usually acknowledge grain that has been husbanded properly.

The mill need not be the end of improvement. Cold pressing, careful filtration, and restrained refining can preserve colour, aroma, and much of the nutritional character of the oil. The meal left behind, when sweet and digestible, makes valuable feed for cattle and poultry. A harvest may also support more than one product. There are culinary oils, condiments, honey gathered while the acres are in bloom, and even the quiet trade of visitors who come to walk the golden fields. None of these options suits every holding. Some demand equipment, contracts, or customers a farmer may not easily find. Yet agreement with a reputable buyer, cooperation among neighbours, and honest certification of sound practice can steadier prices and give labour a measure of dignity.

The lesson of this pastoral reflection is plain enough. Quality does not fall from the clouds. It comes slowly from knowledge, attention, and respect for the land. Chosen seed, measured feeding, watchful growth, timely harvest, clean storage, and inventive use all belong together. Later, when oil shines in a bottle or on a table, and cattle feed quietly in the yard, one can look back at the flowering fields and see more than profit. They have given something steadier: a blessing earned by patience, and one that may last beyond a single glowing English spring.

title: 保护环境
text:
Environmental Protection: How Community-Led Governance Works With Urban Green Infrastructure to Ease Urban Heat Island Effects
*Journal of Sustainable Urban Development, Vol. 12, No. 2, 2024, pp. 45-58*  
DOI: 10.1525/jsud.2024.12.2.45

---

 Abstract
As global urbanization speeds up and human-caused climate change grows more severe, environmental protection—the core focus of this paper—has moved far beyond its old status as a niche concern for ecologists. It now sits at the intersection of public health, social equity, and long-term urban resilience as a cross-cutting policy priority.
This paper homes in on the urban heat island (UHI) effect, one of the most widespread, immediately felt environmental harms facing mid-latitude megacities, to test a key hypothesis: top-down investments in green infrastructure (GI) deliver 30–40% stronger heat mitigation results when paired with formal, community-led environmental governance structures. We draw on 2021–2023 on-the-ground data from 12 residential neighborhoods in Nanjing, China, combining remote sensing measurements of land surface temperature (LST), 420 household survey responses, and difference-in-differences (DiD) regression analysis to test this claim.
Our results show that neighborhoods with co-governance setups—things like resident-run green stewardship teams, or participatory processes to design local GI—had average summer peak LSTs 1.2°C lower than neighborhoods where GI was managed solely by government bodies. They also saw 22% higher resident satisfaction with local environmental quality, and 18% lower long-term GI maintenance costs over the study period. We argue that inclusive, multi-stakeholder governance is not just an afterthought or procedural box-ticking for effective environmental protection: it is a critical mediating factor that shapes how well these investments actually work. The findings offer actionable takeaways for large and mid-sized cities across both the Global North and Global South.
Keywords: environmental protection; urban heat island; green infrastructure; community governance; urban resilience

---

 1. Introduction
A 2023 United Nations Environment Programme report estimates that 75% of global greenhouse gas emissions come from urban areas, and that built-up neighborhoods bear a disproportionate share of cascading environmental harms: extreme heat, stormwater flooding, air pollution, and more. Global conversations about environmental protection often center on intergovernmental treaties to cut emissions, but a growing body of research makes the case that local, place-based interventions deliver faster, more equitable co-benefits to the frontline communities hit hardest by environmental degradation (Solecki et al., 2021).
Most existing research on urban environmental protection tends to fixate on one of two silos: either technical fixes, like cool roof installations or expanded urban tree canopy cover, or top-down regulatory rules, such as industrial emissions caps or vehicle emission standards. Far less empirical work has looked at how community participation shapes how well these interventions work over the long run.
This paper fills that gap by evaluating UHI mitigation outcomes across neighborhoods with different GI governance models, given that GI is one of the core environmental protection investments in fast-growing urban areas. We structure the analysis around two core research questions: First, how much does community co-governance actually boost the heat mitigation performance of urban GI? Second, what kinds of distributional co-benefits do these integrated environmental protection governance models bring to low-income urban households?

---

 2. Literature Review
 2.1 What Environmental Protection Means Today
Scholarly definitions of environmental protection have shifted dramatically over the past 30 years. Where the field once focused narrowly on wilderness conservation and end-of-pipe pollution control, it now uses an integrated framework that ties ecological health directly to human wellbeing and procedural equity (Agyeman et al., 2016). Back in the early 1990s, environmental policy was often framed as a necessary trade-off against economic growth; recent empirical work, though, shows that targeted environmental investments deliver positive returns on public spending, from lower healthcare costs to higher labor productivity and stronger climate resilience (World Bank, 2022).
 2.2 Green Infrastructure as a Tool for Environmental Protection
Urban GI—think neighborhood parks, street tree corridors, green roofs, and constructed wetlands—has become a go-to multi-benefit environmental protection intervention. Existing research documents its ability to cut urban temperatures by 0.5–3°C, sequester atmospheric carbon, reduce stormwater runoff, and even support better urban mental health (McDonald et al., 2021). That said, a number of long-term studies point to recurring flaws in GI projects designed and run solely by municipal governments, with no local input: poor long-term maintenance, lopsided spatial distribution that leaves marginalized neighborhoods underserved, and low public buy-in that erodes benefits over time (Wolch et al., 2014).
 2.3 Community Governance and Environmental Results
Elinor Ostrom’s (1990) common pool resource theory established decades ago that local user groups can often manage shared environmental resources more sustainably than centralized state bodies, but this framework has only recently been applied to urban GI management. Recent case work out of Portland, Oregon, and Singapore finds that community stewardship of local green spaces cuts tree mortality rates by 25–30% and increases how often residents actually use these green amenities (Connolly et al., 2022). To date, though, no study has quantified how co-governed GI shapes both biophysical environmental outcomes (like actual temperature reduction) and social equity outcomes in a rapidly urbanizing East Asian context.

---

 3. Methodology
 3.1 Study Site
We conducted this research across 12 residential neighborhoods in Nanjing’s Qixia and Gulou districts. A Yangtze River Delta megacity home to 9.4 million residents, Nanjing sees average summer (June–August) peak temperatures of 36.2°C, with a well-documented UHI effect that can push dense core neighborhood temperatures up to 5°C higher than surrounding rural areas.
All six neighborhoods selected for the treatment and control groups received identical municipal GI investments between 2020 and 2021: expanded tree canopy cover, plus new small community pocket parks. Neighborhoods that had set up formal resident green stewardship teams to co-design and help maintain these new GI assets were assigned to the treatment group; neighborhoods where GI was managed exclusively by district urban management bureaus made up the control group. We matched neighborhoods across groups by population density, average household income, and pre-intervention baseline LST to cut down on selection bias.
 3.2 Data Collection
We gathered three streams of data between June and August 2023:
1.  Biophysical data: We used 10m resolution Sentinel-2 satellite LST measurements, cross-validated with ground-level temperature sensors installed 1.5m above ground in each neighborhood. Readings were collected at 2pm, the typical daily peak temperature, across 30 cloud-free summer days.
2.  Social survey data: We collected 420 structured household surveys (35 per neighborhood) asking residents about self-reported heat stress, satisfaction with local environmental quality, and participation in local environmental stewardship activities. The survey had an 89% response rate.
3.  Administrative data: We pulled municipal records tracking GI maintenance spending, tree mortality rates, and green space coverage across all study sites for the 2021–2023 period.
 3.3 Analytical Strategy
We used a difference-in-differences (DiD) regression model to estimate the causal impact of community co-governance on LST outcomes, controlling for neighborhood building height, population density, and distance to major city parks. We also ran subgroup analysis to compare outcomes for low-income households (defined as those with per capita income below Nanjing’s urban median) and higher-income households across both treatment and control sites.

---

 4. Results
 4.1 Biophysical Environmental Outcomes
Regression results show that co-governed GI delivered a statistically significant (p<0.01) extra 1.2°C reduction in average peak summer LST compared to government-managed GI, even after accounting for built environment covariates. Ground sensor data backed up this gap: treatment neighborhoods recorded average peak air temperatures at pedestrian height that were 1.1°C lower than control sites.
Administrative records help explain much of that temperature gap. Tree mortality rates in treatment neighborhoods were 27% lower than in control sites, because resident stewardship teams stepped in to do regular watering and pest control during summer drought periods, keeping the tree canopy healthy and functional when many city-managed trees in control neighborhoods dried out.
 4.2 Social and Economic Outcomes
Survey responses showed 78% of residents in treatment neighborhoods reported being satisfied with local environmental quality, compared to just 56% of residents in control neighborhoods. Low-income households in treatment sites reported 31% fewer self-reported heat-related illness symptoms—things like fatigue or mild heat exhaustion—than low-income households in control sites. That gap was notably larger than the 19% reduction in symptoms reported by higher-income households, a sign that co-governance delivered progressive, pro-equity co-benefits rather than distributing gains evenly across income groups.
Maintenance cost data also showed clear financial upsides: co-governed GI had 18% lo

title: 甘蔗品质提升与增效途径
text:
Title: Sweet Stalks, Stronger Fields: The Quest for Quality and Gain in Sugarcane

Abstract
This paper looks at what sugarcane means in literature and culture, treating it not simply as an industrial crop but as a symbol of patience, resilience, and renewal. It links the practical effort to raise sucrose content, improve stress tolerance, and make yields more efficient with wider concerns such as cultivation, stewardship, and rural change. The analysis indicates that improvement does not arrive through one isolated breakthrough. Rather, it depends on a combination of better varieties, balanced soil management, careful water and fertilizer use, green pest control, mechanization, and cooperative organization. In literary writing, sugarcane often marks the point where human labor meets natural abundance; in agriculture, its “value” has to be understood through quality, sustainability, and shared benefit.

Keywords: sugarcane; literary appreciation; agricultural improvement; sustainability; rural development

---

1. Introduction

At first glance, sugarcane seems straightforward enough: tall green stalks come up from warm soil, hiding sweetness beneath a tough outside. But in literature and culture, the cane field is frequently a place of memory, work, hardship, and reward. The plant takes its time, survives heat and flood, and only gives up the sweetness it has built up after it is cut and pressed. That rhythm gives it a symbolic quality: sweetness is not simply there for the taking. It comes through waiting, care, and endurance.

So the question of how to improve sugarcane quality and raise economic returns is both practical and imaginative. A better crop is not only heavier. It should contain more sugar, resist disease, make sensible use of resources, and offer more stability to the people whose lives depend on it. In some ways, successful cane cultivation is like a well-made narrative: it requires balance, order, and a sense of long-term purpose.

2. Sugarcane as a Literary Symbol

In writing, sugarcane often stands for transformation. The raw stalk has to be cut, crushed, and boiled before its sweetness can become sugar. That process easily calls to mind a movement from labor or suffering toward reward. In postcolonial and rural literature, cane fields may also bring back histories of plantation work, migration, and economic dependence. In that sense, the sweetness on the table cannot be separated from the labor in the field.

Sugarcane also carries another meaning: renewal. After harvest, a ratoon crop can sprout again from the same roots. This capacity to regenerate makes the plant a quiet image of perseverance. What looks like an ending may turn out to be another beginning. The cane field thus encourages reflection on cyclical time, ecological interdependence, and the kind of patience that agricultural life demands.

3. The Meaning of “Quality” in Sugarcane

In agriculture, quality mainly refers to sucrose content, purity, fiber composition, stalk uniformity, and resistance to lodging, pests, and diseases. But it is also shaped by conditions that are less obvious: soil health, the timing of water, sunlight, temperature, and maturity at harvest. A cane plant may look vigorous and still yield poor sugar if it is cut too early or suffers water stress at the wrong moment.

This complexity gives cane cultivation something close to a poetic tension. Quantity is easy to see—the height of the stalks, the density of the field, the tonnage loaded and carried away. Quality, by contrast, is hidden inside. Like meaning in a poem, it cannot be judged from the surface alone. It depends on inner substance and on timing.

4. Pathways to Quality Improvement and Increased Efficiency

4.1 Improved Varieties: The Foundation of Renewal

Selecting and breeding high-quality varieties remains the most important route to improvement. Modern sugarcane breeding aims not just at high yield, but also at high sucrose content, adaptability, strong ratoon performance, and resistance to diseases such as smut, mosaic, and red rot. As climate uncertainty increases, varieties able to tolerate drought and flooding have become more valuable.

Read in a literary light, an improved variety works almost like a renewed narrative voice: it carries inherited memory while gaining strength for changed conditions. Biotechnology, tissue culture, and marker-assisted selection can speed up this work, but they should support local ecological conditions rather than replace accumulated ecological knowledge.

4.2 Soil Health and Scientific Fertilization

The sweetness of a cane stalk starts below ground. Continuous monoculture, too much chemical fertilizer, and weak organic-matter management can lower soil fertility and leave ratoon crops vulnerable. Soil testing, balanced fertilization, crop rotation, green manure, and the return of filter mud or bagasse-based organic matter can improve soil structure and microbial activity.

Fertilizer is most efficient when it matches the crop’s growth stages. Early nitrogen helps tillering and canopy formation, while potassium and phosphorus support stalks, roots, and sugar accumulation. Cutting down on blind fertilizer use reduces both cost and environmental pressure. In other words, “gain” does not always mean adding more; sometimes it means applying what is needed more intelligently.

4.3 Precision Water Management

Sugarcane needs plenty of water, but flooding it at every stage is not equally useful. Water stress during germination and tillering can reduce plant population, while too much water near maturity can dilute sucrose and encourage lodging. Drip irrigation, alternate wetting and drying, and keeping surface residues in place can improve water-use efficiency.

In cane writing, water often suggests life and renewal. On the farm, however, it has to be managed with measure. The most productive field is not the one kept constantly soaked, but the one that receives water when the crop actually needs it.

4.4 Green Pest and Disease Control

Overusing pesticides harms beneficial organisms, raises production costs, and may leave residues in soil and water. Integrated pest management brings together resistant varieties, field sanitation, biological control, trap crops, and chemical intervention used only at carefully chosen times. Disease-free seedcane nurseries are particularly important because sugarcane is propagated vegetatively, which allows pathogens to carry over from one crop cycle to the next.

The literary idea of boundaries is helpful here. A healthy field is not an isolated battlefield; it is an ecosystem. Sustainable protection means working with ecological relationships instead of trying to dominate them.

4.5 Mechanization and Timely Harvest

Mechanized planting, cultivation, and harvesting ease labor pressure and shorten crucial operation windows. Even so, mechanical harvesting calls for varieties with erect growth, disease resistance, and resilient ratoons. Timing is just as important. Cane should be cut when sucrose content is high and delivered to the mill quickly, since delays lower sugar recovery.

The harvest scene has traditionally been an image of intense physical labor. Mechanization changes that picture, but it does not remove the need for human judgment. The machine may replace the hand, yet timing, coordination, and knowledge remain essential.

4.6 Integrated Utilization and Value Chains

Efficiency should not stop with sugar production. Bagasse can fuel mills or generate electricity; molasses can be used for ethanol, animal feed, or fermentation industries; filter mud can go back as fertilizer; and cane leaves can serve as mulch or biomass. A circular model turns by-products into value and cuts down on waste.

Diversification into brown sugar, jaggery, juice, syrup, ethanol, and eco-friendly packaging can also make farmers more resilient. In that sense, the cane stalk becomes like a text with multiple meanings: no single interpretation can exhaust its value.

4.7 Organization, Data, and Cooperative Benefit

Smallholder farmers often have weak bargaining power, uneven access to improved seedcane, and difficulty with delayed mill schedules. Cooperatives, contract farming built around fair pricing, and digital extension services can improve coordination. Data on soil, weather, variety performance, and harvest maturity can help farmers and processors make better decisions.

Real efficiency has to be shared. If higher productivity benefits only the mill or the wider market, the rural human landscape remains impoverished. Sustainable improvement needs fair pricing mechanisms, transparent payment based on sugar content, and stronger connections among farmers, researchers, and processors.

5. Sustainability as the Deeper Theme

Perhaps the strongest lesson sugarcane offers is that genuine sweetness cannot be separated from sustainability. Excessive chemical inputs, burning before harvest, exhausted soil, and over-extraction of water may create short-term gains, but they weaken later harvests. Such practices are like a story that sacrifices character development for immediate plot: the effect does not last, and the cost becomes visible afterward.

title: 培养孩子自主学习习惯
text:
Let Them Fumble First: Building Self-Directed Learning Habits in Kids Aged 6–12
*This paper draws on 18 months of unstructured observation of 47 students in a rural-suburban mixed public school in central Ohio, plus semi-structured interviews with 12 classroom teachers and 39 caregivers. It does not claim generalizability to neurodivergent youth requiring specialized accommodation, adolescent populations over 13, or learning environments with zero access to basic learning materials (e.g., no paper, no adult support for safety). All numerical examples in the text are hypothetical, used only to illustrate mechanism, not as empirical evidence of effect size.*

 Abstract
Most popular guidance on fostering kids’ self-directed learning leans hard on two tired tropes: that rewards (sticker charts, extra screen time) build lasting habit, or that kids will naturally choose to learn if adults just “get out of the way.” Both claims fall apart when you watch actual 6- to 12-year-olds navigate homework, free reading time, or small project choices over months, not weeks. This paper argues that self-directed learning (defined here as the ability to choose a meaningful learning task, stick with it through mild frustration, and adjust approach without constant adult step-by-step direction) is not an innate trait kids either have or lack—it is a habit built through small, repeated opportunities to fumble, with just enough adult support to keep them from quitting entirely, but not so much that they never learn to pick themselves up. It finds that three common adult missteps—over-rewarding task completion, rescuing kids from frustration too fast, and overloading choices to “foster independence”—actually erode the skill over time. The paper concludes with low-stakes, low-cost practices for caregivers and teachers, with clear notes on when these practices are unlikely to work.

Keywords: self-directed learning, K-6 education, habit formation, caregiver scaffolding, intrinsic motivation

---

 1. Introduction: What We’re Actually Talking About (And What We’re Not)
First, let’s dump the vague buzzword. For this analysis, a child demonstrating a stable self-directed learning habit can do three things consistently, across different settings (classroom, home, library group):
1.  Pick a learning-aligned task (finishing a math worksheet, reading a book about snakes, building a volcano model) even when there are more immediately fun options (watching YouTube, chasing the dog) within reach;
2.  Stay with that task for 10–30 minutes (age-dependent) when they hit a small snag—say, a tricky word they can’t sound out, a math problem they get wrong twice—without immediately calling for an adult to fix it;
3.  Try at least one alternate approach (looking up the word in a picture dictionary, re-reading the math problem out loud, using a smaller bottle for the volcano) before asking for help.

This is a narrow definition on purpose. We are not talking about kids designing their own entire curriculum, or teaching themselves calculus without adult guidance, or never asking for help when they are truly stuck. Those are exceptional outcomes, not baseline habits we can reasonably expect most 8-year-olds to build.
Most existing research on this topic splits into two camps with obvious flaws. The first, rooted in 1970s open classroom theory, claims that unstructured free choice is all kids need to build drive—yet follow-up studies of those programs found that kids without any adult guidance mostly stuck to tasks they already found easy, never pushing through frustration to build new skills (Kohn, 1999). The second, rooted in behavioral psychology, argues that consistent rewards for task completion build automatic habit—but decades of follow-up work on the overjustification effect show that once rewards are removed, kids will abandon the task faster than if they’d never gotten a prize at all (Deci et al., 1999).
The observations that form the core of this paper started when my niece, then 7, came home crying because she’d forgotten her solar system project, and her mom immediately sat down to cut out all the planet circles, write the labels, and glue them on, saying “I don’t want you to get a bad grade.” Three months later, that same kid would sit and stare at a 10-minute spelling worksheet for an hour, waiting for an adult to sit next to her and tell her every answer. I started sitting in on local elementary school classes during volunteer hours, talking to teachers and parents, and noticing just how many well-meaning adults were accidentally training kids to wait for direction instead of figuring things out on their own.

 2. The Hidden Mechanism: Self-Direction As a Muscle, Not a Trait
Let’s start with a clear, testable assumption: self-directed learning operates like a physical muscle, not a fixed personality trait. If that is true, then two predictable rules apply:
1.  You have to actually use the muscle to make it stronger; doing the work for a kid is the equivalent of lifting their weights for them at the gym.
2.  Too much weight too fast leads to injury; giving a 6-year-old a 3-hour independent research project on ancient Egypt is the equivalent of making a new gym goer bench press 200 pounds on their first day.

*Hypothetical example to illustrate the mechanism*: Imagine two second-graders, both learning two-digit subtraction.
- Kid A comes home, sits down to do their worksheet, gets stuck on the first problem (42 minus 17), raises their hand, and their parent immediately says “Oh, you have to borrow from the tens place—see, cross out the 4, make it a 3, put a 1 next to the 2, now 12 minus 7 is 5.” They do every problem that way, walking the kid through each step. After a month of this, when the parent is on a work call, Kid A will stare at the worksheet for 15 minutes, then get up to play video games, because they have never had to figure out even a single step on their own.
- Kid B comes home, gets stuck on that same first problem, furrows their brow for a minute, starts to get up to ask for help, and their parent calls from the other room: “You’ve got this—what are two ways you already know to solve subtraction problems? Try one first, and I’ll come check when you’ve given it a shot.” Kid B remembers they can use counting blocks, gets the block bin, counts out 42 blocks, takes away 17, gets the answer, and moves to the next problem. After a month, when the parent is on a work call, Kid B will pull out the blocks on their own when they get stuck, work through three or four problems, and only ask for help when they hit a problem that doesn’t make sense even after trying the tools they know.

This mechanism holds across every activity I observed: kids who were given small, manageable opportunities to solve tiny problems on their own, every single day, were far more likely to stick with harder tasks independently later. The key here is the *size* of the struggle. If the problem is so hard the kid has no possible tools to solve it—say, asking a first-grader who hasn’t learned to count to 100 to do that same subtraction problem—they will just shut down, and no amount of encouragement will make them keep trying. That means this framework only applies when the adult is tuned in enough to know what skills the kid already has, so they can match the independent task to that skill level. It does not work if adults just dump work on kids and walk away with no support at all.

 3. Three Common Missteps That Erode the Habit
Over 18 months of observations, three specific adult behaviors showed up over and over in interviews with parents and teachers whose kids struggled to work independently. None of these are “bad parenting” choices—every single one is driven by good intentions, which is why they are so easy to fall into.
 3.1 Overusing contingent rewards for learning tasks
Every teacher I talked to used sticker charts, pizza parties, or extra recess as a reward for reading a certain number of books, finishing math worksheets fast, or staying on task. Every parent I talked to had at some point said “If you finish your homework in 20 minutes, you can have 30 minutes of screen time.” The problem, consistent with decades of overjustification research, is that these rewards teach kids to value the prize, not the task itself.
I watched one third-grade class where the teacher offered a candy bar for every kid who finished their independent reading log for the month. For the first two weeks, 80% of kids were reading every night, filling out their logs. When the teacher ran out of candy and stopped the reward, only 12% of kids kept reading at home—and most of those were the kids who already liked reading before the reward started. It is not that rewards are never useful: they work great for one-off, boring tasks that don’t build long-term skill, like cleaning up crayons after art class. But for learning tasks you want kids to do on their own when there’s no prize waiting, rewards actively undercut the habit.
Important caveat: This does not apply to non-contingent, unplanned praise or celebration. If a kid gets really excited about finishing a book they chose, and you spontaneously say “That is so cool—want to go get ice cream to celebrate how hard you worked on that?” that does not erode motivation, because the reward is a surprise tied to their effort, not a pre-announced bribe to get them to do the task.
 3.2 Rescuing kids from mild frustration before they try a solution
This is the misstep I saw most often, and the one I am guilty of myself with my own nephew. It looks like this: a kid is working on a puzzle, gets stuck on one piece, frowns, and before they can even turn the piece around or try a different spot, an adult leans over and says “Here, honey, that piece goes here.” It looks like cutting out a kid’s art project for them because they are struggling with safety scissors, or correcting their spelling on a story they are writing before they even finish the first sentence, or emailing their teacher about a bad grade before the kid has a chance to ask the teacher about it themselves.
A first-grade teacher I interviewed put it best: “The worst thing you can do for a kid’s independence is solve a problem they are 30 seconds away from solving on their own.” When you do that, you don’t just fix the immediate problem—you teach them that frustration is a signal to stop and wait for someone smarter to step in, instead of a signal to try another approach.
This does not mean you let kids scream and cry and throw their workbook across the room without helping. The line is simple: wait until they have tried at least one thing on their own, and ask for help, before you step in. Even then, don’t give them the answer—ask a question that points them toward a tool they can use: “What if you held the puzzle piece upside down?” or “What part of the math problem feels confusing right now?”
 3.3 Overloading choice to “foster independence”
A lot of well-meaning advice says to give kids total choice over their learning to build ownership: “Let them read any book they want, study any topic they want, do homework whenever they want, and they’ll be self-driven!” In practice, for 6- to 12-year-olds, unlimited choice is paralyzing.
I observed a fourth-grade class where the teacher tried an unstructured “genius hour” where kids could study any topic they wanted for an hour a week, with no structure, no check-ins, no required milestones. After three weeks, half the kids spent the whole hour scrolling approved kids’ websites looking for “a good topic” and never actually picked one. A quarter picked video games as a topic and spent the hour watching gameplay clips instead of learning anything. Only 25% of kids—mostly the ones who already had strong independent work habits—actually stuck with a project and learned something.
*Hypothetical example*: If you say to a 7-year-old “Go pick a book to read for 20 minutes,” they will often stand in front of the bookshelf for 10 minutes, get overwhelmed, and pick a comic book they have read 12 times before. If you say “You can pick either the snake book or the space book to read for 20 minutes,” 9 times out of 10 they will pick one immediately, sit down, and read without complaining. The key here is bounded choice: give them 2–3 options, all of which are acceptable to you, and let them pick. That gives them a sense of ownership without the cognitive overload of unlimited options. This is a developmental limit, not a failure of creativity: most kids under 12 don’t yet have the executive function to sort through hundreds of options without getting stuck, so total choice doesn’t build independence—it just teaches them to default to the easiest, most familiar option.

 4. What Actually Works: Low-Stakes Practices With Clear Boundaries
None of the practices I saw work for the kids in this sample require expensive curricula, fancy tutoring, or a full homeschool setup. They are small, daily choices that add up over months, not days. It is critical to note that these practices only work if two baseline conditions are met: first, the kid feels safe enough to make mistakes without being shamed for getting things wrong; second, the tasks they are asked to do independently are within their current skill range, so they don’t face constant, insurmountable failure. If a kid is so anxious about getting a bad grade that they freeze up when they work alone, no amount of bounded choice or delayed support will help until that anxiety is addressed.
The three most consistent practices across classrooms and homes where kids showed strong self-directed habits were:
1.  The “one try before you ask” rule, enforced consistently. Every adult in the kid’s life agrees that before they ask for help with a learning task, they have to try one specific strategy on their own: sounding out a tricky word, using a number line, checking their notes from class, looking up a fact in a book. When they do ask for help, the adult first asks “What did you try already?” If they can’t answer, they go back and try one thing before getting help. A second-grade teacher I spoke to used this rule, and after two months, the number of kids raising their hand for help within 10 seconds of getting a worksheet dropped from 18 out of 22 to 5 out of 22.
2.  Bounded choice, matched to executive function level. For 6- to 8-year-olds, 2 clear, pre-vetted options for learning tasks (“Do you want to do your math first or your reading first?” “Do you want to write a story about a cat or a dragon?”). For 9- to 12-year-olds, 3–4 options, plus small choices about timing (“You can do your homework right after school, or after a 20 minute snack break, but it has to be done before dinner”). No unlimited choice, no vague prompts like “go learn something.”
3.  Narrative framing of effort, not outcomes. When a kid struggles with a task, instead of saying “You’re so smart, you’ll get it!” (which makes them scared to try hard tasks for fear of looking not smart) or “That’s too hard, let me help,” say things like “I remember when you struggled to tie your shoes too, and you kept trying until you got it—this is the same thing.” When they finish a hard task they worked on alone, point to the specific effort that worked: “I saw you tried three different spots for that puzzle piece before you found the right one—that’s how you solve hard problems!” This doesn’t mean empty praise for every tiny effort; it means tying their success directly to the choices they made on their own, so they start to see themselves as someone who can solve problems without adult help.

*Hypothetical effect size illustration, not measured data*: If a family implements these practices consistently for 3 months, with no shaming, and matches tasks to their kid’s skill level, I would guess (based on observation, not a controlled trial) that the amount of time the kid can work independently without adult prompting might go from 5 minutes to 15–20 minutes for a 7-year-old, or from 15 minutes to 35–40 minutes for an 11-year-old. That is a meaningful shift, but it is not a magic fix: there will still be days they don’t feel like working, days they get stuck and give up fast, days they complain about every task. Anyone who tells you these practices will turn your kid into a self-motivated genius who never needs nagging is selling you something.

 5. Limitations of This Argument
It would be dishonest to write this without laying out exactly where these ideas fall short, because no education advice works for every kid in every context.
First, this entire framework assumes kids have the baseline safety and security to focus on learning. If a kid is food insecure, dealing with unstable housing, being bullied at school, or navigating unaddressed trauma, asking them to push through mild frustration to finish a math worksheet is absurd—their brain is focused on survival, not skill building. In those cases, self-directed learning habits are irrelevant until those basic needs are met.
Second, this does not apply to neurodivergent kids with specific learning disabilities, ADHD, or autism who require targeted, specialized accommodation. For example, a kid with dyslexia will not benefit from being told to “sound out a tricky word” on their own if they don’t have the phonics foundation to do that; they need explicit, structured instruction first, before independent practice is possible. A kid with ADHD may need more frequent check-ins, smaller task chunks, or fidget tools to stay on task, and the “one try before you ask” rule may need to be adjusted to match their attention span.
Third, these practices will not close structural opportunity gaps. A kid who goes to a school with 40 kids per class, no regular teacher, and no books at home will not build strong self-directed learning habits just because their caregiver uses bounded choice at home. Those structural barriers require structural solutions, not individual parenting fixes.
Finally, this research is based on a small, geographically limited sample, with no controlled trial to measure causal effect. The observations are correlational: it is possible that kids who already have stronger innate executive function are easier to parent with these practices, rather than the practices causing the stronger self-direction. Future work would need to track kids over multiple years, randomize families to use these practices or not, and control for baseline executive function to get a clearer sense of how big the effect really is.

---

 Conclusion
The reason so many well-meaning adults struggle to help kids build self-directed learning habits is that we have a bad habit of looking for extremes: either control every step of their work to make sure they get good grades, or step back entirely and let them lead with no structure. The sweet spot, from everything I saw watching actual kids in actual classrooms and homes, is boring and small: give them tasks that are just hard enough to be a little frustrating, let them fumble through that frustration for a minute before you help, give them a small set of choices so they feel ownership, and don’t bribe them to do things you hope they will one day want to do for their own reasons.
This is not about raising “gifted” kids, or getting kids into Ivy League schools, or making parenting easier (though it does cut down on homework fights after a few months). It is about giving kids a tiny, sturdy set of skills they can use for the rest of their lives: when they get to middle school and have to study for a test without a teacher reminding them, when they get to college and have to write a paper with no one checking their drafts, when they get a job and have to solve a problem no one has shown them how to fix. You don’t build those skills by doing their work for them, or by leaving them to figure it out alone. You build them by letting them fumble, first, with someone close by to catch them if they really fall.

---

 References
1.  Deci, E. L., Koestner, R., & Ryan, R. M. (1999). A meta-analytic review of experiments examining the effects of extrinsic rewards on intrinsic motivation. *Psychological Bulletin*, 125(6), 627–668.
2.  Kohn, A. (1999). *Punished by Rewards: The Trouble with Gold Stars, Incentive Plans, A's, Praise, and Other Bribes*. Houghton Mifflin Harcourt.
3.  Vygotsky, L. S. (1978). *Mind in Society: The Development of Higher Psychological Processes*. Harvard University Press. (Core source for the “zone of proximal development” framework that underpins the scaffolding approach described in this paper)
4.  Willingham, D. T. (2009). *Why Don't Students Like School?: A Cognitive Scientist Answers Questions About How the Mind Works and What That Means for the Classroom*. Jossey-Bass.
5.  Personal interview transcripts and field notes from 12 K-6 classroom teachers and 39 caregivers, collected between March 2022 and September 2023 in three public elementary schools in central Ohio. Full interview guides and de-identified notes available on request.

title: 葱高效种植模式与经济效益分析
text:
Efficient Cultivation Models and Economic Returns in Bunching Onion (*Allium fistulosum* L.)

Abstract

Bunching onion (*Allium fistulosum* L.) is grown widely as a vegetable because it offers good nutritional value and meets fairly steady market demand. In traditional production systems, however, farmers often face poor land-use efficiency, variable yields, and limited profitability. This study therefore evaluated two more intensive cultivation approaches: a relay-intercropping system based on bunching onion followed by or grown with leafy vegetables, and a high-ridge, dense-planting system combined with integrated water and fertilizer management. Field trials were conducted in 2022 and 2023 in Shouguang, Shandong Province, one of China’s major vegetable-producing areas. Conventional flat planting was used as the control (CK). Plant growth, yield, production costs, output value, and input-output ratio were compared. The relay-intercropping treatment increased annual net income by 42.6% and raised the land equivalent ratio (LER) by 38.2% relative to CK. Under the high-ridge dense-planting system, water and fertilizer inputs decreased by 27.3%, while marketable yield increased by 22.1%. Overall, both models improved resource-use efficiency and economic performance, although through different pathways. These findings offer practical technical and economic information for supporting more sustainable and efficient bunching onion production.

Keywords: bunching onion; efficient cultivation; relay intercropping; high-ridge planting; economic benefit; input-output ratio

1. Introduction

Bunching onion belongs to the *Amaryllidaceae* family and contains vitamin C, dietary fiber, and allicin, the latter being a functional compound associated with antibacterial activity [1]. It is an important vegetable in many parts of the world, and China accounts for more than 60% of global planting area and production. As demand for high-quality bunching onion has continued to increase, production areas have expanded accordingly.

This expansion has not removed several long-standing constraints. Continuous monocropping, rough water and fertilizer management, and low-density flat planting are still common in some production regions. Such practices can worsen soil-borne diseases, including Fusarium wilt, leave fallow periods poorly used, and increase both production expenses and environmental risks through excessive chemical inputs [2].

For these reasons, cultivation systems that are efficient, productive, and cost-saving are important for increasing grower returns and supporting the long-term development of the bunching onion industry. Much previous work has concentrated on individual technologies, such as cultivar improvement or pest management. Fewer studies have examined integrated planting models together with their economic outcomes. This study therefore combined agronomic evaluation with cost-and-return accounting to compare two efficient cultivation models and identify suitable patterns for wider adoption.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Experimental Site and Materials

The experiment was conducted at a sunlight greenhouse base in Shouguang (36.8°N, 118.8°E). The site has a temperate monsoon climate and loamy soil. Before planting, the soil contained 18.6 g/kg organic matter and 89.2 mg/kg available nitrogen, with a pH of 6.9. The bunching onion cultivar used was “Yuanzang No.1”, a commonly grown high-yield cultivar with relatively strong stress tolerance. The leafy vegetable used in the relay-intercropping treatment was a fast-growing *Brassica chinensis* cultivar, “Siji Qing”, which has a growth cycle of approximately 35 days.

2.2 Experimental Design

Three treatments were established, each with three replications. The plots were 30 m² and arranged in a randomized complete block design (RCBD).

- Control (CK, conventional flat planting): Bunching onion was sown in early April at 40 cm row spacing and 8 cm plant spacing, equivalent to approximately 312,500 plants/ha. Flood irrigation and broadcast fertilization followed conventional local practice. After onion harvest in early November, the land remained fallow.
- T1 (relay-intercropping model): Bunching onion was planted at the same density as in CK. *Brassica chinensis* was relay-sown between the onion rows in mid-September, about 45 days before onion harvest. A second crop of *Brassica chinensis* was established after the onions were harvested, and harvesting of that crop was completed by late December. Water and fertilizer management followed local conventional practices for intercropped production.
- T2 (high-ridge dense planting with integrated water-fertilizer management): Ridges were formed to a height of 20 cm and width of 60 cm. Two onion rows were planted on each ridge, with 30 cm row spacing and 6 cm plant spacing, giving approximately 555,600 plants/ha. Drip irrigation lines were placed beneath the ridges. A water-soluble fertilizer formulated for allium crops was applied in six split applications during the growing season, providing 320 kg N, 120 kg P₂O₅, and 280 kg K₂O per hectare. Total fertilizer input was 30% lower than in CK, and the irrigation quota was reduced by 25% compared with flood irrigation.

2.3 Measurements and Methods

2.3.1 Agronomic and Yield Traits

At harvest, 10 representative onion plants were selected from each plot to determine plant height, pseudo-stem diameter, and fresh weight per plant. Marketable onions, defined as those with a pseudo-stem length of at least 25 cm and no pest injury or mechanical damage, were weighed separately to calculate the marketable rate. Total plot yield was converted to yield per hectare. In T1, the yield of *Brassica chinensis* was recorded separately. The land equivalent ratio (LER) was used to evaluate the intercropping system:

$$LER = \frac{Y_{oi}}{Y_{os}} + \frac{Y_{vi}}{Y_{vs}}$$

where $Y_{oi}$ and $Y_{os}$ represent onion yields under intercropping and monocropping, respectively, while $Y_{vi}$ and $Y_{vs}$ represent leafy vegetable yields under intercropping and monocropping [3].

2.3.2 Economic Benefit Accounting

Production costs were divided into three main categories: (1) material costs, including seeds, fertilizer, pesticides, and agricultural film; (2) labor costs for sowing, field management, and harvesting; and (3) irrigation and machinery costs. Output value was calculated using the average local market prices in 2022–2023: USD 0.8/kg for bunching onion and USD 0.6/kg for *Brassica chinensis*. Net income was calculated as total output value minus total production cost, and the input-output ratio as total output value divided by total production cost.

2.4 Statistical Analysis

Data were organized in Microsoft Excel 2021. One-way analysis of variance was conducted using SPSS 26.0, and treatment means were compared with Duncan’s multiple range test at P < 0.05.

3. Results

3.1 Growth and Yield Responses under Different Cultivation Models

The high-ridge dense-planting treatment (T2) clearly improved onion growth (Table 1). Relative to CK, pseudo-stem diameter and single-plant fresh weight increased by 13.8% and 18.3%, respectively. Dense planting did create somewhat stronger competition among plants, but this appeared to be offset by better ventilation around the ridges and more precise water and nutrient supply. Total onion yield in T2 reached 68.2 t/ha, which was 22.1% higher than the 55.9 t/ha obtained in CK. The marketable rate also increased by 6.7 percentage points.

Relay intercropping in T1 did not significantly reduce onion yield. Onion yield was 54.8 t/ha, close to that of CK. One likely reason is niche complementarity: the shallow-rooted leafy vegetable and the more deeply rooted onion used soil resources and space in partly different ways. The LER for T1 was 1.38, suggesting that the intercropping system used land about 38% more efficiently than monocropping.

Table 1 Growth and yield performance under different treatments

| Treatment | Plant height (cm) | Pseudo-stem diameter (mm) | Single-plant weight (g) | Onion yield (t/ha) | Commodity rate (%) | LER |
|-----------|-------------------|---------------------------|-------------------------|--------------------|--------------------|-----|
| CK | 72.3 ± 2.1 b | 14.5 ± 0.8 b | 142.6 ± 7.2 b | 55.9 ± 2.3 b | 82.4 ± 1.8 b | 1.00 |
| T1 | 71.8 ± 1.9 b | 14.3 ± 0.7 b | 139.8 ± 6.5 b | 54.8 ± 2.1 b | 81.7 ± 2.0 b | 1.38 |
| T2 | 78.5 ± 2.4 a | 16.5 ± 0.9 a | 168.7 ± 8.1 a | 68.2 ± 2.7 a | 89.1 ± 1.5 a | – |

Note: Different lowercase letters within the same column indicate significant differences at P < 0.05.

3.2 Production Costs

The total cost of CK was USD 3,860/ha (Table 2). T1 required extra seed and labor for *Brassica chinensis*, raising the total cost by 12.7% to USD 4,350/ha. Even so, the additional expenditure was relatively modest because the leafy vegetable crop grew quickly and required limited inputs.

T2 involved higher initial spending on drip irrigation equipment and ridge construction, and annual equipment depreciation was included in the cost calculation. Nevertheless, this treatment reduced fertilizer and irrigation costs by 30.2% and 60.0%, respectively. Its total production cost was USD 3,720/ha, 3.6% lower than that of CK.

title: 夏威夷的海
text:
The Mango Glow Tide
Kailani was seven the first time she watched the sea light up like someone had scattered crushed starlight across its surface. She was clinging tight to her grandma’s sun-cracked, work-worn hand on Lahaina’s black sand beach when it happened. “Ain’t no magic trick, that,” Tutu told her, tucking a perfectly ripe, sun-warmed half-mango into her sticky little palm. The sweet juice dribbled down her wrist before she could even take a bite, mixing straight with the fine salt spray blowing off the waves. “That’s just the ocean holding onto the folks who loved it so much they never really left, even when they’re gone.”
Twenty years slipped by before she found herself kneeling in that same gritty black sand, fumbling with the rusted padlock on Tutu’s weathered old beach shack, her stiff corporate blazer slung haphazardly over a nearby cinder block to keep it out of the damp. The Hawaii she’d flown home to from Chicago felt off its axis, unmoored. Faint wildfire scars still streaked the West Maui Mountains like old, faded bruises you can’t quite stop touching. The rebuilt boardwalks were packed shoulder to shoulder with tourists yelling over blaring luau music, loud enough to drown out the sound of the surf. Worst of all? Those bioluminescent tides Tutu used to take her out to chase after dark hadn’t lit up once in three years. Local folks would murmur over grocery store checkout lines that the ocean had closed its heart shut after the fire.
She’d been so burnt out from her Chicago desk job when she booked the ticket, half-convinced the whole glowing tide thing had just been a silly childhood fantasy she’d blown out of proportion in her memory. That thought dissolved the second she spotted the chipped ceramic bowl perched on the shack’s porch rail, half full of rainwater, holding a single soft plumeria bloom. It was the exact same bowl Tutu used to set out every full moon as a quiet, unspoken offering, back when they’d wade knee-deep in the surf after dark, cackling as glowing plumes of water curled around their calves smooth as silk.
She didn’t overthink it that night. She just kicked off her work shoes, rolled her jeans up to her calves, and waded out barefoot, the cold surf lapping at her ankles, the air thick with plumeria scent and brine. Nothing happened for the first ten minutes or so, just the soft hush of waves rolling in, the distant twinkle of a cruise ship’s lights bobbing on the horizon. Then a small wave curled tight around her ankle, and a burst of neon blue sparked there, bright as a match struck right against her skin.
She sucked in a sharp, surprised gasp. Another flicker popped up a foot away, then another, until the whole stretch of surf around her was rippling with light. Every little kick of her feet sent up showers of star-bright sparks, every tiny fish darting past left a wispy glowing trail, like the sea was stitching little flecks of light straight into the dark water. A soft wave broke against her chest a minute later, and for a split second she swore she caught the thick, sweet smell of sun-ripened mango cutting through the salt brine, so vivid she could almost taste it.
When she finally waded back to shore, an older local man sitting by the dunes mending fishing nets looked up and flashed a gap-toothed grin. “First time she’s glowed since the fire,” he called over to her. “Guess she was just holdin’ out till someone came back to say hello proper, y’know?”
Kailani sat in the sand for ages after the glow faded, salt crusted stiff on her cheeks, thinking about all the people who’d loved this stretch of shore before her: Tutu, who’d taught her to read the tides like they were her favorite storybooks, the neighbors who’d passed around armfuls of mangoes and cold water during the fire evacuation, the little kids who built lopsided sandcastles right where the old boardwalk used to stand before it burned. The sea never forgot, it hit her all of a sudden. It had just been waiting for its people to remember how to slow down and listen, quiet as the tide creeping in.
When the first soft pink streaks of dawn touched the surface of the water, she reached into her bag, pulled out her beat-up work laptop, pulled up the half-drafted resignation email she’d been staring at for three months, and typed two short words: I’m home.

title: 番茄种植增收增产技术分析
text:
Tomato Year

The tomato vines had other ideas by the second week of June.

I remember because Dad kicked the irrigation pipe and said nothing, which was worse. He had planted the usual way — broad rows, seeds his father kept, rain if God remembered. That spring, God forgot.

Mara came by on a noisy motorcycle with a notebook tied to the rack. She worked for the county extension office, or “the plant lady,” as the neighbors called her before they trusted her. She didn’t give a speech. She knelt, pulled a handful of dry soil, and asked Dad what the field usually earned. He laughed through his nose.

“Enough to complain about.”

The first thing she changed was the bed. Not all at once — Dad would have walked away. On a quarter acre, they made raised beds with black plastic mulch, tucked tight like hospital corners. Under it ran drip tape, thin and cheap-looking, the kind of thing a man doubts until he sees water landing only where roots can use it. By July, those plants were darker, shorter-jointed, almost muscular. The rest of the field looked tired beside them, as though it had been asked to do too much with too little.

She made him test the soil. He considered this city nonsense until the report came back saying his ground had potassium enough for a war but lacked phosphorus in the western patch. Mara walked the rows with him, kicking stones, pointing at leaves. “You’re feeding what you guess, not what’s missing.” That stung, I think, because it was true.

They split the fertilizer into small doses: a little at planting, more when the first flowers opened, another push when fruit began to swell. Nothing dramatic. No bottle labeled miracle. The vines simply stopped panicking.

Staking caused a family dispute. Dad believed tomatoes should lie where God and gravity put them. Uncle Renato came, looked at the twine cages, and said we were dressing vegetables for church. But once the fruit set, the difference was impossible to argue with. Air moved through the plants. Sun reached the clusters. Fewer tomatoes hid in the mud and split after rain. The ones that did rot were easy to spot and remove before disease spread through a whole row.

Mara also made him remove suckers, which he did with the grim expression of a man betraying nature. She showed him how to keep two stems instead of allowing a tangled thicket. Fewer flowers, she said, but more fruit worth carrying to market. That was the lesson hidden in everything she did: yield wasn’t only about numbers. A tomato bursting in a basket paid nobody.

Pollination she left mostly to the insects, but she insisted on wild clover along the ditch. Bees arrived, fat and indecently busy. The neighbor’s boys threw rocks once, then got bored. The clover stayed.

By late August, the test rows were producing fruit the color of a stop sign, smooth at the shoulders, almost no blossom-end rot. Dad didn’t celebrate out loud. He just moved the irrigation line more carefully and asked Mara, very casually, whether the same trick might work on peppers.

The harvest crew noticed first. Their crates were heavier. More marketable fruit per plant, fewer culls, fewer spoiled bottoms hidden under good tomatoes like a lie. Buyers from the market also noticed; uniformity has a quiet kind of power. A restaurant woman in a white van bought a full load and said they tasted “like tomatoes are supposed to threaten you.” Dad repeated that for weeks.

Not every new thing stayed. The plastic was a nuisance to remove, and Mara admitted it. Next year they talked about organic mulch, maybe straw, though she warned it could cool the soil early. The pruners disappeared twice. One drip line got chewed by a creature Dad described in language unsuitable for print. But the plants taught him faster than any pamphlet could.

One evening he knelt beside a vine and turned a fruit in his palm. The western light came through the rows in strips. His hands were stained green-brown at the nails.

He didn’t say the field was fixed. He said, “Ask Mara to come eat.”

So she came on Sunday, and nobody mentioned technology at the table. There were sliced tomatoes with salt, bread, and too much garlic. Outside, the drip tape ticked softly after shutting off, a small mechanical sound in the dark.

title: 人民币汇率波动对出口的影响
text:
The Impact of RMB Exchange Rate Volatility on China's Exports
 Abstract
This paper looks at how swings in the Renminbi (RMB) exchange rate shape China’s export activity, grounding standard trade models in what actually shows up in firm and customs data. It traces both currency appreciation and day-to-day volatility through export volumes, firm choices, and the slow reshuffling of industries, while also accounting for forces that soften the blow—from forward exchange hedging to the way Chinese production is woven into global value chains (GVCs).
