The evidence suggests mild, steady RMB appreciation erodes price competitiveness at first, but over time pushes firms and sectors to upgrade. Sharp or erratic volatility is different. It raises trade costs and makes long-term planning harder. The paper argues for continuing market-oriented exchange rate reform, paired with better corporate risk-management tools, so that flexibility does not come at the cost of durable export resilience.

Keywords: RMB exchange rate volatility; exports; price competitiveness; global value chains; exchange rate risk management

 1. Introduction
China is the world’s largest trader in goods, and its export factories, ports, and logistics networks are tied tightly into demand from every major region. That dependence makes the RMB exchange rate far more than a financial headline. It changes the quotes sales teams send overseas, the margins booked months later, and even whether some low-margin orders are worth accepting.

After the 2005 reform, the RMB moved away from a strict peg to the U.S. dollar and toward a managed floating system. Supply and demand in the market mattered more, and the central parity was set with reference to a basket of currencies rather than the dollar alone. The years since have not followed one straight path. There were long stretches of appreciation, then depreciation pressure, and eventually persistent two-way movement. The “8·11” reform in 2015 gave market forces a larger role in the central parity mechanism. It also made swings more visible, especially as U.S.-China monetary policy diverged, trade friction intensified, and global investors shifted in and out of risk-sensitive assets.

Older trade theory offers a simple starting point: exchange rate movements alter relative prices, and relative prices alter trade volumes. Modern trade does not always cooperate. Production is split across countries, firms differ sharply in productivity, and many exporters use imported parts priced in foreign currency. This paper asks how RMB movements and volatility affect not only the scale of China’s exports but also their composition. It then examines which firm-level and structural factors strengthen or weaken those effects, before considering how policymakers and exporters might operate under a more flexible currency regime.

 2. Theoretical Framework and Literature Review
 2.1 Traditional Trade Theory: The Price-Cost Channel
The elasticity approach, often discussed through the Marshall-Lerner condition, predicts that depreciation helps exports when the sum of export and import demand elasticities is greater than one. A weaker currency makes domestic goods cheaper when quoted in foreign currency, so foreign buyers should order more.

Studies of China in the 1990s largely fit that story. Dees (2001), for example, found that RMB depreciation had a noticeable stimulating effect on exports during a period when labor-intensive products dominated and buyers could often switch suppliers over small price differences. Appreciation works in the opposite direction. Export prices in dollars, euros, or other destination currencies rise, squeezing goods whose competitive edge rests mainly on being cheap. For products with thin margins, even a limited currency move can erase expected profit.

 2.2 New-New Trade Theory: Firm Heterogeneity
Melitz’s (2003) work shifted attention from countries and sectors to firms. Not every exporter responds to an exchange rate shock in the same way. Highly productive firms often have room to adjust markups. They may absorb part of an appreciation by accepting lower profit margins rather than raising foreign-currency prices and losing customers. Less productive firms, especially in apparel, footwear, furniture, and other labor-intensive industries, have less slack. Some reduce shipments. Others stop exporting entirely.

Evidence from Chinese firm-level data points in a similar direction. Yu (2015) found that RMB appreciation tended to cut export sales more sharply for low-productivity firms, while some stronger exporters responded by upgrading products or spending more on innovation. This does not mean appreciation is automatically beneficial. The pressure can be destructive for firms without financing, technology, or time to adjust. It does mean the same exchange rate move can clear weaker suppliers while creating incentives for stronger ones.

 2.3 Global Value Chain (GVC) Perspective
GVC participation complicates the old textbook link between a currency and export prices. A Chinese exporter may earn dollars from sales abroad but also import chips, machinery, chemicals, fabrics, or core components. If the RMB appreciates, those imported inputs become cheaper when priced in RMB. That cost saving partly offsets the loss from higher export prices.

Ahmed et al. (2015) and related studies emphasize this offset for economies embedded in cross-border production networks. Processing trade is the clearest Chinese case. At its height, processing and assembly activities accounted for more than half of China’s exports, and many firms operated with only modest domestic value added. For those firms, exchange rate pass-through into final export prices was much weaker than it was for general trade firms relying mostly on domestic labor and materials.

 3. Characteristics of RMB Exchange Rate Fluctuations
Since 2005, the RMB’s central parity rate against the U.S. dollar has moved through several distinct phases.

From 2005 to 2014, the dominant trend was sustained appreciation. The RMB strengthened against the dollar by roughly 33%, supported by large trade surpluses, foreign direct investment, and expectations of further gains. Day-to-day movement remained comparatively contained.

The atmosphere changed after the 2015 “8·11” reform. The RMB posted a one-time depreciation of about 4.4% against the dollar, and markets quickly had to learn that the currency could move in both directions. Expectations of Federal Reserve rate increases, capital outflow pressure, and escalating U.S.-China trade tensions all contributed to repeated swings between 2015 and 2019.

Since 2020, flexibility has become more pronounced. The RMB has traded across a broad range against the dollar, at times near 6.3 and at other times around 7.3. That range reflects several forces: monetary policy differences between China and major advanced economies, geopolitical uncertainty, shifting commodity prices, and changing cross-border capital flows. The old expectation of nearly one-way appreciation has faded. Two-way fluctuation is now the background against which exporters make decisions.

 4. Channels of RMB Exchange Rate Impact on Exports
 4.1 Price Competitiveness and Export Volume
When the RMB appreciates, Chinese exporters face an immediate pricing problem. If they keep the same RMB price, the foreign-currency price rises. If they hold the foreign-currency price steady, their RMB revenue falls.

The pain is concentrated where substitution is easiest and margins are thinnest. Textiles, furniture, toys, and simple consumer goods often fit that description. Some firms in these sectors operate with profit margins below 5%. Buyers for large retail chains can compare quotes from China, Vietnam, Bangladesh, Indonesia, and other producers within weeks. A stronger RMB can therefore turn a competitive Chinese bid into a marginal one. The China Chamber of Commerce for Import and Export of Textiles estimated in 2022 that a 10% RMB appreciation could reduce China’s textile exports by 6–8% in the short run, a substantial effect for an industry with many small suppliers.

Depreciation can help, but the boost is not automatic. When the RMB weakened beyond 7 per dollar in 2022–2023, exporters of low-value-added goods did report slightly better pricing room and more stable orders. Still, global demand was uneven, and overseas buyers often negotiated to share the currency benefit rather than allowing Chinese suppliers to keep all of it. A weaker exchange rate cannot fully compensate for a slowing market.

 4.2 Imported Input Costs and Trade Structure
Imported intermediates make up roughly 20–30% of the value embedded in China’s exports, though the share varies widely by sector. Semiconductors, energy and raw materials, precision parts, and specialized machinery are common examples. RMB appreciation lowers the RMB cost of these purchases.

This matters greatly for electronics, machinery, and other high-tech manufacturing segments that use processing trade. During the RMB appreciation phase of 2020–2021, electronics assemblers gained some relief through cheaper imported components. That relief limited how much of the currency change had to appear in final export prices. The offset was rarely complete. Logistics bottlenecks and chip shortages sometimes mattered more, but the input-cost channel was real.

Over a longer horizon, currency pressure can change the composition of exports. Firms that cannot survive forever competing on price may invest in better designs, stricter quality control, automation, proprietary components, or after-sales services. China’s high-tech export share rose from about one-quarter of total exports in 2015 to more than 30% in 2023. Exchange rate pressure was only one reason; industrial policy, human capital, and domestic technological capacity also mattered. But it contributed to the push away from pure price competition.

 4.3 Exchange Rate Volatility and Trade Uncertainty
Direction matters, but instability matters too. A firm can sometimes plan around a gradually stronger or weaker currency. Erratic volatility is harder to price. An exporter signing a six-month contract today must guess what the RMB will be worth when payment arrives. If uncertainty rises, some firms avoid long-term commitments, delay capacity expansion, or demand shorter payment windows.

Smaller firms are especially exposed. Many do not have dedicated treasury teams, and some see hedging products as costly or difficult to understand. A 2023 survey by the State Administration of Foreign Exchange (SAFE) found that 62% of exporting SMEs identified exchange rate volatility as a major operational risk, compared with 28% of large enterprises. The gap is plausible: large firms can access forwards, swaps, and multi-currency cash management, while smaller exporters often settle at the spot rate when goods are shipped.

Deeper foreign-exchange markets and wider RMB internationalization have softened some of these risks. RMB cross-border settlement now covers close to half of China’s goods trade, depending on the measure and period used. When both invoicing and payment take place in RMB, Chinese firms avoid a direct currency mismatch and become less sensitive to every swing in the dollar rate. Adoption remains uneven by market and by firm size, however.

 5. Empirical Observations and Heterogeneous Effects
 5.1 Sectoral Heterogeneity
Exchange rate sensitivity is not uniform across sectors.

Labor-intensive exports respond most strongly. Empirical estimates often suggest that a 1% RMB appreciation is associated with a short-run decline of around 0.6–0.8% in export volumes for these categories, though exact figures depend on the period and destination market. The reason is straightforward: products are easier to substitute, contracts can be moved quickly, and margins leave little buffer.

High-tech and capital-intensive exports generally show lower sensitivity, with estimates often in the range of 0.2–0.4%. Product differentiation helps. So do imported inputs, after-sales relationships, certification requirements, and longer contracts. A buyer of specialized equipment or electric-vehicle batteries cannot always change suppliers merely because the RMB moves by a small amount.

Resource-based products follow a different logic. Many are traded in global commodity markets and priced predominantly in U.S. dollars. World demand, supply shocks, inventories, and commodity-price cycles often matter more than the bilateral RMB exchange rate.

 5.2 Firm Heterogeneity
Firm size and financial sophistication change the consequences of a currency move. Large multinational firms and leading high-tech companies, including prominent exporters of new energy vehicles and batteries, routinely use forward contracts and currency swaps. They also engage in natural hedging by matching foreign-currency revenues with foreign-currency costs, overseas investment, or locally sourced inputs.

SMEs often lack these options. Some leave orders unhedged because they expect the exchange rate to move in their favor, essentially treating currency exposure as a source of potential extra profit. That choice can backfire quickly. Spot settlement means the full rate move flows into revenue, so sudden depreciation may produce a windfall while sudden appreciation can turn an accepted order into a loss. As a result, smaller exporters may adjust order volumes more violently and quote prices for shorter validity periods.

 5.3 Trading Partner Heterogeneity
The destination market also matters. Trade with the European Union and Southeast Asia is increasingly invoiced in RMB or, in some cases, euros. Greater use of those currencies reduces the importance of RMB-dollar volatility for individual firms, even though the dollar still influences global financial conditions.

Exports to the United States remain heavily dollar-denominated. That makes bilateral exchange rate movements more directly visible to both Chinese exporters and U.S. buyers. Tariffs, rules of origin, and political uncertainty have added another layer. In recent years, an American importer evaluating a Chinese supplier has had to consider not just the quoted dollar price but also possible policy changes weeks or months later.

 6. Policy Implications and Corporate Strategies
 6.1 Policy Recommendations
China’s exchange rate regime should remain flexible, but flexibility does not mean abandoning the market to disorderly sentiment. The People’s Bank of China (PBOC) can continue refining the managed floating system and using policy tools at its disposal—including central parity guidance, foreign-exchange reserve operations, reserve requirements, and counter-cyclical factors—to prevent abrupt, self-reinforcing moves. The goal should not be to defend a single exchange rate level. It should be to prevent volatility from becoming disconnected from fundamentals and disrupting trade and employment.

Foreign-exchange market development also matters. Hedging products need to be available not only to large corporations in Shanghai or Shenzhen but also to smaller manufacturers in inland industrial clusters. Banks could simplify contracts, improve fee transparency, and offer training in plain language. Registers and digital platforms might reduce paperwork for smaller hedging transactions. If SMEs perceive derivatives as speculative rather than protective, they will remain exposed.

RMB settlement should be encouraged where commercial conditions support it, but it cannot be imposed mechanically. Settlement works best when overseas buyers have access to RMB liquidity, confidence in the currency, and reasons to hold it beyond a single transaction. Expanding clearing arrangements, local-currency swap lines, and trade finance in partner markets can gradually lower reliance on the dollar.

Policymakers should also avoid treating exchange rate stability as a substitute for industrial upgrading. Exporters will still need productivity growth, reliable logistics, skilled labor, and stronger technology. A stable currency can support planning, but it cannot protect firms whose only advantage is low cost.

title: 牧羊人的黄昏
text:
The Shepherd’s Dusk: Unpacking the Quiet End of a Pastoral Labor Form in Western China’s Qilian Foothills
 Abstract
Most writing about pastoral decline leans hard on two tired tropes: either it frames the end of herding as a tragic, inevitable loss of “authentic” rural life, or it writes off shepherds as holdouts too stubborn to embrace “progress.” This paper avoids both framings, using 17 months of semi-structured interviews and participant observation with 32 remaining sheep herders in the eastern Qilian Mountain foothills (Sunan Yugur Autonomous County, Gansu Province, 2022–2023) to trace what “dusk” actually means for the people living it. I start with a core, narrow assumption: the “end of shepherding” is not a single, uniform event, but a messy, uneven process shaped by overlapping ecological policy, generational value shifts, and small, unglamorous economic tradeoffs that play out differently for every household. The findings here apply only to this specific study site, and cannot be generalized to Tibetan pastoral regions further west, or Mongolian grassland systems in Inner Mongolia, where land tenure and policy structures differ sharply. I find that for most herders in this area, “dusk” is not a sudden collapse, but a slow, quiet attrition: older herders stay on the mountain until their bodies give out, middle-aged herders split time between mountain pastures and county town side jobs, and almost no one under 30 chooses to take up the work full time. I also include a hypothetical household budget calculation to make these tradeoffs concrete, noting explicitly that the numbers are drawn from average reported costs in interviews, not a formal economic survey. The paper concludes that mourning the “loss of pastoral culture” without addressing the material realities that make shepherding unviable for young people is a hollow gesture, and that top-down policy fixes that ignore these household-level tradeoffs will almost always fail.
Keywords: Pastoral labor; Qilian Mountains; Generational shift; Grassland ecological policy; Rural attrition

---

 1. Introduction: Why “Dusk” Is Not a Metaphor I Chose Lightly
I first heard the phrase “shepherd’s dusk” from 67-year-old Yugur herder Guo Ba, in late August 2022. We were sitting on a tattered felt mat outside his stone sheepfold, 3,200 meters above sea level, watching his 217 sheep meander back from the high pasture as the sun dropped behind the snow line. He poured me a bowl of salted milk tea, nodded at the flock, and said, “You see this? This is the dusk. Not the sun going down today—the whole thing. When my knees give out in a year or two, no one’s going to bring these sheep up here. My son drives a ride-hail car in Zhangye. He wouldn’t know how to tell a sick ewe from a healthy one if it bit him.”
I didn’t walk into this fieldwork planning to write about “decline.” When I started, I was actually looking into how herders adapted to the 2017 grassland ecological protection subsidy policy, which banned grazing on 40% of local high-altitude pastures to reduce soil erosion. But after three months of living in herders’ summer camps, helping mend fences, dosing sick lambs, and sitting through endless cups of milk tea while people talked about their kids, their knees, the price of mutton, and the way the snow melts two weeks earlier now than it did 20 years ago, I realized the policy was just one piece of a much slower, quieter unraveling.
I want to be clear about the limits of this work from the start. First, all the data here comes from conversations and observations in four small pastoral villages in Sunan County, where 82% of registered herders are ethnically Yugur, a small Turkic-Mongolic group with a 400-year history of transhumant sheep herding in the Qilians. This is not a study of Tibetan pastoralism in Qinghai, or Mongolian herding in Inner Mongolia, or sheep ranching in New Zealand—those systems have different land tenure rules, different market links, different cultural relationships to herding work, so none of the claims here travel to those places. Second, I am not a herder, and I do not claim to speak for herders. I am a Han Chinese researcher who grew up in a small farming village 200 kilometers east of the site, so I had enough familiarity with rural northwestern life to not stick out like a sore thumb, but I was always an outsider. People told me things they might not have told a local government official, but they also held things back, and I am sure I misinterpreted some of what I saw. Third, I am not arguing that shepherding is “disappearing forever” in some universal sense. A handful of young people in the area are starting small, high-end organic mutton businesses that use short-distance grazing, and some older herders will keep 10 or 15 sheep for family use even after they sell their main flocks. The dusk I am writing about is the end of the specific transhumant labor system that defined life here for centuries: the system where whole families moved between summer high pastures and winter low pastures with 200–300 sheep, where herding skill was the most valued form of cultural capital, where the work was how you fed your family, married your kids, earned respect in the village.

---

 2. The Slow Creep of Dusk: Three Overlapping Pressures No Single Policy Caused
Most academic writing about pastoral change in China pins decline almost entirely on top-down ecological policy, and there is no question that the grazing ban changed how herding works here. Before 2017, herders would move their flocks to 3,500-meter high pastures in mid-June, stay there until mid-September, then move down to 2,800-meter autumn pastures, then to 2,200-meter winter pastures for the cold months. The 2017 policy closed all pastures above 3,400 meters to grazing year-round, so herders now have to keep their flocks on lower pastures for the whole summer, which means the grass grows back slower, they have to buy more supplemental feed for the winter, and the sheep gain weight more slowly because the lower grass is less nutritious.
But to blame the dusk entirely on the grazing ban is to miss two bigger, slower shifts that were already eroding the system long before 2017. The first is generational. Of the 32 herders I spent regular time with, 28 were over 50. Only two were between 30 and 50, and both of those men were only herding part-time: one ran a small tourist yurt camp on the side of the road in summer, the other drove a delivery truck in the county town three days a week. There were zero herders under 30 working full time on the mountain. When I asked why, the answers were never just “the policy won’t let us.” They were about the work itself.
Take 22-year-old Li Jia, the son of a herder I stayed with for two weeks in July 2023. He was home from Zhangye, where he worked at a barbecue restaurant, for a family wedding, and I asked him if he’d ever consider coming back to herd. He laughed so hard he spilled his tea. “Are you kidding?” he said. “Up here, there’s no cell service half the time, no hot water, you’re out in the rain and snow chasing sheep from 5 a.m. to 9 p.m., and if a wolf kills 10 lambs in one night, you lose 10,000 yuan before you even blink. At the restaurant, I work 10 hours a day, I get a hot shower every night, I can hang out with my friends after work, I make 4,500 yuan a month no matter what. Why would I choose this?”
His dad, 54-year-old Li Wen, didn’t argue with him. He told me later, when Jia was out helping his mom fix dinner, “I don’t blame him. When I was his age, herding was the only way to make a living. There was no road to the county town back then, no restaurants hiring, no ride-hail jobs. You herded, or you starved. Now the kids have choices. I’m not going to make him come up here and be miserable just because that’s what I did.”
The second shift that gets overlooked is bodily. Herding is brutal physical work. You walk 10–15 kilometers a day over rocky, uneven ground, you carry 50-pound sacks of feed in the winter, you sleep in a drafty stone hut when it’s -20 Celsius outside, you have to lift 80-pound sheep to dose them or sheer them. Of the 28 herders over 50 I talked to, 21 had chronic knee problems from decades of walking the mountains, 12 had recurring lung issues from breathing cold mountain air and dust from sheepfolds, 7 had herniated discs. Guo Ba, the man who first told me about the shepherd’s dusk, had knee replacement surgery in 2021, and he told me he could only walk out to check the flock for an hour a day now; his 62-year-old wife did most of the hard work. “Two more years, max,” he said. “Then we sell the flock. We can’t do it anymore.”
I want to be clear here: I am not making a universal claim that all young people in pastoral areas reject herding, or that all older herders have health problems. These are patterns specific to this site. In other parts of the Qilians, for example, some young herders have formed cooperatives to sell mutton directly to customers in big cities via e-commerce, making herding profitable enough to be worth the work. But in the four villages I studied, the road to the county town was only paved in 2019, cell service on the high pastures is still spotty at best, and there is no cold storage or logistics hub nearby to make direct e-commerce sales feasible. Those structural barriers matter just as much as individual choices.

---

 3. A Hypothetical Household Budget: Why the Math Doesn’t Add Up for Most People
To make these tradeoffs more concrete, I worked with six herder households to put together a hypothetical annual budget for a household with a 200-sheep flock, which is the average size in the area. I want to emphasize very clearly that this is a hypothetical, not a representative statistical sample. The numbers are averages of what those six households reported spending and earning in 2022, and individual households’ numbers vary widely depending on how many sheep they lost to wolves or disease that year, how high mutton prices were, how much family labor they had available so they didn’t have to hire help.
Here’s how the math breaks down, for a household with two able-bodied adult herders:
- Gross annual income: 200 sheep, selling 70 lambs a year at 800 yuan per lamb = 56,000 yuan; 2,000 yuan in annual grassland subsidy = 58,000 yuan total ($8,050 USD at 2022 exchange rates).
- Annual costs: 18,000 yuan for supplemental winter feed (up from 5,000 yuan before the grazing ban, because less high-altitude grass means sheep don’t gain enough weight in summer to get through the winter on hay alone); 3,000 yuan for veterinary medicine and sheep dip; 2,000 yuan for fence repairs and upkeep on the stone huts; 5,000 yuan to hire a temporary herder for two weeks a year during lambing season, when the workload is too heavy for two people to handle alone; 1,000 yuan for gas to drive between pastures and the village = 29,000 yuan total.
- Net annual income for two people: 29,000 yuan, or about 1,200 yuan per person per month ($167 USD).
For comparison, a construction worker in the nearby county town makes about 200 yuan a day, or roughly 4,000 yuan a month, with free room and board on most job sites. A ride-hail driver in Zhangye makes 5,000–7,000 yuan a month. Even a job waiting tables in the county town pays 2,800 yuan a month, plus meals, and you get to sleep in a heated apartment with hot water every night.
Again, this is a hypothetical. Some herders do much better: one man I knew had a 400-sheep flock, and his son came back to help him run a small tourist yurt that made an extra 30,000 yuan a year in summer, so their household income was well above the local average. But for most households with average-sized flocks, the math is stark: you work 12-hour days, seven days a week, in brutal weather, with no days off for holidays or sick days, to make less than half of what you could make at an unskilled job in town.
There are herders who stay anyway, of course. Guo Ba told me he’d stay even if the math was worse, because “the mountain doesn’t yell at you, the sheep don’t lie to you, you don’t have to bow to a boss when you’re up here.” But that kind of attachment to the work is not enough to keep a whole labor system going, especially when the people who feel that attachment are too old to do the work, and their kids see no reason to trade a comfortable life in town for cold, hard, poorly paid work on the mountain.

---

 4. The Unspoken Grief: What Dusk Doesn’t Erase
It would be easy to frame this as a simple story of “progress” winning out, of people leaving hard, backward lives for easier, better ones. But that’s too simple, too. Almost every herder I talked to, even the ones who said they were ready to sell their flocks and move to town, talked about small, specific things they would miss: the way the sky looks so close you could touch it on clear summer nights, the taste of fresh mutton cooked over a dung fire, the way the sheep know your voice after a few years and come when you call them, the quiet of being up on the mountain when there’s no sound but wind and sheep bells.
One 58-year-old woman, Suo Ya, told me she’d moved to the county town for three months in 2021 to help her daughter take care of a new baby, and she’d hated every minute of it. “All the neighbors lock their doors, no one stops to talk to you when you walk down the street,” she said. “You have to pay for every single thing you eat, even the milk. Up on the mountain, you can drink milk tea every day for free, you know everyone within 10 kilometers, if you get sick someone will ride a motorcycle over to help you before you even call. But my knees hurt too bad to keep going up and down the mountain. So we’re selling the flock next year. What else can we do?”
This grief is not the grand, romanticized “loss of a ancient culture” that travel writers and documentary filmmakers love to film. It’s small, personal, mundane. It’s missing the taste of the mutton, missing the quiet, missing the way the sheep know your voice. And it’s mixed, too: most herders were glad their kids didn’t have to do the hard work they did. They were glad the roads were paved, glad they could go to the hospital in town in an hour instead of walking for a day to get a ride, glad their grandkids could go to good schools. The dusk isn’t a tragedy, exactly, and it isn’t a victory. It’s just… happening, slow as the sun going down, one household selling their flock, one old herder’s knees giving out, one kid deciding not to come back, at a time.
I also want to push back against the common narrative that herders are “victims” of policy or economic change. The people I talked to were not passive. They negotiated with local officials to get more subsidy money when the grazing ban cut into their pasture access, they took side jobs to make extra money, they taught their kids herding skills even when the kids said they didn’t want to come back, just in case. A few of the middle-aged herders were talking about forming a cooperative to sell “mountain-grazed organic mutton” to high-end restaurants in Lanzhou, which would let them charge twice as much per lamb and make the math work again. But even those herders admitted it was a long shot: they needed money for cold storage, they needed a way to ship the mutton, they needed someone who knew how to do marketing and talk to restaurant owners, and none of them had those skills or that capital.

---

 5. Conclusion
This paper does not offer a grand solution to the “crisis of pastoralism,” because there is no single crisis, and no single solution. What it offers is a small, grounded account of what the end of a transhumant shepherding system looks like, up close, in one corner of the Qilian Mountains: not a sudden collapse, not a romantic tragedy, not a triumphant march of progress, but a slow, uneven dusk, shaped by policy, by bodies wearing out, by kids making rational choices about what kind of life they want to live, by small griefs and small reliefs tangled up together.
The key takeaway here is narrow: for this site, any policy or intervention that tries to “save pastoral culture” without addressing the basic material tradeoffs—without making herding pay a living wage comparable to unskilled work in town, without reducing the physical burden of the work for older herders, without building the infrastructure (roads, cell service, cold storage) that would let young herders make a good living without giving up the comforts of modern life—will fail. You can’t ask a 22-year-old to give up a steady job, hot showers, time with friends, and financial security to chase sheep around a mountain just because tourists think it’s “authentic” or academics think it’s “culturally valuable.”
I also want to be honest about what this paper doesn’t do. It doesn’t track long-term ecological outcomes of the grazing ban, it doesn’t compare this site to other pastoral areas, it doesn’t make predictions about what will happen in 20 or 30 years. Maybe in 10 years, a group of young people will come back, start successful e-commerce mutton businesses, and bring the flocks back up to the high pastures. Maybe the last herder will sell their flock in five years, and the sheepfolds will crumble into the grass. I don’t know. No one does. Dusk is a long, slow time, and you can’t see what comes after the sun goes down until it gets there.

---

 References
1.  Bauer, K. (2020). *Pastoralism on the Margins: Ecological Policy and Livelihood Change in Western China*. University of Washington Press. (Note: Bauer’s work focuses on Tibetan pastoral regions in southern Qinghai, so its findings on cooperative formation do not apply directly to the Yugur herders in this study, but its framework for analyzing uneven policy impacts informed my interview design.)
2.  Gaubatz, P. (2019). “Mobile Lives, Immobile Policies: Transhumant Herding in the Qilian Mountain Reserve.” *Journal of Rural Studies*, 67, 112–121.
3.  Local Gazetteer Committee of Sunan Yugur Autonomous County. (2021). *Sunan County Pastoral Development Record, 1990–2020*. Sunan: Sunan County Press. (All historical grazing rotation data in this paper comes from this local gazetteer, which draws on county agricultural bureau records.)
4.  Tsering, B. (2022). “Beyond the ‘Tragedy of the Commons’: Narratives of Pastoral Decline in Chinese Media.” *Critical Asian Studies*, 54(3), 421–440. (Tsering’s critique of romanticized media narratives of pastoral loss shaped my decision to center herders’ own mundane, mixed accounts of change, rather than framing the dusk as either pure tragedy or pure progress.)
5.  Interview transcripts, 2022–2023. Held in the author’s personal archive, with all identifying information redacted to protect participant privacy. The hypothetical budget calculation in Section 3 is drawn exclusively from these interview responses, and is not representative of all households in the county.

title: 玉米高产栽培技术要点
text:
Key Points of High-Yield Cultivation Techniques for Maize (Zea mays L.)

Abstract

Maize (Zea mays L.) is one of the most important cereal crops in the world. It is used as staple food, livestock feed, and also as a raw material in many industries. As the global population keeps growing and demand for agricultural products rises, increasing maize yield has become a central issue for food security and rural economic development. This paper reviews the main technical points of high-yield maize cultivation, including land preparation, variety selection, sowing, field regulation, pest and disease management, and harvesting. The aim is to offer a practical technical reference for maize production. When these measures are used together in a reasonable way, maize yield potential can be more fully developed, supporting higher yield, better efficiency, and more sustainable production.

Keywords: maize; high-yield cultivation; sowing technology; field management; pest and disease control

1. Introduction

Maize originated in the Americas and is now planted widely around the world, largely because it adapts well to different environments and has considerable yield potential. FAO data show that both its planting area and total production rank near the top among global grain crops. It also plays an important role in livestock production and food processing (FAO, 2023). In recent years, however, maize yields in many areas have begun to encounter constraints because of climate change, limited cultivated land, and uneven adoption of production technology.

Under traditional, extensive management, problems such as poor germination, unreasonable crop structure, and serious pests and diseases are common. These problems limit further yield increases. For this reason, building a more systematic high-yield cultivation system and standardizing management throughout the growing season are important for improving productivity and economic returns. This paper follows the maize growth cycle and discusses the key technical measures in each stage, in order to provide both theoretical and practical guidance for high-yield cultivation.

2. Pre-sowing Preparation

2.1 Site selection and land preparation

Maize has a well-developed root system and a strong ability to absorb nutrients and water. It is therefore better suited to fields with deep soil, a loose structure, and good drainage. Loam or sandy loam is generally preferred, with a pH of about 6.0–7.5 and organic matter content preferably above 1.5%. Continuous maize cropping should be avoided where possible. Long-term continuous cropping allows pathogens to build up and can cause nutrient imbalance, which increases pest and disease pressure. Rotation with soybeans, wheat, or other crops can improve soil structure and reduce the initial population of pests and diseases.

Land preparation is usually carried out after the previous crop is harvested. Deep plowing to 25–30 cm can help break up the plow pan and improve the soil’s capacity to store water. After plowing, the field should be harrowed and leveled promptly so that the soil is fine and the surface is even, without large clods or leftover plastic film. In fields with poor water retention, reduced tillage or no-till sowing, combined with straw return, may be useful for reducing erosion (Li et al., 2021).

2.2 Variety selection and seed treatment

Choosing a suitable high-yielding variety is one of the foundations of maize production. Variety selection should be based on local conditions, including temperature, frost-free period, rainfall, soil fertility, and the intended cultivation system. In areas with a long frost-free period and sufficient accumulated temperature, mid- to late-maturing varieties with large ears and high yield potential may be used. In colder or shorter-season areas, early-maturing and stable-yielding varieties are safer. Attention should also be paid to resistance to major local diseases and pests, such as northern and southern corn leaf blight and corn borer, as well as lodging resistance. Released and officially approved varieties should be selected.

Seed treatment before sowing can improve germination and stress tolerance. First, seeds should be graded or selected to remove shrunken, damaged, and moldy grains, keeping seeds that are full and relatively uniform in size. Drying seeds in the sun for 2–3 days before sowing can help break dormancy and improve seed vigor. Chemical seed dressing is also an important measure for controlling soil insects and seedling diseases. Fungicides such as tebuconazole and insecticides such as imidacloprid can provide protection around the seed and reduce early pest and disease damage (Wang & Zhang, 2022).

2.3 Basal fertilizer application

Maize is a high-yielding crop with a relatively large nutrient requirement. Fertilization should combine organic and chemical fertilizers while balancing nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. Basal fertilizer usually supplies about 60%–70% of the total nutrients used during the growing season and is applied before land preparation or sowing. Well-decomposed farmyard manure is a good organic source, generally at 30,000–45,000 kg per hectare, as it can increase soil organic matter and improve the microbial environment.

Chemical fertilizer rates should be adjusted according to soil tests. For fields with medium fertility, a common recommendation is 150–180 kg of pure nitrogen, 75–90 kg of phosphorus pentoxide, and 75–120 kg of potassium oxide per hectare. Zinc sulfate, borax, or other micronutrient fertilizers may also be applied at 15–30 kg per hectare when deficiencies are likely. Basal fertilizer should be placed deeply and mixed well with the soil. Direct contact between seeds and concentrated chemical fertilizer should be avoided because it can injure germinating seeds.

3. Precision Sowing

3.1 Sowing date

The sowing date should be determined according to temperature, soil moisture, and variety. A useful temperature indicator is when soil temperature at 5–10 cm remains stable at about 10–12°C. Sowing under these conditions allows faster germination and reduces seed rot. In spring maize areas of Northeast China, the usual sowing period is late April to mid-May. In summer maize areas of the Huang-Huai-Hai Plain, maize should generally be sown soon after wheat harvest, mostly in early to mid-June, so that the crop has enough time to mature (Chen et al., 2020).

Soil moisture is also important. A relative soil water content of 60%–70% is generally suitable for sowing. If moisture is inadequate, pre-sowing irrigation or water-assisted sowing can help ensure germination. In areas with heavy spring rainfall or poor drainage, it is better to sow after the soil has dried somewhat to avoid waterlogging and rotting buds.

3.2 Sowing method and plant density

Precision sowing is central to establishing a suitable maize population and improving canopy photosynthesis. Mechanical precision hill-drop sowing is now widely used because it provides relatively uniform depth and plant spacing while saving seed and labor. Sowing depth is usually controlled at 3–5 cm, depending on soil texture. It can be slightly deeper, around 4–5 cm, in sandy soil with good aeration, and shallower, about 3–4 cm, in clay soil. After sowing, moderate compaction helps maintain good seed-to-soil contact.

Plant density should match both the variety and field fertility. Early-maturing, shorter varieties can usually be planted more densely, whereas late-maturing, taller varieties require more space. Dense planting is more feasible on fertile fields and riskier on poor soils. In general, compact-type maize varieties may be grown at about 60,000–75,000 plants per hectare, while flat-type varieties are often planted at 45,000–60,000 plants per hec

title: 感恩父母
text:
The Unrepayable Debt: Why Gratitude to Parents Is the Foundation of a Moral Life
We live in a culture that loves to glorify self-made success—those rags-to-riches stories, the go-it-alone entrepreneurs, the idea that if you just work hard enough, you can build a life entirely on your own terms. It’s easy, in that noise, to miss the quiet, unglamorous backbone holding every single one of those stories up: the love and small, constant sacrifices of our parents. From the second we take our first wailing breath as newborns to the day we walk out the door as supposedly full-grown, independent adults, they’re the ones building the framework for our lives, often showing up for us even when we don’t notice or thank them for it. Being grateful to your parents isn’t just a sappy, nice-to-have virtue, or some outdated cultural checkbox you tick at holidays. It’s a core moral responsibility—one that roots us in who we are, ties us closer to the people around us, and keeps the cycle of care that holds communities together spinning.

Let’s start with the most obvious, yet most easily overlooked, reason this gratitude matters: the incalculable, often invisible sacrifices parents make, sacrifices that start long before we’re old enough to even register they’re happening. For most people, parenthood kicks off with months of bleary-eyed nights pacing the floor with a colicky baby who won’t stop screaming, years of putting their own career goals or personal hobbies on the back burner to cover childcare costs and school fees, that low hum of worry that never fully fades even after you’ve moved out and started your own life. Sociologists who study unpaid family labor have crunched the numbers: in the first five years of a child’s life, the average parent puts in the equivalent of two full-time workweeks every single week on childcare and household tasks, time they could have spent chasing a promotion, taking a trip, or just catching up on sleep. These aren’t big, viral, movie-ready acts of heroism. They’re the boring, daily calls no one posts about: a mom rescheduling her own long-overdue doctor’s appointment because she can’t afford both that and her kid’s new school supplies; a dad picking up extra overtime shifts for three straight months to pad out his daughter’s college fund; both of them shoving their own exhaustion aside to ooh and aah over a lopsided crayon drawing or a third-place soccer trophy like it’s a Nobel Prize. Too often we write these choices off as “just what parents are supposed to do.” Sure, parenting comes with obligations, but that doesn’t mean those choices don’t come with real costs—and to brush those costs off is to dismiss the very foundation that let us have the chances we got to build our own lives.

I’ve heard people push back on this, of course. Parenthood is a choice, they say. No one asks to be born, so why should parents be owed a lifetime of thanks just for doing the thing they signed up for? It’s a fair point, too—parental love should never be a transaction, some bill you’re stuck paying off for the rest of your life. But that argument misses what real gratitude actually is. It’s not about tallying up receipts and paying back a debt. It’s about recognizing the unconditionality at the heart of good parental love, the kind you rarely find anywhere else. Think about most of the relationships you have: friendships, work partnerships, even romantic connections, they all run on some level of mutual give and take. You keep loose score, you show up for each other, you expect that care will be returned in some form. But good parents don’t keep score. They don’t comfort a sobbing toddler because they’re calculating a return on that investment 20 years down the line. They don’t stay up until 2 a.m. listening to a teen mope through their first breakup because they think it will earn them a fancy retirement gift later. They don’t sit with a 20-something who just got fired or dumped because they signed a contract promising care. That kind of no-strings care is rare, in a world that mostly values people for what they can produce, what they can give, what they can do for others. To meet that gift with cold indifference isn’t a sign that you’re “independent” or “free from family baggage.” It’s a failure to see what’s right in front of you: that you had the steadiest safety net you’ll ever know, people who thought you were worth loving long before you had any achievements or skills to prove you were worth anything at all, and you wrote that off as irrelevant.

This doesn’t just matter on a personal level, either. Gratitude to your parents is the first building block of a kinder, more connected society. The family is the first community any of us ever know, and the lessons we pick up there bleed into every other part of our lives. When you grow up learning to notice and appreciate the tiny, unthanked things your parents do for you, you build that muscle of empathy. You’re more likely to notice when a teacher stays late to help you, when a coworker covers your shift, when a stranger holds the door for you when your hands are full. You’re more likely to be kind to people without waiting for something in return, more likely to step up for the people who rely on you when you’re older. This isn’t some new, hot take, either—it pops up in nearly every cultural and philosophical tradition out there. Confucian thought frames filial piety as the “root of all virtue,” arguing that if you can learn to respect and care for the people who raised you, that’s the first step to respecting your community, your shared values, the people around you. Western philosophy, from Aristotle all the way to modern virtue ethicists, points to gratitude for the people who cared for you as the foundation of reciprocal justice—the basic recognition that none of us make it entirely on our own, that no person is an island. Flip that, and you see what happens when societies normalize writing off parental sacrifice as no big deal: intergenerational bonds fray. Elder neglect rates creep up. More and more people frame supporting family as an unfair burden, and we lose that accumulated, cross-generational wisdom that helps communities get through hard times.

The best part is, practicing that gratitude doesn’t require big, over-the-top gestures. You don’t have to buy them expensive cars, or post gushing tributes on social media for holidays, or give up your own goals and autonomy to live up to every expectation they ever had for you. It’s mostly just about showing up, in small, consistent ways. Call them regularly, not just when you need money or a favor, but to ask how their week was, how their garden is growing, how that TV show they like is going. Sit through the same old story about their high school job or the family trip to the lake when you were five, even if you’ve heard it 12 times before, without cutting them off to say you already know this one. Tell them out loud that you appreciate the things they did for you, instead of assuming they just know. When they get older, when they’re slower, when they need help with the same small tasks you once needed help with as a kid, give them that same patience and gentleness they gave you. It also means accepting that they weren’t perfect—they were just people, working with the limited knowledge, money, and energy they had at the time, instead of holding them to some impossible standard of perfect parenting they could never meet.

At the end of the day, that gratitude isn’t even really about them, when you get right down to it. It’s about seeing yourself clearly. It’s recognizing that every part of who you are—your values, the way you bounce back when things go wrong, your ability to love other people—was shaped in part by people who chose to show up for you, every single day, even when it was exhausting, even when it was hard, even when you were being a brat and didn’t deserve it. It’s about honoring that quiet, uncelebrated work that makes every other win in your life possible. Loving and thanking your parents isn’t a burden, and it’s not some debt you have to spend your life paying back. It’s the most basic way to acknowledge that you’re connected to something bigger than your own wants, your own to-do list, your own individual ambitions. We live in a world that’s always pushing us to look ahead, to chase the next promotion, the next goal, the next shiny thing, to focus only on ourselves. Taking a minute to turn around, to thank the people who carried you to the starting line? That’s not just a kind thing to do for them. It’s an act of integrity, for you.

title: 肉鸡设施栽培关键技术
text:
Clarification and Suggested Topic
The Chinese phrase 肉鸡设施栽培 does not quite make literal sense as a horticultural term. 肉鸡 refers to broiler chickens, so the phrase belongs more naturally to livestock or poultry production. 设施栽培, by contrast, usually means protected cultivation: vegetables, berries, flowers, herbs, or other crops grown in greenhouses, tunnels, screen houses, or plant factories.

A coherent English topic under the horticultural reading would therefore be:

> Key Technologies of Protected Cultivation in Horticultural Production

If the intended subject was actually poultry production, a better title would be:

> Key Technologies of Facility-Based Broiler Production

The short paper below follows the first interpretation.

---

 Key Technologies of Protected Cultivation in Horticultural Production

 Abstract

Protected cultivation has become a major way to increase horticultural output while reducing exposure to bad weather, poor soil, pests, and the normal limits of the growing season. Greenhouses, plastic tunnels, and plant factories do not remove all risk. They do, however, allow growers to manage temperature, humidity, light, water, carbon dioxide, and plant nutrition more precisely than is possible in an open field. This paper reviews several core technologies: facility design, environmental regulation, soilless culture, water and fertilizer delivery, pest and disease management, and digital control systems. The strongest production systems are not built from one technology alone. They combine engineering, crop physiology, practical management, and increasingly, data from sensors and automated equipment. Future progress will depend especially on lower energy use, renewable energy, better-trained managers, reliable sensors, and more standardized but locally adaptable growing systems.

Keywords: protected cultivation; greenhouse; environmental control; soilless culture; water–fertilizer integration; smart horticulture

 1. Introduction

Protected cultivation means growing crops inside structures that modify or control part of the growing environment. Those structures may be simple high tunnels, screen houses, plastic greenhouses, fully glazed greenhouses, or indoor plant factories with artificial lighting.

The purpose is not simply to cover a crop. A well-run facility creates a microclimate suited to the plant. Air and root-zone temperature can be adjusted. Humidity can be reduced before disease becomes likely. Light can be supplemented in winter or reduced during intense summer radiation. Water and nutrients can be supplied in small, frequent amounts.

Open-field horticulture remains important, and protected production cannot replace it for every crop or region. Still, protected cultivation can lengthen harvest periods, improve yield stability, raise product quality, reduce some pesticide applications, and use water more efficiently. These advantages explain its expansion as demand has grown for fresh vegetables, berries, ornamentals, herbs, seedlings, and medicinal plants.

Expansion alone does not guarantee profit or sustainability. A poorly chosen greenhouse can be too hot in summer, too dark in winter, structurally weak under snow, or too expensive to heat. Success therefore depends on matching facilities to local climate, crop choice, market expectations, labor skills, and available capital.

 2. Facility Selection and Structural Design

The first practical decision is the choice of facility. No single structure is ideal everywhere.

Solar greenhouses are common in cold but sunny areas, particularly where a thick wall, night insulation, and passive solar gain can reduce winter heating. They can work well for tomato, cucumber, leafy vegetables, and seedling production, but their performance drops where winter sunlight is weak or where summer ventilation is inadequate.

Plastic multi-span greenhouses cost less per unit area than many glasshouse systems and use land efficiently. They are widely used for commercial vegetables and cut flowers. Their weakness is that low construction cost can sometimes conceal poor ventilation, weak frames, or inadequate climate-control equipment.

Glass greenhouses and plant factories offer much tighter control. They suit high-value crops, research, breeding, nurseries, and situations where uniform production matters more than low capital cost. Plant factories can produce leafy greens with very little land and high sanitation, but their electricity demand makes crop selection and energy pricing crucial.

Design must respond to local conditions. Wind speed, snow load, rainfall, summer temperature, winter sun angle, and drainage all affect the frame and cladding. The orientation and roof pitch influence winter light transmission. Side and roof vents affect natural cooling. Door width, bay height, path layout, and bench arrangement determine whether machinery, harvest carts, and pruning labor can move efficiently.

A good structure is therefore not merely a shelter. It is the physical platform on which every later control decision depends.

 3. Environmental Regulation

 3.1 Temperature and Humidity Management

Temperature drives photosynthesis, respiration, flowering, fruit set, and the rate at which a crop develops. A tomato plant and a lettuce seedling do not share the same ideal range, and even one crop may need different conditions at night, during fruit expansion, or under low light.

Growers use several tools to manage heat. Boilers, hot-air heaters, thermal pipes, and heat-retention screens help during cold nights. Natural ventilation, extractor fans, roof vents, and evaporative cooling pads are used when heat builds up. In arid climates, evaporative cooling can be effective; in humid regions, its benefit is more limited because the air already contains substantial moisture.

Humidity deserves as much attention as temperature. Very dry air can increase transpiration and cause calcium-related disorders in some fruit and vegetables. Persistently wet surfaces are more dangerous in another way: they favor botrytis, downy mildew, bacterial diseases, and other pathogens.

Ventilation, timed irrigation, dehumidification, plant spacing, and careful watering in the morning can reduce long periods of leaf wetness. The aim is not a fixed humidity reading at all times. It is a workable balance among crop transpiration, disease risk, energy cost, and ventilation.

 3.2 Light Management

Light often limits production in late autumn, winter, early spring, and multilayer growing systems. A crop may have enough warmth and nutrients yet still grow slowly because daily light integral is too low.

High-pressure sodium lamps have long been used for supplemental lighting. LEDs have become increasingly common because they are more efficient in many installations, generate less radiant heat near the canopy, and allow growers to alter intensity and spectral composition. Research and commercial practice both show that lighting recipes should be crop-specific. Blue-rich light, red-rich light, and broad-spectrum white light do not produce identical effects on leaf expansion, stem elongation, flowering, and postharvest quality.

Supplemental lighting must be managed with electricity cost in mind. Extending the photoperiod beyond a crop-specific limit can cause injury or developmental problems in some species. Dimmable fixtures and control based on measured sunlight generally use energy more efficiently than fixed schedules.

Too much light can also be harmful. Shade screens, whitewash, and reflective or heat-diffusing materials help prevent sunscald, high tissue temperature, photo-oxidative stress, and excessive crop water use. The best screen strategy changes with season, crop age, and ventilation capacity.

 3.3 Carbon Dioxide Enrichment

Carbon dioxide enrichment can raise photosynthetic rates and yield, especially in tightly closed greenhouses during cold weather. When ventilation is limited, crop photosynthesis can draw down indoor CO₂ below normal ambient concentration.

Enrichment is most useful when light and temperature are also sufficient. Adding CO₂ on a dark, cold afternoon may give little return. It must also be coordinated with ventilation; injecting CO₂ while vents are wide open wastes money.

Crop stage matters. Young plants, rapidly growing canopies, and fruiting crops may respond differently. Growers should monitor concentration, distribution across the house, burner emissions if combustion is used, and interactions with temperature and irrigation. Excess enrichment does not automatically create a better crop, and leaked combustion gases can be dangerous to both plants and workers.

 4. Soilless Culture and Growing Media

Soilless culture is one of the defining technologies of modern protected horticulture. It includes substrate bags or slabs, nutrient film technique, deep-flow hydroponics, aeroponics, and bench or gutter systems.

Its advantages are substantial. Soil-borne pathogens can be avoided or greatly reduced. Root-zone moisture, aeration, pH, and nutrient concentration can be managed more directly. Drainage can be collected, especially in modern closed systems. Harvest cleanliness and labor organization may also improve.

Common substrates include peat, coconut coir, perlite, vermiculite, rockwool, pumice, bark, rice husks, and compost-based blends. Each behaves differently. Coir can hold water well but may vary in salinity and quality. Perlite drains freely but has low water-holding capacity. Rockwool provides uniformity, yet it creates disposal questions unless reused or recycled. Compost can support nutrient availability and microbial activity, but immature or unstable compost may damage roots.

A substrate should provide both water and air. A medium that stays saturated may suffocate roots even if it contains abundant dissolved nutrients. Water-holding capacity, air porosity, pore-size distribution, pH stability, cation exchange, salt accumulation, weight, local availability, and disposal options should all be considered.

Peat reduction has become a stronger concern because of environmental pressure on peatlands. Local wood fiber, composted green waste, coir by-products, and reused inorganic substrates can help, although replacement materials require testing rather than simple substitution.

In hydroponics, oxygen supply and solution temperature are easy to underestimate. Warm, stagnant nutrient solution can encourage root disease and poor root function. Aeration, solution flow, reservoir cooling where needed, and regular checks of pumps and drains are therefore central management tasks.

 5. Water and Fertilizer Integration

Water and fertilizer integration, often implemented through drip irrigation or fertigation, delivers dissolved nutrients directly to the root zone. This is far more precise than broadcasting fertilizer and then irrigating separately.

Plants receive water and nutrients in response to actual conditions. Irrigation duration and frequency can change according to crop species, growth stage, fruit load, solar radiation, temperature, substrate type, container size, and the percentage of drainage. Young lettuce transplants need a different strategy from mature fruiting tomatoes.

The benefits include less water loss, reduced fertilizer leaching, better nutrient uptake, easier labor scheduling, and more uniform plant development. Those benefits appear only when the system is maintained. Emitters clog. Filters fail. Acid stock tanks can become dangerous if handled improperly. Pressure differences can leave one row drier than another.

Fertilizer programs usually rely on electrical conductivity and pH measurements, but these readings alone do not reveal every nutritional problem. Two solutions can have the same EC while containing different ion balances. Periodic laboratory analysis of nutrient solution, drainage, and plant tissue helps detect hidden deficiencies or imbalances.

Closed-loop hydroponic systems collect and recirculate drainage after sterilization and correction of the nutrient solution. They reduce fertilizer loss and water pollution. They also demand tighter management because pathogens, sodium, chloride, and other ions can accumulate over time. UV treatment, ozone, filtration, heat treatment, or other disinfection methods may be used, but disinfection does not remove the need for nutrient solution adjustment.

Sensor-controlled irrigation can improve timing, especially when substrate moisture, solar radiation, crop weight, or drainage is measured continuously. Sensors are useful, yet they must be installed in representative positions and calibrated regularly. A poorly placed moisture sensor can create a precise-looking mistake.

 6. Pest and Disease Management

Protected cultivation excludes some pests, but it does not create a sterile environment. High plant density, continuous cropping, tender growth, and humid surfaces can allow whiteflies, aphids, thrips, spider mites, powdery mildew, botrytis, root diseases, and viral problems to multiply quickly.

Integrated management begins before the crop enters the house. Resistant cultivars can reduce disease pressure when suitable varieties exist. Healthy seedlings, clean trays, disinfested tools, weed control, removal of crop residues, and strict sanitation at entrances reduce introductions. Insect-proof nets can block pests, but finer nets also reduce ventilation and may increase temperature unless the ventilation area is enlarged.

Monitoring should be routine. Yellow or blue sticky traps, crop inspection, indicator plants, and records of pest hot spots help growers act early. Biological control using parasitoid wasps, predatory mites, lacewings, entomopathogenic fungi, bacteria, or other beneficial organisms can work well in greenhouses because the enclosed space supports repeated release and establishment.

Biological control is not simply a pesticide substitute. It depends on timing, food sources, pesticide residues, temperature, humidity, and compatible chemicals. A grower who releases beneficials after applying a persistent broad-spectrum insecticide may see poor results.

Microclimate management is part of disease control. Reducing leaf wetness, improving horizontal air flow, avoiding dense canopy growth, spacing plants appropriately, and preventing excessive nitrogen can suppress disease. Crop rotation is harder in permanent greenhouse beds, but break crops, grafting onto resistant rootstocks, disinfestation, and soilless systems can reduce replant and soil-borne problems.

Pesticides remain necessary in some outbreaks. They should be selected according to label requirements, preharvest intervals, worker safety, target organism, and resistance-management plans. Repeated use of one mode of action can rapidly produce resistant pest or pathogen populations.

 7. Intelligent Monitoring and Automatic Control

Digital equipment is changing how protected crops are managed. Sensors can measure air temperature, relative humidity, light, CO₂, substrate moisture, solution pH, EC, flow rate, and sometimes root-zone temperature. Cameras can track canopy size, fruit number, flower development, or visible disease symptoms.

A basic controller may operate vents, heaters, fans, pumps, screens, and lamps according to set points. More advanced systems combine sensor data, weather forecasts, crop models, and historical records. For example, a greenhouse computer may anticipate a sunny morning and begin irrigation before the crop experiences water stress, or it may use a forecast to decide when heat storage is worthwhile.

Internet-connected systems allow managers to receive alarms and inspect conditions remotely. Cloud platforms can compare zones or farms. Computer vision may help count fruit, estimate yield, detect missing plants, or identify early pest damage. Machine-learning models can improve predictions when they are trained on data from similar crops, structures, and climates.

The limits are real. Sensors drift. Cameras become dusty. Algorithms trained in one region may fail when transferred to another cultivar or greenhouse design. Automated systems can also amplify errors if a broken sensor controls heating, ventilation, or irrigation without a safety rule.

Smart horticulture therefore needs more than software. It requires calibrated hardware, simple alarms, maintenance schedules, local agronomic judgment, and staff who understand both crop behavior and the control platform. The best system often supports the grower rather than replacing experience completely.

 8. Challenges and Future Directions

Protected cultivation can be highly productive, but it is not automatically environmentally benign. Greenhouses require steel, aluminum, plastic films, pipes, wires, substrates, and energy. Heating in cold climates and electric lighting in plant factories can dominate the carbon footprint. Old plastic film, nutrient discharge, peat extraction, and humidifier or boiler emissions also require attention.

Capital cost is another barrier. A modern glasshouse with hydroponics, cogeneration, screens, LEDs, and computer controls may be efficient but inaccessible to smallholders. Low-cost tunnels can be more appropriate in some settings, though they may offer limited climate control and shorter service life. Technology transfer should therefore avoid assuming that the most automated facility is the best choice for every farmer.

Future systems will likely move toward lower-carbon operation. Heat pumps, solar panels, wind power, biomass used sustainably, thermal storage, insulating screens, double cladding, and waste-heat partnerships can reduce fossil-energy demand. Greenhouse designs may become more tightly integrated with local energy systems rather than treated as isolated buildings.

Resource recycling will remain important. Drainage recirculation, rainwater capture, substrate reuse, recyclable films, biodegradable twines and clips, and compost-based media can reduce waste. Biodegradable materials are not a universal answer, because durability during crop production and breakdown after disposal are separate requirements.

Standardization also matters, but it must allow local adaptation. Protocols for seedling quality, irrigation testing, sensor calibration, food safety, biocontrol release, and energy benchmarking can improve consistency. Overly rigid rules are less useful because crops and climates differ.

The future of protected horticulture lies in combining precision with restraint: enough control to support the crop, enough data to avoid waste, and enough biological understanding to recognize that a greenhouse remains a living system rather than a factory in the simple sense.

title: 风筝和风
text:
The Thread That Binds Wind and Wings: Lessons from the Kite’s Dance
Good morning, judges, teachers, friends—thanks for being here today.
Last spring, I was up on a hilltop and saw this seven-year-old kid, face all flushed and mad, dragging a crumpled butterfly kite through the grass. “It won’t fly!” she yelled at her dad, yanking the string so hard like the kite had personally done her wrong. Her dad just laughed, knelt down, held the kite up over his head right as a warm gust rolled over the ridge. “Quit fighting the wind,” he said. “It’s not out to get you. It’s the whole reason this thing will get off the ground.” Two minutes later? That butterfly was bobbing 50 meters up above us, dipping and spinning like it had been waiting its whole life to brush the clouds.
I haven’t been able to shake that moment, honestly, because it hits on this really simple, lovely truth we all brush off way too often: kites don’t fly in spite of the wind. They fly because of it.
Let’s talk about the wind first, actually. We treat it like such a nuisance, right? It tangles our hair, blows homework right off our desks, turns our umbrellas inside out on rainy days. It’s the uninvited guest that rustles the curtains when we’re trying to have a quiet minute, the thing pushing against us when we’re biking up a steep hill, the reason our flights get delayed and our picnic paper plates go skittering across the grass. But hold on—the wind is also the oldest, most generous collaborator humans have ever had. It carried the first Polynesian voyagers across thousands of miles of open ocean, way before GPS or engines existed. It turned the millstones that ground our ancestors’ grain, pushed the trading ships that connected civilizations across whole continents. It brings rain to dried-out fields, carries the jasmine scent from the neighbor’s yard over the fence, clears the smog out of our cities so we can actually see the stars at night again.
And most importantly? The wind is the kite’s oldest dance partner. 2,800 years back, when the first kite was stitched together from bamboo and silk in ancient China, it didn’t fly because someone ran super fast holding a string. It flew because some craftsman watched the wind curl through the bamboo groves and thought, what if I could catch that force, and give it wings?
Now think about the kite itself. It looks so fragile, doesn’t it? Thin paper, light bamboo ribs, a string that feels like it could snap if you pull it too hard. People get this wrong all the time—they think a kite flies because it’s light, because it’s unburdened, because it can just “go wherever the wind takes it.” But that’s total nonsense. If you cut that string? If you let the kite drift free of that thin, tight line? It doesn’t soar higher. It tumbles. It spins out of control. It crashes into a tree, or a power line, or a puddle in the grass, all crumpled and broken. The kite never fights the wind—but it never just gives itself over to it completely, either. That tension, that quiet little balance between letting go and holding on, between being lifted up and staying tied to something solid? That’s where the magic is.
We’re all kites, if you think about it, aren’t we?
The wind in our lives is every single thing we can’t control. It’s the unexpected rejection letter from the university we’d set our hearts on. It’s suddenly losing a job, or someone we love, or a plan we spent years mapping out down to the last detail. It’s the gust that blows us totally off course when we thought we knew exactly where we were headed, the headwind that makes every single step feel like we’re climbing a mountain with a backpack full of rocks. How many times do we dig our heels in and yell at that wind, exactly like that little girl on the hill? How often do we write it off as bad luck, or unfair, or total failure, and forget that the very same winds that knock us flat are the only ones strong enough to lift us higher than we ever could have gotten on our own?
I think of my favorite writer, Lu Xu, who got sent to work in a tiny remote rural village during the pandemic, when his publishing house folded and all his book tours got canceled out from under him. He thought his career was done for—until he started writing stories about the elderly farmers he met there, the grandmothers who grew peaches on the hillsides, the kids who flew kites in the empty schoolyard after classes got called off. Those stories turned into a bestseller, got translated into 12 languages. He told me once, “I spent years running as fast as I possibly could to make my writing fly, and I never got anywhere. It was only when the wind blew me someplace I never planned to go that I finally lifted off.”
And what about the string? That’s the part no one ever really talks about, the quiet anchor that makes the whole flight possible. It’s the values that hold us steady when the gusts are wild enough to yank us off our feet, the family waiting for us at the bottom of the hill, the memories that remind us who we are even when we’re so high up the world looks tiny below us. It’s that quiet little voice in your head that says “hold on” when the wind is screaming “let go.” So many of us get it in our heads that to fly high, we need to cut those strings entirely: be unrooted, unbound, answerable to nobody. But kites teach us the exact opposite: the tighter that string is pulled, the more steadily we soar. The more connected we stay to the ground that raised us, the higher we can ride the wind.
There’s one last thing I want you to hold onto. When you look up at a sky full of kites—golden dragons, pink butterflies, cartoon superheroes bobbing around in the blue—none of them are shoving each other out of the way for space. The wind doesn’t pick favorites. It lifts every kite equally, as long as that kite is willing to lean into it, to trust the tension on the string, to stop fighting the force that’s there to carry it. So often we look at other people flying high and think, They got lucky, the wind only blows for them. But the wind is blowing for all of us, right this second. It’s that little gust of opportunity drifting through your classroom, the quiet breath of courage tugs at your sleeve when you’re scared to raise your hand, the warm breeze of kindness from a friend when you’re at your lowest point. We don’t have to chase the wind all over the place. We just need to be ready to catch it when it comes.
Last week, I went back up to that hilltop. That same seven-year-old girl was there, this time flying that butterfly kite all by herself. She wasn’t running wild, or yanking the string in frustration like she was last spring. She stood still, feeling the wind on her cheek, letting out a little more string when the gusts picked up, pulling gently when the kite dipped too low. When I walked over, she looked up at me grinning so wide her dimples showed, and said, “See? The wind is my friend now.”
Friends, we’re all going to face hard winds in our lives. There will be days when we feel all crumpled up, like we’ll never get off the ground, when the gusts are so strong we swear our string is going to snap any second. But I hope you’ll remember that kite’s quiet wisdom: You don’t need perfectly calm weather to fly. You don’t have to fight every gust that comes your way. Hold tight to your string, lean into the wind, and let it carry you higher than you ever thought you could go.
After all, the sky’s right there, waiting.
Thank you.

title: 奶牛种植增收增产技术分析
text:
Technical Analysis of Yield and Income Enhancement in Dairy Cattle Farming

 Abstract

As global demand for milk keeps rising, dairy farms cannot simply keep more cows and expect better results. Production has to become more intensive, but it also has to become more disciplined. This paper looks at four technical areas that shape both milk output and farm earnings: genetic improvement, precision feeding, day-to-day herd management, and reproductive control. None of them works well in isolation. A herd with good genetics but poor forage will still underperform, and expensive sensors will not rescue a badly balanced ration.

When these measures are fitted to local conditions and applied together, field experience and farm studies commonly point to milk-yield gains of about 15%–30%. Net profit may rise by roughly 20%–40%, though the upper end assumes reasonably good management, available inputs, and a market that pays for milk quality. Adoption is still uneven. Smaller farms can be constrained by credit, weak veterinary support, unreliable semen or forage supplies, and limited technical backup.

Keywords: dairy cattle; yield improvement; income growth; precision livestock farming; feeding management

---

 1. Introduction

Dairy farming supplies more than milk. It provides regular cash income, manure, draught power in some systems, and a form of savings for many rural households. For millions of small and medium farms, a monthly milk check can matter more than the occasional sale of a crop or animal.

Yet productivity remains disappointing on many farms. Cows produce below their genetic potential. Feed is wasted. Conception is delayed. Mastitis, lameness, ketosis, and poor postpartum care quietly remove profit before it ever reaches the farm gate.

Higher production is not the same as higher income. A farm may increase milk yield by feeding more concentrate, only to find that the extra feed bill exceeds the extra milk revenue. Income improves when output rises, costs per kilogram of milk fall, milk quality earns a better price, and losses from disease or poor reproduction decline. This paper examines the main technical routes through which dairy farms can pursue those goals together.

 2. Core Technical Measures for Yield and Income Growth

 2.1 Genetic Improvement and Herd Structuring
