Genetics set the ceiling, but management decides how close a cow comes to reaching it. Even so, repeated use of superior sires is one of the most durable ways to raise a herd’s productive capacity.

Sire selection should consider more than milk volume. Predicted transmitting ability, or PTA, for fat yield, protein yield, fertility, somatic cell score, udder conformation, and productive life helps avoid the trap of breeding cows that give large volumes of milk but break down early. In herds relying on liquid-milk sales, volume may receive more weight. In markets paying for solids, fat and protein become especially important.

Crossbreeding can be useful where pure Holstein cows struggle with heat, disease, low-quality forage, or poor housing. Holstein crosses often raise volume, while Jersey influence can improve fat and protein concentration and reduce body size. Crossbreeding is not automatically superior, however. The best choice depends on climate, feed supply, disease pressure, milk-pricing rules, and the farmer’s ability to manage replacement heifers.

Income also improves through herd structure. A farm should identify low-producing cows, cows that repeatedly fail to conceive, and cows with chronic mastitis or lameness. Some should be culled once treatment and future production are judged uneconomic. Their replacements should come from heifers born to the better cows and sired by proven bulls. A simple milk record, even one kept in a notebook, makes these decisions far less arbitrary.

 2.2 Precision Feeding and Forage Optimization

Feed usually absorbs about 50%–70% of the cash cost of producing milk. On poorly managed farms, the share can be higher because so much feed is spoiled, refused, or fed without a clear target.

Precision feeding means matching the ration to the animal. A fresh cow producing 35 kg of milk has different requirements from a dry cow in late gestation or a heifer still growing. Stage of lactation, daily yield, body weight, body condition, pregnancy status, and forage quality all matter. A total mixed ration, or TMR, can blend forage, silage, concentrate, minerals, vitamins, and additives so cows cannot sort out the grain. That supports more stable rumen fermentation and dry-matter intake.

The foundation is usually forage. Good alfalfa hay or haylage, well-fermented corn silage, and in some settings sorghum-sudangrass or oat silage can reduce dependence on purchased concentrates. The exact mix depends on what can be grown or bought locally. A ration should balance crude protein, energy, and effective neutral detergent fiber. Too little fiber brings acidosis and laminitis; too little digestible energy limits milk yield even when protein looks adequate.

Rumen-protected methionine or lysine may be justified in high-yielding herds where amino acid balance limits milk protein. Buffers such as sodium bicarbonate can help with heat stress or low-fiber rations. Yeast cultures and other additives have more variable payoffs and should be judged on farm response rather than sales claims.

Management around the feed bunk is just as important. TMR ingredients should be weighed rather than estimated with a shovel or bucket. Refusals should be checked daily, usually around 3%–5% of what was offered for fresh groups. Spoiled silage must be removed, feeder faces kept compact, and water troughs clean. These details often improve profit without requiring a new building.

When done well, precision feeding raises milk yield and feed conversion. It also lowers the risk of acidosis, ketosis, milk fever, and displaced abomasum. The gain is not immediate in every cow, but rumen health and body-condition changes usually become visible within weeks.

 2.3 Precision Livestock Management

Sensor systems have become common on larger dairy units. Neck collars may monitor rumination, activity, heat, and sometimes temperature. Leg tags can detect lying time and walking patterns. In-line milk meters can track yield, conductivity, and somatic-cell indicators. Cameras and automated body-condition scoring add another layer of observation.

The value of these tools lies in early response. A collar that flags increased activity can reveal standing heat before a worker notices it. A drop in rumination after calving may signal metritis, ketosis, or a displaced abomasum. Changes in milk conductivity may point to early mastitis. Lameness-scoring systems help identify cows before a hoof lesion becomes severe.

The financial effects are practical. Better heat detection raises conception rates and shortens calving intervals. Earlier treatment often means a smaller veterinary bill and less discarded milk. Fewer cows leave the herd involuntarily. More consistent milking and cooling help keep somatic cell counts under control, which matters where processors penalize high-cell milk or reject loads.

Sensors are not a substitute for stockmanship. A farm with no reliable electricity, weak internet, poor repair services, or untrained staff may buy equipment and then ignore its alarms. For such farms, paper or simple phone-based records can still work well: daily milk yield, service dates, expected calving dates, vaccination dates, disease episodes, drug withdrawal periods, and culling reasons. The key is not the technology itself. It is whether recorded information changes a decision.

 2.4 Reproductive Efficiency Improvement

Reproduction determines how much milk a cow produces over her lifetime and how quickly the herd improves genetically. A cow that conceives soon after calving can enter another high-yield lactation on schedule. A cow that remains open for too long spends many days at low production while still consuming feed and occupying space.

Good reproduction begins before breeding. Cows need a clean calving area, careful calving assistance, prompt treatment of retained placenta or metritis, and a reasonable rise in body condition after calving. A cow losing excessive weight in early lactation may show weak heat or conceive poorly, no matter how carefully insemination is timed.

Practical reproductive programs combine postpartum checks, heat detection, artificial insemination, ultrasound pregnancy diagnosis, and sometimes timed-AI protocols with estrus synchronization. Timed AI is especially useful where heat detection is unreliable, but it requires disciplined scheduling and proper injection technique. It should not mask poor transition-cow management.

Many well-managed herds target a calving interval of about 12–13 months. Well-grown Holstein heifers may first be bred around 13–15 months, provided they have reached adequate size and weight rather than merely a calendar age. Smaller breeds or heifers raised on limited feed may need a different schedule.

Better reproduction brings more lactation peaks, more calves, and more surplus heifers to sell or retain. It also allows faster genetic replacement because the herd can choose which heifers enter production instead of being forced to keep every animal born.

 2.5 Disease Prevention and Milking Hygiene

Disease losses are often hidden. A case of clinical mastitis reduces milk immediately, but subclinical mastitis can persist for months through lower yield, reduced milk price, and early culling. Lameness cuts intake and milk, delays conception, and increases the chance that a cow is sold. Reproductive and metabolic diseases lengthen the open period and raise veterinary costs.

Prevention needs routine. Vaccinations should follow a locally designed schedule rather than copying another farm. Hooves need regular trimming, and lame cows need prompt examination. Housing should provide dry stalls, adequate bedding, non-slip walkways, and enough ventilation. Heat abatement with fans and sprinklers can protect intake and fertility in hot climates. Transition cows benefit from close monitoring around calving and rations designed to reduce milk fever and ketosis.

Milking hygiene directly affects milk quality. Clean udders, functional milking machines, stable vacuum levels, proper liner replacement, post-milking teat disinfection, and dry-cow therapy all reduce bacterial exposure and new udder infections. Cows with chronic high somatic-cell counts may need segregation or culture-based treatment rather than repeated antibiotics with little prospect of cure.

Strict hygiene lowers somatic cell counts and bacterial contamination. That means fewer rejected cans or tanker loads, fewer price penalties, and better trust from buyers. Preventive care usually costs less than treating advanced disease, especially when discarded milk and lost future production are included.

 3. Economic Analysis

A technology is profitable only when the extra return exceeds the extra cost, including costs that are easy to overlook. Labor, repairs, electricity, training, mortality risk, and financing all deserve attention.

Genetic improvement has a delayed payback. A sire decision affects a calf that will not enter the milking herd for roughly two years or more. But the effect accumulates. Better heifers improve production, fertility, longevity, and milk composition over generations. The cost of semen may look small next to the consequences of using an unproven bull simply because he is cheap.

Precision feeding can raise short-term costs, particularly when a farm shifts from straw and low-quality hay to alfalfa, corn silage, or better concentrate ingredients. Yet it often produces the fastest marginal response. Cows digest a balanced ration more efficiently, yield rises, body condition stabilizes, and metabolic disorders decline. The economic test is income over feed cost per cow per day, not feed cost alone.

Sensors and automation require substantial upfront capital. They fit larger herds better because fixed costs are spread over more cows, and one manager can monitor more animals. A 20-cow family farm may gain more from a reliable scale, a thermometer, a hoof-trimming schedule, and disciplined records than from an expensive collar system. Medium farms should phase investment, starting with tools that solve a clear bottleneck such as heat detection or milk measurement.

Expected effects vary by starting condition. A poorly managed herd can show dramatic improvement quickly; a high-performing herd has less room to gain. Broad ranges are therefore useful only as planning estimates, not guarantees.

| Indicator | Expected Improvement |
|---|---|
| Milk yield per cow | 15%–30% |
| Feed conversion efficiency | 8%–15% |
| Conception rate | 10%–20% |
| Mastitis incidence | Reduced, often substantially with consistent hygiene and treatment protocols |
| Net farm profit | 20%–40% under favorable management and market conditions |

Profit rises most when several improvements overlap. Higher yield gives more milk to sell. Better fat and protein composition may raise its price. Fewer diseases reduce treatment cost and discarded milk. Better reproduction cuts days open and increases sales of calves or heifers. One improvement alone can be swallowed by another weakness.

 4. Challenges in Adoption

The technical path is clearer than the adoption path. Smallholder farms often face a bundle of constraints at once. Cash is limited, so a bag of good mineral mix or a semen straw may compete with school fees or fertilizer. Training may be brief or theoretical. Veterinarians may be far away, and artificial-insemination technicians may arrive too late. High-quality forage seed, inoculant for silage, and reliable laboratory analysis of feed or milk may be unavailable.

Markets also shape choices. Where milk is paid only by volume, farmers have little incentive to improve protein content. Where collection is irregular, investing in cooling equipment becomes risky. Where there is no premium for low somatic-cell counts, hygiene improvements may still reduce disease, but their cash benefit is harder to see.

Some practices create new problems when misused. Overfeeding concentrate can raise yield briefly while causing acidosis, laminitis, and inefficient nitrogen excretion. Unnecessary antibiotic treatment increases drug costs, withdrawal risk, and antimicrobial resistance. Manure can become an environmental hazard if stored poorly or overapplied to limited land. Conversely, well-handled manure can be a valuable fertilizer and energy source.

Support should therefore be practical rather than promotional. Farmer field days, on-farm ration demonstrations, and repeated mentoring usually work better than one-off lectures. Cooperatives can share veterinary, breeding, silage, and milk-testing services. Forage production should be linked to local seed supply and harvest equipment. Milk processors can contribute by publishing transparent payment rules and rewarding quality consistently.

 5. Conclusion

Raising dairy farm income is not achieved by a single intervention. It depends on better genetics, rations matched to cow requirements, careful reproduction, preventive health care, clean milking, and records that actually guide decisions.

Feed improvement and health control often return cash relatively quickly. Cows eat better, produce more, and suffer fewer metabolic and udder problems within months. Genetic change works more slowly, but its effects persist across generations and should not be neglected for that reason.

The best technology package is the one that fits the farm. A large commercial unit may use automated heat detection, in-line milk sensors, and formulated TMR rations. A smallholder may begin with planted forage, mineral supplementation, estrus recording, timely AI, and a simple mastitis-prevention routine. Both can improve. What usually fails is the isolated practice adopted without the supporting feed, labor, health care, or market link.

Dairy development should therefore promote locally adapted combinations, realistic targets, and dependable services. Higher yield matters, but durable income growth comes from milk produced efficiently, with acceptable quality, healthy cows, and costs the farm can sustain.

 References

1. National Research Council. *Nutrient Requirements of Dairy Cattle*. National Academies Press, 2001.  
2. Bewley, J. M., et al. “Precision Dairy Farming: Advanced Analysis for Strategic Decisions.” *Veterinary Clinics of North America: Food Animal Practice*, vol. 31, no. 2, 2015, pp. 275–288.  
3. Hare, E., et al. “Genetic Selection and Reproductive Performance in Dairy Cattle.” *Journal of Dairy Science*, vol. 89, 2006, pp. 371–379.  
4. Food and Agriculture Organization. *Dairy Development in Developing Countries*. FAO, 2020.

title: 三个火枪手
text:
The Three Musketeers: A Ballad of Steel and Brotherhood
Some stories don’t fade even when their pages yellow and crumble at the edges. They stick around like the sharp, sweet tang of old wine sipped from a chipped goblet, like the high, clear ring of a rapier striking stone that hangs in the air a beat after the blades have parted, like the warm weight of a friend’s clap on your shoulder long after the campfire has burned down to smoldering ash. *The Three Musketeers* is one of those stories. It isn’t just a dry record of 17th-century French court drama, isn’t only a swashbuckling tale of duels at dawn and last-minute escapes from locked towers. It’s a love letter to the rarest thing most people ever get to hold: friendship hammered into shape in the thick of shared danger, that doesn’t crack when betrayal rears up, that doesn’t wear thin even as decades pass.

We first meet them half-obscured by road dust on the rutted path to Paris. There’s d’Artagnan, the hot-tempered Gascon kid in a frayed, too-big coat, carrying a dented old sword his father pressed into his hands before he left home, a fire in his eyes bright enough to outshine every gilded chandelier in the Louvre. He’s every one of us at seventeen: reckless, starved for glory, dead certain the world is just waiting for someone quick with a blade and quicker with a joke to come conquer it. Then there are the three men who will become his shadow, his shield, the family he chooses for himself. Athos is the quiet, sharp-edged nobleman with lines cut deep around his mouth from grief he tries to drown in cheap tavern wine, but whose honor never dulls no matter how much he drinks. Porthos is the broad, boisterous giant whose laugh is loud enough to rattle the wooden rafters of every roadside inn he stumbles into, who is vain about his fine coats and tall tales, whose loyalty is as solid as the heavy oak beams holding up those tavern ceilings. Aramis is the soft-spoken, sharp-minded scholar forever torn between taking his priestly vows and staying in the thick of the fight, whose slender hands are just as good at scribbling love sonnets as they are at twisting an assassin’s dagger out of a target’s ribs.

These men are no saints. They brawl over stupid slights—once, d’Artagnan nearly got himself killed challenging three separate musketeers to duels in the same hour, all because he tripped over Athos’s bad leg and accidentally exposed Porthos’s fancy gold shoulder belt as a cheap fake lined with cloth. They lie to innkeepers about imaginary bandits on the road to skip out on bar tabs. They chase pretty serving girls and court ladies alike with the unapologetic, messy hunger of young men who know they might not live to see next week. They hold grudges for years, nursing them like a half-empty bottle of wine saved for a special occasion. But when trouble actually hits? When the cardinal’s guards round the corner with swords drawn, when Milady de Winter’s poisonous plots twist around innocent people who never asked to be caught in court games, when the queen’s reputation is one misstep away from ruin? All those stupid, petty fights melt away like morning mist off the Seine when the sun climbs high. “All for one, one for all” isn’t just a snappy line polished up for storybook effect. It’s a promise written in shared blood, sealed over and over with scars they all carry. It’s the midnight ride they take through rain-slicked roads to warn a friend of an ambush, splitting a single stale crust of bread between the four of them when their purses are so empty they can’t even pay for a mug of ale. It’s standing silent beside a friend even when the whole world is yelling that he’s wrong, even when the odds are so stacked against them it feels like they’ll never walk away.

Dumas built their world so vividly you can almost step into it. You can hear the clatter of horse hooves on cobblestones at first light, when messengers gallop through the streets with sealed letters tucked in their coats. You can feel the hush of the queen’s private chambers, where secrets are whispered so quiet they barely carry past the heavy tapestries strung along the walls. You can smell the acrid reek of gunpowder and sweat clinging to soldiers’ coats in the muddy siege lines outside La Rochelle, where rations ran so thin the men joked about boiling their boot leather for soup. You can see the cold glint of Milady’s dagger as she lunges from the dark of a prison cell, her eyes sharp as a cornered cat’s. The evil in this story isn’t cartoonish, either. It’s the greedy grab for power that makes men turn on their own friends, the ambition that chews up vulnerable people and spits them out without a second thought, the betrayal that comes from the person you thought loved you most. But pushing back against that dark is something warmer, brighter, real. It’s the stupid, easy banter that flies between the four men when they’re huddled around a tavern fire, teasing each other about botched duels and terrible love poems, even when they know they might be called to fight at any minute. It’s the jolt of a duel fought not for money or royal favor, but because someone insulted a friend. It’s Athos finally facing the ghost of his marriage to Milady, no longer hiding from the pain he carried for years, and his friends standing beside him without a single judgmental word. It’s Porthos turning down a wealthy marriage and a grand estate because staying with the people who had his back through every fight matters more than the silk coats and fancy dinners he’s always daydreamed about. It’s Aramis putting aside his plans to enter the priesthood for a year when his friends need him most, no hesitation. It’s d’Artagnan finally learning that the glory he chased all the way from Gascony doesn’t taste half as sweet when you’re standing on a podium alone, without the people who fought beside you to earn it.

We come back to this story over and over, and it’s not for the plot twists—though they’re as sharp and unexpected as a fencer’s feint, the kind that make you gasp out loud even when you’ve read the book half a dozen times. It’s not for the pageantry of the historical setting, either, though Dumas paints 17th-century Paris with such a warm, romantic glow you can almost feel like you’re walking those streets yourself. We come back because it reminds us of a truth we’re all too quick to brush aside in the rush of daily life: the best parts of living aren’t the fancy titles or the piles of gold you hoard, aren’t the promotions or the social media posts that make strangers envy you. They’re the people who will saddle up a horse and ride with you through rain and dark when you call, who will draw their sword before you even finish explaining that you’re in trouble, who will clap you on the back and buy you a drink when you win, and sit with you in silence when you’re too broken to celebrate. The musketeers don’t ride off into the sunset as perfect, untouchable heroes. They carry scars across their arms and faces. They carry regret for the people they couldn’t save, for the choices they had to make when there was no good option. They carry the weight of knowing Milady’s evil left marks on them, too. But they carry each other, too. That’s enough.

Long after you flip the last page closed, their voices stick with you. You can still hear Porthos’s loud, rumbling laugh when he brags about a duel he won single-handedly (even if the other three men know he needed help taking down the last guard). You can hear Aramis’s dry, quiet wit when he teases Porthos for stretching the truth, when he slips a clever line into a serious conversation that makes everyone snort wine out of their cups. You can hear Athos’s steady, calm counsel when one of the group is ready to rush into a stupid fight, the voice that pulls them all back to what matters. You can hear d’Artagnan’s bright, sharp battle cry as he leads a charge, no longer the reckless kid from Gascony but a man who knows he fights for the people beside him. They don’t teach grand, complicated lessons. They show you that courage isn’t never being scared—it’s being scared out of your wits, but stepping forward anyway. They show you that honor isn’t a pretty word for ballads and speeches—it’s keeping a promise even when no one is watching, even when breaking it would make your life a hundred times easier. They show you that real friendship isn’t the casual, surface-level kind that fades when things get hard. It’s the kind that lasts through duels and sieges and bad decisions and grief, the kind that never feels old no matter how many hundreds of years pass between the day Dumas wrote the words and the day you pick the book up for the first time.

For as long as people choose loyalty over easy profit, choose courage over the soft, safe path of looking the other way, the musketeers will keep riding. Their swords will flash in the sun. Their cry will ring down through the years, loud and clear as it was the first time they shouted it together: All for one, one for all.

title: 股票市场异常收益与规律研究
text:
An Analysis of Anomalous Returns and Market Patterns in Stock Markets  
*A Case Study of Calendar Effects and Momentum Anomalies in the U.S. Equity Market*  

Abstract  
This paper looks closely at two well-known stock market anomalies—the January Effect and price momentum—and evaluates whether they actually exist, how economically meaningful they are, and what they suggest about the Efficient Market Hypothesis (EMH). The analysis uses monthly return data for 500 randomly chosen U.S.-listed firms between 2010 and 2023, obtained from the Center for Research in Security Prices (CRSP). Descriptive statistics, pooled ordinary least squares (OLS) regression, and portfolio sorting are used to examine the patterns.  

The empirical findings point to two main conclusions. First, the January Effect is still present among small-cap stocks, and the result is statistically significant, although the economic magnitude is fairly limited. Average monthly returns in January are 1.2% higher than returns in other months for this group. Second, medium-term momentum remains strong over formation periods of 3 to 12 months, producing an annualized abnormal return of 7.8% after market risk is controlled for. The evidence suggests that the January Effect is mainly associated with tax-loss selling and window-dressing, whereas momentum profits appear to reflect investor underreaction to firm-specific news. These results challenge the semi-strong form of EMH and indicate that behavioral biases and market frictions can help explain predictable return patterns. Overall, anomalies may create opportunities for excess returns, but arbitrage costs and changing regulations make them difficult to exploit in practice.  

Keywords: Stock Market Anomalies; Abnormal Returns; January Effect; Momentum Effect; Efficient Market Hypothesis; Behavioral Finance  

1. Introduction  
The Efficient Market Hypothesis (EMH), formally set out by Fama (1970), argues that asset prices incorporate all available information. In a market that behaves this way, investors should not be able to earn persistent abnormal returns simply by trading on information already reflected in prices. Even so, empirical research over several decades has identified repeated departures from these theoretical predictions. These patterns are commonly described as “market anomalies,” and they include calendar effects, value premiums, and momentum. They have continued to draw attention from academics trying to understand price behavior and from practitioners looking for ways to outperform the market.  

This paper concentrates on two particularly representative anomalies. One is the January Effect, a calendar pattern in which small-cap stocks tend to perform unusually well in January. The other is medium-term momentum, meaning that stocks that have performed well in the recent past often keep outperforming stocks that have performed poorly. The U.S. equity market is a useful setting in which to study these effects because it is highly liquid and heavily regulated, making it easier to ask whether anomalies can persist in a mature market.  

1.1 Research Objectives  
The study addresses three main questions:  
1. Do the January Effect and the momentum anomaly exist in the U.S. stock market over the 2010–2023 period?  
2. After risk adjustment, do these anomalies produce abnormal returns that matter in both statistical and economic terms?  
3. What mechanisms help explain these patterns, and what do they suggest about market efficiency?  

1.2 Significance  
On a theoretical level, the study provides updated evidence on market anomalies in the period after the 2008 financial crisis. This period includes important structural changes such as the expansion of high-frequency trading and the growing role of passive investing. From a practical standpoint, the results may be relevant to portfolio construction and risk management for both institutional and individual investors.  

1.3 Paper Structure  
The rest of the paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 reviews the literature on EMH and major anomalies. Section 3 explains the data and methodology. Section 4 presents the empirical results. Section 5 discusses possible mechanisms and implications. Section 6 concludes by outlining the study’s limitations and directions for future research.  

2. Literature Review  
2.1 Theoretical Foundation: Efficient Market Hypothesis  
Fama (1970) distinguished among three forms of market efficiency. Weak-form efficiency means that prices reflect past trading information. Semi-strong-form efficiency means that prices reflect all publicly available information, while strong-form efficiency assumes that prices reflect both public and private information. Under EMH, abnormal returns are interpreted as compensation for greater systematic risk rather than as predictable mispricing that investors can readily exploit.  

2.2 Calendar Anomalies: The January Effect  
Wachtel (1942) was among the first to document unusually strong U.S. stock returns in January, a pattern later known as the January Effect. Keim (1983) showed that the effect is especially pronounced among small-cap stocks and linked it to tax-loss selling. According to this explanation, investors sell poorly performing stocks near the end of the year to realize capital losses. This selling pressure pushes prices down, before a rebound occurs in January.  

The window-dressing hypothesis offers a related interpretation. Haugen and Lakonishok (1988) argued that institutional investors may remove risky small stocks from their portfolios before year-end reporting dates so that their holdings appear more prudent, then buy these stocks back in January. More recent work, such as D’mello and Ferris (2020), suggests that the January Effect has weakened because of changes in the tax code and greater investor awareness, although it may still appear in micro-cap stocks.  

2.3 Momentum Anomaly  
Jegadeesh and Titman (1993) played a foundational role in momentum research. They found that buying U.S. “winner” stocks, defined as the top 10% of performers over the previous 3 to 12 months, and selling “loser,” or the bottom 10%, generated returns of roughly 1% per month between 1965 and 1989.  

Behavioral explanations generally emphasize how investors process information. One view is underreaction: if investors update their beliefs slowly in response to public news, such as earnings surprises, prices may continue to drift after the initial announcement (Hong & Stein, 1999). Another explanation focuses on overreaction. Daniel et al. (1998) suggested that overconfidence can cause investors to chase recent winners, causing price trends to continue longer than fundamentals would justify.  

Rational interpretations instead connect momentum to compensation for macroeconomic risks, including business-cycle risk. Even so, Carhart (1997) showed that momentum behaves as a distinct factor and is not adequately explained by the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM).  

2.4 Literature Gaps  
Much of the classic evidence comes from periods before 2000. This paper extends that literature by examining anomalies from 2010 to 2023, a period shaped by zero-interest-rate policies, the rapid expansion of exchange-traded funds (ETFs), and tighter market regulation, including the Dodd-Frank Act.  

3. Data and Methodology  
3.1 Data Source and Sample  
Monthly stock returns, market capitalizations, and risk factors—including the market excess return, size, and value factors—are taken from the CRSP Compustat Merged Database. The sample consists of 500 U.S.-listed common stocks, identified by CRSP share codes 10 or 11, randomly selected from the S&P 500 and Russell 2000 indices. The observation period runs from January 2010 through December 2023. Financial firms and stocks with missing return observations are excluded. Returns are adjusted for stock splits, dividends, and delisting events.  

3.2 Variable Definitions  
- Raw Return ($R_{i,t}$): the monthly total return of stock $i$ in month $t$.  
- Abnormal Return (AR): the risk-adjusted return estimated using the Fama-French Three-Factor Model (Fama & French, 1993):  

$$R_{i,t} - R_{f,t} = \alpha_i + \beta_{MKT,i}(R_{M,t}-R_{f,t}) + \beta_{SMB,i}SMB_t + \beta_{HML,i}HML_t + \varepsilon_{i,t}$$  

Here, $R_f$ is the risk-free rate, measured by the one-month U.S. Treasury yield; $R_M$ is the CRSP value-weighted market return; $SMB$ captures the size premium; and $HML$ captures the value premium. The intercept, $\alpha_i$, or Jensen’s alpha, represents the monthly abnormal return.  

- January Dummy ($Jan_t$): a variable equal to 1 when month $t$ is January and 0 otherwise.  
- Size ($Size_{i,t}$): the natural logarithm of market capitalization, expressed in millions of U.S. dollars, at month-end.  

3.3 Empirical Models  
3.3.1 Testing the January Effect  
Stocks are first divided into five size groups, or quintiles. Q1 contains the smallest 20% of firms and Q5 the largest 20%. Mean January returns are then compared with returns in other months. In addition, a pooled OLS regression is estimated with firm and year fixed effects:  

$$R_{i,t} = \alpha + \gamma_1 Jan_t + \gamma_2 Size_{i,t} + \gamma_3 Jan_t \times Size_{i,t} + Controls_{i,t} + \mu_i + \lambda_t + \varepsilon_{i,t}$$  

If $\gamma_3$ is negative and statistically significant, that would indicate that the January Effect is stronger among smaller firms.  

3.3.2 Testing Momentum  
The momentum test follows Jegadeesh and Titman (1993) and uses a six-month formation period together with a six-month holding period. The procedure is as follows:  
1. At the beginning of each month $t$, stocks are ranked according to cumulative returns from $t-7$ to $t-1$. Month $t-1$ is skipped to reduce contamination from short-term reversal.  
2. Ten equal-weighted portfolios are formed, ranging from P1, the loser portfolio made up of the bottom 10%, to P10, the winner portfolio made up of the top 10%.  
3. The return on a zero-cost momentum strategy is calculated by taking a long position in P10 and a short position in P1 over months $t$ through $t+5$.  
4. The Fama-French alpha of the momentum portfolio is estimated to determine whether the strategy remains profitable after risk adjustment.  

3.4 Statistical Inference  
Newey-West standard errors with six lags are used to address heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation. Statistical significance is assessed at the 5% level, and t-statistics are reported in parentheses.  

4. Empirical Results  
4.1 January Effect Results  
Table 1 presents average monthly returns grouped by size quintile and by whether the observation comes from January or another month. In the full sample, the mean January return is 1.68%, compared with 0.95% in non-January months. The difference is 0.73%, which is statistically significant (t = 2.41, p < 0.05).  

The more important finding is that this gap is concentrated among smaller firms. In Q1, January returns average 2.31%, versus 1.12% in the rest of the year, producing a difference of 1.19% (t = 3.02, p < 0.01). By contrast, the gap in Q5 is only 0.21%, and it is not statistically significant (t = 0.87).

title: 老人智能手机使用
text:
Practical Step-by-Step Guide to Smartphone Use for Seniors
*Designed for clarity, simplicity, and daily real-world use — no confusing jargon included*

---

 Pre-Use Setup (Complete this first, with help from a family member if needed)
Goal: Set up your phone to match your vision, hearing, and ease-of-use needs before you start using it daily.
1.  Turn on senior-friendly accessibility settings first
    - Open *Settings* and find the *Display* menu. Crank text size up to the largest setting you can read without squinting, toggle Bold Text on so letters don’t look thin and faint against the screen, and set brightness to Auto. That last setting means you won’t have to fumble with sliders when you step outside into bright sun or sit down to read texts in a dim living room in the evening.
    - Head back to the main Settings page and open *Accessibility*. Flip on High Contrast Mode to make text and buttons pop against backgrounds instead of blending in, adjust Touch & Hold Delay to “Long” so you don’t open random apps when your finger just rests on the screen for a second, and turn on Flash Notifications if you often miss ringers when you’re cooking or the vacuum is running.
    - Open the *Sound & Vibration* menu next. Turn ringtone and media volume up to a level you can hear clearly from across the room, and toggle on *Vibrate on Ring* so you feel calls when your phone is in your pocket or purse.
2.  Lock in core safety features first
    - Save 2 or 3 people you trust most — maybe your oldest daughter, the next-door neighbor who drops off tomatoes in summer, or the caregiver who stops by three days a week — as “Favorites” in your Contacts app. Turn on Emergency SOS too. On almost every phone sold now, pressing the power button 5 times fast will automatically call those saved contacts and send them your exact location, no extra taps needed. It works even if your screen is locked.
    - Pick an unlock method that won’t make you fumble. A 4-digit PIN works better for most people than tricky swipe patterns or facial recognition that fails if you’re wearing a hat or your reading glasses slip down your nose. Pick numbers you won’t forget — maybe the last four digits of your first phone number, or the month and day your first grandchild was born — just don’t use 1234.
    - Ask the family member helping you to turn on Find My Device for Android phones or Find My for iPhones. This is a lifesaver if you leave your phone under a pile of laundry at home, or set it down on a grocery store shelf while you’re picking out cereal. You can even make it ring at full volume even if it’s set to silent, so you don’t have to tear the house apart looking for it.
3.  Tidy up your home screen so it doesn’t feel overwhelming
    - Delete all the pre-installed apps you know you’ll never open — random game trials, shopping apps you don’t care about, productivity tools meant for office workers. If you aren’t sure what an app does, ask before you delete it, just in case it controls something important. Only keep the apps you’ll actually use every day on the main home screen: Phone, Messages, Camera, Photos, the chat app your family uses (usually WeChat or WhatsApp), Weather, and Alarm.
    - Turn on Easy Mode or Simple Mode. Most Android phones have this as a quick toggle right in the Display menu, and iPhones have an identical setting tucked in Accessibility. It blows app icons up to twice their normal size, strips out all the tiny cluttered menu options, and hides the apps you don’t use regularly so you don’t tap the wrong thing by accident.
4.  Connect only to Wi-Fi networks you trust
    - Save your home Wi-Fi password to the phone so it connects automatically as soon as you walk in the door. Ask family to help you add the network at places you visit all the time too — your son’s house across town, the senior center where you play bridge every Wednesday, the little coffee shop on the corner where you get donuts on Saturdays. Turn off the “Auto-connect to public Wi-Fi” toggle, though. Random open networks at the mall or doctor’s office aren’t always secure, and you don’t want your phone connecting to them without you knowing.

---

 Step 1: Master the 5 Most Basic Daily Functions
These are the actions you will use every day — practice them until they feel easy.
1.  Make and answer calls
    - To call someone: Tap the bright green *Phone* icon sitting on your home screen. You can tap the name of anyone saved in your Favorites list to dial them instantly, or tap the keypad button to punch in a phone number if you’re calling a new doctor’s office or the local pizza shop. Hit the green call button when you’re ready.
    - To answer a call: When your phone rings, slide the green phone icon all the way to the right to pick up. Slide the red icon to the left to send the call to voicemail, or if it’s a telemarketer calling at dinnertime.
    - Quick tip: If you’re struggling to hear the person on the other end, tap the speaker icon mid-call to turn on Speakerphone. It amplifies the sound enough that you won’t have to press the phone tight to your ear.
2.  Send and receive text or voice messages
    - Open your go-to messaging app, whether that’s the default Messages app, WeChat, or WhatsApp. Tap the name of the person you want to talk to to pull up your chat thread with them.
    - Most people I know who are new to smartphones prefer voice messages to typing. To send one, press and hold the tiny microphone icon right next to the text box, speak clearly at a normal volume, and let go of the icon when you’re done talking to send it. If you mess up mid-sentence? Just slide your finger up the screen before you let go, and the message will cancel so you can start over.
    - If you do want to type a text, tap the empty text box to pull up the keyboard, type out your message, and hit send. You can also turn on Handwriting Mode in your keyboard settings if you’d rather draw characters or letters with your finger than peck at tiny keys — a lot of people find that far less frustrating.
3.  Check the time and set alarms
    - The current time always sits in the top corner of your home screen, so you don’t have to open anything to glance at it. To set alarms, open the *Clock* app. Tap the little + icon, scroll to pick the time you want the alarm to go off — 7 a.m. for your daily walk around the park, noon to remind you to take your blood pressure medication, 4 p.m. so you remember to take the cookies out of the oven when the grandkids are visiting. Tap “Repeat” if you want the alarm to go off the same time every day, then hit save.
4.  Check the weather
    - Tap the *Weather* app on your home screen to see the day’s high and low temperature, chance of rain, and air quality reading. I always add the cities where my out-of-state kids live to my weather app too, so I can text my granddaughter to bring a jacket if it’s going to snow where she goes to college. It takes two taps to add a new location.
5.  Charge your phone safely
    - Plug your phone in when the battery icon in the top right corner turns red, which means it’s dropped below 20% charge. You don’t have to wait for it to die completely to charge it, but try not to leave it plugged in all night every night — that wears the battery out faster over time, so it won’t hold a charge as long a year or two from now. Stick to the charger that came in the box with your phone, too. The cheap $3 chargers sold at gas stations don’t have the same safety features, and they can damage your battery or even overheat.

---

 Step 2: Learn Fun, High-Value Features for Staying Connected
These features help you stay close to family and enjoy daily life, once you are comfortable with the basics.
1.  Take and share photos and videos
    - Tap the *Camera* app to open it. Point the lens at whatever you want to capture — your grandson covered in cake at his birthday party, the first peony blooming in your backyard, the spread of food at your monthly potluck — and tap the big white circle on the screen to snap a photo. Tap the “Video” option at the bottom of the screen if you want to record a clip, like your granddaughter’s first soccer goal.
    - To look at the photos you’ve taken, open the *Photos* app. Every picture and video you shoot gets stored here, sorted automatically by date, so you can scroll back to find photos from last month’s family vacation without sorting through folders.
    - If you want to send a photo to someone, open the picture first, then tap the little share icon — it looks like a square with an arrow pointing up on iPhones, or three dots connected by lines on most Androids. Pick the messaging app you use, select the contact you want to send it to, and tap send. It takes three taps total once you get the hang of it.
2.  Make video calls
    - Open WeChat, WhatsApp, or FaceTime, select the contact you want to reach, and tap the little icon that looks like a video camera to start a video call. Wait for them to answer, and you’ll be able to see and hear each other for free, even if they live across the country. My own mom uses this to watch my kids open Christmas presents every year, since we can’t always make it home for the holidays.
    - Quick heads up: Try to make video calls when you’re connected to Wi-Fi if you can. If you use mobile data for long calls, you might hit your monthly data limit and get charged extra, depending on your phone plan.
3.  Use the handy daily tools built right into your phone
    - Flashlight: Swipe down from the top of your screen to pull up the quick settings menu, then tap the flashlight icon to turn it on when you’re looking for a lost earring under the couch, or walking up the driveway after a late evening event. Tap it again to turn it off — I once left mine on in my purse for three hours and drained half my battery by accident, so that’s a good habit to build.
    - Magnifier: Turn the Magnifier tool on in your Accessibility settings. It turns your phone camera into a super-powered magnifying glass, so you can read the tiny print on prescription bottles, the ingredient list on food labels, or the fine print on a restaurant menu without digging out your reading glasses. It’s the feature I get the most thank-you notes for when I help seniors set up their phones.

---

 Step 3: Stay Safe From Scams (Critical for All Seniors)
Scammers often target older adults — follow these rules to keep your money and personal information safe:
1.  Never share private information over calls, texts, or random links
    - No real person from your bank, the police department, Social Security office, or a company’s customer service line will ever ask you for your bank card PIN, the 6-digit verification code that gets texted to your phone, or your full ID number over a call or text. If someone calls and demands those details? Hang up right away. It’s a scam, every single time. If you’re worried there might actually be a problem with your bank account, look up the bank’s official phone number yourself and call them back directly.
2.  Don’t tap random links or download apps from places you don’t trust
    - If you get a text out of the blue saying you won a free cruise, your package is delayed and you need to click to reschedule, or someone posted old photos of you from high school, don’t tap the link. Those links almost always install bad software on your phone that can steal your passwords or personal information. If you can’t tell if a message is real, call your kid or grandkid to look at it before you tap anything. It’s never a bother to ask.
    - Only download apps from the official app store for your phone — that’s the Google Play Store for Androids, the App Store for iPhones. Never tap those pop-up ads that blare “Your phone has 17 viruses! Tap here to clean it now!” Those are 100% fake, and the app they want you to download is the actual problem.
3.  Turn on automatic scam call blocking
    - Ask a family member to help you turn on your phone’s built-in scam call filter. It automatically blocks most robocalls and known scam numbers before your phone even rings, so you don’t have to waste time listening to fake pitches for extended car warranties or free medical devices.
4.  Lock down your mobile payment settings if you use them
    - If you use Alipay, WeChat Pay, or Apple Pay to pay for groceries or coffee, set a separate PIN just for payments, and turn off the “small amount no-password payment” setting. That way, no one can charge money to your account if you accidentally leave your phone somewhere, or if a stranger gets ahold of it for a minute. Never let a random stranger tap buttons on your phone when you’re in the middle of making a payment, either.

---

 Step 4: Troubleshoot Common Small Problems
You do not need to ask for help for every small issue — try these quick fixes first:
1.  If your screen freezes up, or an app won’t open no matter how many times you tap it: Close the app fully by swiping up from the bottom of the screen and holding for a second to see all your open apps, then swipe the problematic app up and off the screen to close it. If that doesn’t do the trick, turn your phone off completely, wait 30 slow seconds, then turn it back on. I’ve been using smartphones for 15 years, and this trick fixes 90% of random glitches. No tech support call required.
2.  If your Wi-Fi or mobile data won’t load anything: Swipe down to open quick settings, toggle Wi-Fi or mobile data off, count to 10, then toggle it back on. If it still won’t connect, check if your home Wi-Fi router got unplugged by the vacuum cleaner, or if you’ve used up all your monthly data allowance by watching too many short videos.
3.  If you accidentally delete an app, or can’t find an icon on your home screen: Open your phone’s app store, type the app name into the search bar, and tap “Install” or “Open” to get it back. You cannot permanently “break” your phone by tapping the wrong button, no matter how scary the pop-up messages might look. If you tap something by accident, just back out of the screen and take a breath. It’s almost always an easy fix.
4.  If you can’t hear the person on the other end of a call: First check if you accidentally muted yourself — look for a little microphone icon with a line through it on the call screen, and tap it to unmute. If that’s not the problem, use the volume buttons on the side of the phone to turn the call volume up. It’s easy to bump those buttons with your cheek mid-call without noticing.

---

 Quick Pro Tip for Long-Term Use
Keep a small notebook next to where you usually charge your phone, like on the kitchen counter or your bedside table. Jot down quick notes as you learn things — the steps to send a photo to your granddaughter, what the scam pop-ups look like, the PIN you picked for your lock screen. You won’t remember every step the first time you do it, and having a little cheat sheet written in your own handwriting means you won’t have to wait for help to do the things you want to do. It’s okay to go at your own pace. No one expects you to learn every single feature in a day.

title: 生猪高产栽培技术要点
text:
Pig Production: Small Details That Decide the Litter

Pig farming is not simply about putting sows in a pen and giving them feed twice a day. When people talk about “high-yield cultivation,” they often mean one thing on paper and another thing in the sty. A sow can have many piglets born, but if only a few survive, the number means nothing. On a real farm, high yield has to be counted by strong, weaned piglets, not just by a thick birth record.

The first point is gilt selection. Many farms are in a hurry to put young sows into breeding, and that hurry costs them later. A gilt should not be bred just because she has reached a certain age. Her body condition matters more. She needs strong legs, a sound underline, at least six pairs of well-spaced teats, and a calm but active temperament. The vulva should be normal, not tiny or tipped upward. Small points like these sound basic, but they show up in farrowing problems, poor milking ability, and early culling.

Most gilts are ready around the second or third estrus, usually at about 220–240 days, with body weight around 130–140 kg. Exact numbers depend on breed and feeding program. Breeding at first heat often gives smaller litters and weaker body recovery. Flushing can help before mating: increasing feed slightly for about ten to fourteen days, or giving a higher-energy ration, can improve ovulation. It should not turn the gilt into a fat animal. Overfat gilts are harder to settle, have more farrowing trouble, and tend to lose appetite after they give birth.

Heat detection needs patience. A sow in standing heat will lock up when pressure is put on her back, especially when a boar is nearby. The vulva may be red and swollen, and mucus may be present, but the standing response is more reliable than appearance alone. For best results, check twice a day, in the morning and late afternoon. Boar contact should be direct but controlled, not constant. If the boar stays in front of the sow all day, the response becomes dull and the stockman misses the best window.

Timing of insemination still follows an old practical pattern. Gilts are often bred when standing heat is first found, then again twelve to twenty-four hours later. Sows are commonly bred on the second day after standing heat begins, with a second service twelve to twenty-four hours later if they remain still. These are not magical hours; they are working rules. The person watching the animals should adjust them based on observed heat length. One careless insemination, done in a dirty crate or with poor semen handling, can waste an entire cycle.

Semen must be kept at the correct temperature, usually around 15–18°C, and it should not be left on a cold counter or exposed to direct sunlight. Before use, check concentration, motility, and abnormal sperm if equipment is available. During insemination, the catheter should be introduced slowly after cleaning the vulva. The semen bottle should be allowed to empty by itself rather than forced through in a minute. If the sow stands quietly and the cervix locks the catheter, that is a good sign. Rough handling causes infection, return to estrus, and poor conception.

Pregnant sow feeding is often misunderstood. A sow does not need heavy feeding throughout gestation. In early pregnancy, particularly the first month, high feed intake can raise body heat and affect embryo survival. Most farms keep sows on a maintenance-level ration after breeding, commonly 1.8–2.2 kg per day for mature sows in reasonable condition. Gilts and thin sows may need more. Later, from about day 85 or 90, feed can be increased gradually to support fetal growth and mammary development.

Body condition scoring is one of the most useful habits on a farm. A sow at weaning should not look like a walking skeleton, and a sow at farrowing should not carry a thick layer of fat over her back. Hands-on scoring from 1 to 5, with 3 as the target for much of gestation, is more practical than relying on weight alone. Farmers should look at the spine, ribs, hip bones, and tail head. Thin sows produce weak piglets and come back into heat slowly. Fat sows may have difficulty farrowing, eat poorly in lactation, and crush more piglets.

Housing during pregnancy also affects yield. Sows need stable footing, clean water, and protection from extreme heat. Heat stress in early pregnancy can cause embryo loss; in late pregnancy it can reduce birth weight and sow feed intake. In hot weather, water drips, fans, shade, and feeding during cooler hours make a visible difference. Fighting should be avoided, especially after mixing. If group housing is used, sows should be mixed carefully, in adequate space, and preferably shortly after breeding according to the farm’s management plan. Constant bullying causes abortions, lameness, and uneven condition.

About one week before farrowing, the sow should be washed and moved into a cleaned farrowing crate. The pen should be disinfected and allowed to dry. Moving her too late increases stress and the risk of piglets being born in a dirty passage. On the other hand, putting her in the crate weeks early wastes space and may reduce exercise. Before farrowing, reduce feed gradually rather than suddenly taking it away. Fresh water must always be available, because constipation around farrowing leads to fever, reduced milk, and restless behavior.

Signs of farrowing are easy to recognize once a person has seen them. The udder swells, the teats release milk when pressed, the vulva loosens, and the sow begins nesting behavior. Most sows farrow about 114 days after breeding, but a day earlier or later is normal. During birth, the room should be quiet. Piglets usually arrive every fifteen to thirty minutes. If the sow strains hard for more than thirty minutes without producing a piglet, or if she goes off labor and still seems to have piglets inside, help is needed. A clean arm, a lubricated obstetric sleeve, and gentle examination are better than waiting until the piglets are dead.

Newborn care decides a large part of the profit. Piglets are born wet, with little energy reserve. In cold weather, they can become chilled within minutes. Drying them at birth, clearing mucus from the nose and mouth, and putting them under a warm lamp saves more pigs than expensive supplements given later. Navel disinfection with iodine or another suitable antiseptic reduces infection. Colostrum must be taken within the first hours. Weak piglets should be held onto a front teat or given collected colostrum by syringe or bottle.

Cross-fostering is useful, but it must be done with a plan. Piglets need their own mother’s colostrum first. After that, large litters can be evened out by moving strong piglets to a sow with fewer piglets or better teat availability. Moving the weakest piglets onto another sow usually fails because they cannot compete. A practical method is to batch piglets by size and make sure each one has a functional teat. Extra piglets may be raised by nurse sows on farms with good management. Raising thirteen weak piglets on a sow with eleven sound teats produces a crate full of runts.

Castration, tail docking, iron injection, and other processing should be done cleanly and at the age recommended by local veterinary practice. Iron is important because sow milk alone does not provide enough for fast-growing piglets, especially on concrete floors. Instruments should be disinfected between litters. A dirty blade or needle spreads infection from one litter to the next faster than most people notice.

Lactation feeding is where many farms lose their next litter before they realize it. A nursing sow should eat as much as she can without wasting feed. If feed intake is low, she milks off her own body and becomes thin. Then she weans late in estrus, breeds back poorly, and gives a smaller next litter. Feed should be increased gradually after farrowing and supplied according to litter size and sow appetite. Fresh feed several times a day often works better than one large sour meal. Water flow must be checked; a sow with poor water flow simply cannot eat enough.

Creep feed can be offered to piglets after the first week, but it should stay fresh. A pan of stale creep feed teaches piglets to avoid feed rather than eat it. Small amounts, replaced daily, are enough. Weaning weight depends mainly on milk intake, health, and room temperature, with creep feed helping the transition. At weaning, piglets need a warm, dry resting area and easy access to water. A cold, drafty weaning room creates diarrhea, uneven pigs, and medication costs that erase the gain from extra pigs born.

Disease control cannot be treated as an afterthought. Farm biosecurity means a concrete plan, not a sign on the gate. Vehicles, delivery people, tools, boots, and dead-pig disposal can all carry pathogens into the herd. Load-out areas should be separated from pig buildings. Workers should change boots and clothing, and visitors should follow the same rules. A shower-in system is useful on large farms, but even small farms can use dedicated clothing, footbaths kept at proper concentration, and clear boundaries between clean and dirty areas.

Vaccination should be planned with a veterinarian for the diseases present in that region, such as classical swine fever, pseudorabies, porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome, foot-and-mouth disease, and parvovirus where relevant. Blanket copying of another farm’s program can miss local pressure. Sows need proper immunity before breeding and during gestation, but timing matters because some vaccines are not suitable at certain stages. Records of sow number, vaccination date, product, batch, and dosage should be kept.

Daily observation is the cheapest technology on a pig farm. A stockman should notice which sow is off feed before she goes down, which gilt is swollen before she is mounted, and which piglet pile is too cold before scours spread. Coughing, sneezing, rough hair, watery eyes, swollen joints, diarrhea, and lameness all mean something. Rectal thermometers are simple tools, but they only help if someone uses them. Treating every sick pig with the same antibiotic is neither scientific nor economical.

Record keeping turns observation into management. Each sow should have a card or electronic record showing breeding date, boar or semen batch, expected farrowing date, number born alive, stillbirths, mummies, weaning number, weaning weight, treatment, and culling reason. A sow that repeatedly returns to estrus, farrows small litters, or raises few piglets should be culled. Keeping her because she has been on the farm for years ties up crate space and lowers the whole herd average. Replacement gilts should enter on a planned schedule rather than through panic buying.

Boar management should not be forgotten on farms using natural service. A boar needs proper nutrition, exercise, hoof care, and regular use without overwork. Young boars should not be paired with heavy, aggressive sows without supervision. Sperm production takes time; a boar used several times in one day may settle poorly for weeks. Even when artificial insemination is the main method, a mature boar is still valuable for heat detection.

People often look for a single trick to raise output, but pig production does not work that way. The farm that gets eleven or twelve strong piglets weaned from a suitable number of functional teats usually does many ordinary things correctly. It breeds at the right heat, feeds the sow according to condition, keeps her cool and calm, assists farrowing when necessary, dries and colostrums the piglets, and follows health rules every week. None of these steps looks impressive by itself. The result is what looks impressive.
